About 92% said they had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, while 97% said the same about District Attorney Kim Sabol.The vote is the latest fallout from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A.Some show a modified bug zapper being used to shock three apprentice firefighters while on duty in 2024. Other videos show water being dumped on two firefighters and a dead raccoon placed inside a fire vehicle.A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation, though they disputed the characterization of hazing and said the incidents were "consensual" pranks that were done "all in good fun." “It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," said Hutchinson. “We’re all still friends," added Boudrias. Boudrias, Hutchinson, and Baldwin's firings sparked outcry from firefighters, former firefighters and community members, many of whom felt the punishment was too harsh. In Wednesday's Fire Board meeting, those community members packed the Fire Administration building, many of whom held signs or wore shirts in support of the three firefighters. "Not only have they lost their jobs, but they also lost their reputations," said one public commentator. "We need to restore faith in this fire district," said another. "I think it speaks loud and clear, exactly like the confidence vote that was reported to us. There was a large desire to have a change in leadership, and we delivered that today," said St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board member James Clasby. Lee had signaled days earlier that his tenure could be coming to an end. 15 letter to the board, Lee wrote that it may be time to consider a “mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition," adding "the position of fire chief requires confidence." During the meeting's discussion, fire board member and business owner Travis Leonard said that gave him reason to begin the motion to Fire Lee. "Coming from the private sector, anytime an employee gives their notice, I terminate them; I found they've checked out," said Leonard. After terminating Lee’s contract, the board appointed Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim fire chief. The district also plans to hire a recruiter to conduct a search for Lee’s permanent replacement."I am excited to move this district forward, to begin the healing process of the issues that we’ve been dealing with, as of recent, and to instill trust,” Langel said.Lee's departure comes with a high cost to the district. His severance package is expected to total about $350,000.The leadership change also comes as the firefighters union continues negotiations with the district in an effort to reinstate three veteran firefighters who were fired. Union Representative Ryan Sapp said he believed Lee's termination is a "positive step forward.""I think moving forward, the ultimate goal here is to just move forward and get things back to a level field and continue providing the services to our community," Sapp told investigative reporter Kate Hussey. "The biggest thing today is we worked together and came together as a local — glad to see my membership stepped up and let their voices be heard." The Fire Board is also searching for a replacement district attorney, who submitted her notice of retirement amid the ongoing controversy.

entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. William Reaves Execution Jack Wu's Reporter Notebook Before the execution 5:45 p.m. Notes say 29 people in the room, including 16 spectators: 8 men and 8 women. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Kevin Delisle are listed. The room is white, with no windows. A large viewing window takes up most of one wall. The room is quiet, with muffled talking heard on the other side of the glass. The door to the execution chamber is the same color as the wall, with covered glass and a tan border. Reaves is lying face-up, with his feet toward the witnesses. Three men in suits are in the room; one is on the phone. A spectator in the second row puts his hand on his wife’s shoulder. The man on the phone hangs up. Asked for any final words, Reaves says, No, I do not. Notes describe heavy breathing, his mouth opening and multiple IVs in his left arm. He is bound by brown leather straps. A man in a white shirt says "Reaves, Reaves" while shaking his shoulder. A man in the room is taking notes. (The note doesn’t specify further.) 6:11 p.m. A doctor walks in, puts a hand on Reaves’ face and shines a flashlight in his eyes. The doctor checks Reaves’ heart with a stethoscope. Notes say his face is blocked from view for 10 to 20 seconds. The doctor leaves; the man with the phone makes a call. Reaves is pronounced dead, and the curtain drops. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother is expected to be among the witnesses. Flowers said the brother told him Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. See also: 124 cats, some deceased, surrendered in disturbing Port St. Lucie hoarding case Reaves’ attorneys fought the execution to the end. In court filings, they argued he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Department of Corrections is expected to hold a briefing after the execution. CBS12 News is at Florida State Prison and will update this story.

entry.title: 2 vehicles sought in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run investigation, police say
entry.summary: The Port St. Lucie Police Department has released new information in its investigation of a hit-and-run crash that left a 63-year-old man seriously injured earlier this month on Oct. 9. Detectives now believe the victim may have been hit by two separate vehicles near the intersection of Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard. According to police, one vehicle was traveling northbound while the other was traveling southbound at the time of the incident. The crash occurred at approximately 12:56 a.m and the victim, a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, was found unconscious in the roadway suffering from severe head injuries. In a previous update, police said surveillance video from a nearby business captured the incident and showed what investigators believed to be a white four-door sedan striking the man before leaving the scene without stopping. As detectives continued reviewing evidence and surveillance footage, investigators developed information indicating a second vehicle may also have been involved in the crash. Police are now working to identify both vehicles and their drivers. Investigators have released images of the vehicles and are asking for the public's help. Anyone who recognizes either vehicle, was in the area around the time of the crash, witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or surveillance video from the area is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

entry.title: WHERE'S WALTER? Having a day of discovery at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast
entry.summary: This week, I visited a place where learning and fun go hand in hand: the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast. From the moment I walked in, I could tell this wasn't your typical museum. Instead of looking at exhibits from behind a rope or glass case, kids are encouraged to jump in, get involved and learn by doing. As I explored the museum, I discovered exhibits designed to teach important life skills in creative and engaging ways. From learning about money and budgeting to exploring different careers and practicing job skills, every corner of the museum offered a new opportunity to learn something useful. WATCH: WHERE'S WALTER? Discovering the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast One of my favorite stops, of course, involved the weather. As a meteorologist, I was excited to check out the museum's WPTV weather simulator and hurricane simulator. It was fascinating to see how children can experience weather concepts in a hands-on environment and gain a better understanding of the science behind storms and hurricanes. What impressed me most was how interactive everything was. Kids aren't just reading signs or watching demonstrations. They're solving problems, making decisions, using their imaginations and building confidence along the way. The museum creates an environment where learning feels more like an adventure than a lesson. Whether they're exploring future careers, practicing financial skills or learning about science and weather, children are gaining valuable experiences that can help them throughout their lives. My visit was a great reminder that some of the best learning happens when you're having fun. By rolling up their sleeves, asking questions and trying new things, kids can discover skills and interests they never knew they had. If you're looking for a family-friendly destination on the Treasure Coast that combines education, creativity and fun, the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast is definitely worth a visit. That's where I was!

entry.title: Republicans split over condemning controversial Ramaswamy ad targeting Amy Acton
entry.summary: A campaign ad in Ohios governors race is drawing criticism from Democrats and some Republicans and raising questions about how far negative campaigning should go. The ad, paid for by Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamys campaign, features Democratic nominee Amy Actons birth mother calling her daughter a liar. RELATED STORY | Democrat Amy Actons estranged mother calls her liar in ad, court documents say otherwise The ad has drawn particular attention because Actons mother lost custody of her when Acton was a child amid sexual abuse allegations involving the man her mother was with at the time. Republican Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina sharply criticized the ad, calling it the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said the ad needs to come down, but he would not be rescinding his endorsement of Ramaswamy. Acton worked for DeWine as the state's health director during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance were also asked about the controversy but did not condemn the ad. I know nothing about it, Trump said. But I hear the mother went very rogue on the daughter, doesn't have a lot of respect for the daughter. Trump later added, It's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much. But I don't think that has anything to do with Vivek. RELATED STORY | Barack Obama to campaign with Ohio Democrats as he expands his outreach ahead of Election Day Vance defended Ramaswamys decision to air the commercial. Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar, Vance said. Acton herself condemned the ad, telling CNN that it has 'crossed everyone's boundaries.' The controversy has extended beyond Ohio, prompting a broader debate about negative political advertising. There was no indication that Ramaswamys campaign planned to pull the ad. Republican Sen. John Husted of Ohio also criticized the decision, telling The Associated Press he would not have aired the commercial.

entry.title: Teachers in Palm Beach County worry voter confusion over a ballot referendum could lead to sizeable pay cut
entry.summary: In less than two weeks, voters in several school districts in Florida will decide whether to renew a local $1 million property tax referendum that is directly tied to teacher pay. For band teachers like Amrutha Murthy, the suspense and concern are building. 'We love our students and we want to be able to provide for them, but we don't want it to come at our cost of living, says Murthy. The Park Vista High School instructor is one of nearly 900 teachers in the Palm Beach County School District who could face an average pay cut of $8,000 a year if voters choose not to renew the referendum that first passed in 2018. WATCH: Teachers in the Palm Beach County School District are relying on voters to keep jobs and pay Teachers in the Palm Beach County School district are relying on voters to keep jobs and pay Some educators say they're worried the property tax renewal supplement will be confused with the highly controversial Amendment Three Property Tax measure. The 'referendum to continue ad valorem levy for school safety, teachers and operational needs' is different. It helps to pay the salaries of music, art and physical education teachers as well as teachers of specialty programs like culinary and aviation. In addition, the Palm Beach County School District says the money is also used to help fund additional security measures and personnel and provide a behavioral health professional at every school. 'It's been a huge boost for teachers in Palm Beach County because it literally creates a more livable situation,' says Gordan Longhofer, president of the Classroom Teachers Association. By next school year, the Palm Beach County School District says some of these teaching positions could be eliminated if the referendum fails. Veteran educators like Marie Chrisphonce could lose the maximum $10,00 annual amount because of their years of experience. She is hoping to keep her job and pay intact. 'It's scary because that's a lot of pay. It's paying the bills. It's very scary,' says Chrisphonce. While Chrisphonce already has a second job, Murthy says with her busy band schedule, there's just no time. Teachers say they can only hope for a forte of support when voters head to the polls next month.

entry.article_text: Martin County’s Airport Noise Advisory Committee is scheduled to meet at 9 a.m. Thursday at Witham Field’s Airport Administration Building to review nighttime flight activity and noise concerns. The committee advises the county on airport noise and possible mitigation measures. The airport recorded 7,474 takeoffs and landings in September, including 1,224 jet operations. Of those, 258 took place during the voluntary curfew, which runs from 11 p.m. The airport reported a 96.55% compliance rate. The county also sent 20 letters to aircraft operators about nighttime activity; the report does not specify how many flights, if any, were considered violations. Residents say private jet traffic can increase when flight restrictions are imposed in Palm Beach County during President Donald Trump’s visits to Mar-a-Lago, affecting their quality of life. The committee is also scheduled to receive an update on the Residential Sound Insulation Program, which aims to reduce aircraft noise inside eligible homes near the airport. The agenda does not list a proposal to change the voluntary curfew or a vote on airport rules. If you would like to review the agenda for the meeting, CLICK HERE. This is a developing story.

entry.title: High surf and red flag warnings put St. Lucie County beaches under high hazard advisory this week
entry.summary: A red flag warning was cautioning swimmers about dangerous surf at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park, where waves between four and six feet we're crashing along the shoreline Wednesday. Fort Pierce Inlet State Park was among several beaches in St. Lucie County under a red flag high hazard warning. The conditions are tied to a low pressure system off the eastern U.S. coast in the mid-Atlantic. 'The sea was angry today my friends,' Fort Pierce resident Lee Bertucelli said. St. Lucie County Ocean Rescue says conditions like these make it more important than ever to swim at a lifeguarded beach. There are two in St. Lucie County, at Pepper Park and Waveland Beach. Officials say both will likely be flying red or double red flags for the next few days. 'It was very windy and very choppy and it's really challenging because you have to negotiate all of the chop,' foil surfer Lisa Rose said. 'I went in, not with my surfboard, but like, to my waist and it's just, it's rough and it's just not super safe for like I'm sort of a beginner so not safe for me, but like, some of the other surfers have definitely been out,' surfer Jodi Riley said. 'I went in, you know, not too far. The waves were fun, but again not too far, didn't want to deal with rip tides or anything else,' Bertucelli said. The county says rip currents are possible in these conditions. If you find yourself stuck in one, Ocean Rescue says don't panic and swim parallel with the shoreline. entry.title: 'This is a mistake': Swimmers react to possible elimination of IRSC swimming and diving
entry.summary: It is as dominant a college sports program as there is anywhere in the country, and it's located on the Treasure Coast. WPTV received several emails from concerned residents that the plug may soon be pulled on this diving dynasty. We're learning the Board of Trustees at Indian River State College are looking to possibly eliminate the men's and women's swimming and diving teams. WATCH BELOW: IRSC swimmers react to possible elimination of program Swimmers rally to save IRSC swim and dive teams This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. WPTV listened to sophomore swimmer Kalla Hall, who came to the college from Australia, joining the decorated and prestigious swimming and diving team under head coach Sion Brinn. The team has produced multiple Olympians, including Brinn. Hall was first nationally at the 100-meter freestyle last year. 'I knew I'd wanted to be an Olympian,' Hall said. entry.summary: St. Lucie County fire chief terminated after months of controversy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 to terminate fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause after months of controversy, hazing allegations, and a no-confidence vote. Interim Chief Paul Langel said, "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job. Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process." The decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced for allegedly turning a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and using it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three firefighters ultimately lost their jobs. One of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, said, "I think it was a step in the right direction. I don’t think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department." The disciplined firefighters have called the termination retaliation for previous complaints they filed against district leadership. When asked about the possibility of the terminated firefighters regaining their jobs, Langel said, "I believe that there’s always scenarios that would unfold and happen. I’ve got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics." The board voted to appoint Langel as interim chief. He is a familiar face in the district, with 30 years of experience. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early. entry.title: Treasure Coast group marks 50 years of friendship, service to community
entry.summary: The Treasure Coast (FL) Chapter of The Links, Incorporated is celebrating 50 years of friendship and service in 2026, marking five decades of volunteerism, education, advocacy and philanthropy across the region. Chartered October 30, 1976, by 22 women, the chapter serves Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties. Its approved chapter background reports more than 125,000 volunteer service hours over its history. The chapter works with schools, health providers, civic organizations and nonprofits to address local needs. The chapter organizes its work through five national program facets: Services to Youth, The Arts, National Trends and Services, International Trends and Services, and Health and Human Services. A signature health initiative Launched in 2011, Linking Together Against Syndrome X addresses metabolic syndrome and risk factors associated with diabetes, heart disease and stroke. Activities have included free community health symposiums, Womens Red Dress heart-health education, screenings, nutrition and oral-health education, healthy-lifestyle coaching, and Walk for Healthy Living. The chapters approved background reports more than 1,450 people served through its health symposium over more than 13 years. Florida Community Health Centers, Inc. is a documented partner. According to the chapters 2023-2024 program report, it provided blood glucose and blood pressure screenings, waist-circumference assessments, and COVID-19 testing and education. Other community partners have contributed venues, clinicians, outreach and health education. The 2023-2024 report describes more than 3,000 people educated through the wider Syndrome X initiative over its history and reports broader educational outreach of more than 50,000 people, including public-health campaigns in collaboration with Florida Community Health Centers, Inc. In that report, 90% of surveyed respondents rated educational delivery excellent. Supporting youth and students The chapter supports student learning and career exploration through scientist-led STEAM education and interactive STEAM Day exhibits at the Indian River State College Planetarium. Its scholarship program supports graduating seniors in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties, considering academic achievement, financial need and leadership. Typical annual awards are approximately $1,000 per recipient per county, and the chapter has also supported renewable four-year scholarships for students attending historically Black college

entry.title: Trump’s trade fight with Canada hits home along Maine border
entry.summary: Along Maines northern border, ties between the United States and Canada have long extended beyond trade. Families live on both sides, and businesses depend on customers crossing the border. A golf course, the Aroostook Valley Country Club, even straddles the international boundary. But Northern Mainers say President Donald Trumps trade fight with Canada is straining those cross-border relationships and raising economic concerns in communities like Fort Fairfield, located about two miles from the international boundary. Retiree John Foster, who lives in Fort Fairfield, told Scripps News Group that his towns location puts it in a particularly difficult position. The economics certainly is a big deal for us, he said Wednesday. Most towns, he explained, in the U.S. have a 360-degree area that they can haul business from. The political fallout could also carry implications for incumbent Republican Susan Collins , who has represented Maine in the U.S. Senate since 1997 and is seeking re-election in the November midterms. Foster, who is retired and has family on both sides of the border, said he has supported Collins every time shes run. Now, he says he wont vote for Collins, though he said he still considers himself a Republican. What changed? Trump, Foster said flatly. The Congress is not doing their job; they're not standing up, he added. The economic dispute has included U.S. tariffs, some up to 50%, on Canadian goods and retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada, adding to tensions between the longtime allies. Those tensions are visible plainly at the Aroostook Valley Country Club, which nearly entirely lies in Canada, but runs along the American border. On Wednesday, a parking lot on the American side of the border across from the clubhouse was empty and partially overgrown. A golf course, the Aroostook Valley Country Club, even straddles the international boundary.But Northern Mainers say President Donald Trump’s trade fight with Canada is straining those cross-border relationships and raising economic concerns in communities like Fort Fairfield, located about two miles from the international boundary.Retiree John Foster, who lives in Fort Fairfield, told Scripps News Group that his town’s location puts it in a particularly difficult position.“The economics certainly is a big deal for us,” he said Wednesday.“Most towns,” he explained, “in the U.S. have a 360-degree area that they can haul business from.”RELATED STORY | Heating oil costs test political loyalties in northern Maine“[Half] of that is all Canada,” adding, “a lot of that is not coming here.”The political fallout could also carry implications for incumbent Republican Susan Collins, who has represented Maine in the U.S. Senate since 1997 and is seeking re-election in the November midterms.Foster, who is retired and has family on both sides of the border, said he has supported Collins “every time” she’s run.Now, he says he won’t vote for Collins, though he said he still considers himself a Republican.What changed?“Trump,” Foster said flatly.“The Congress is not doing their job; they're not standing up,” he added.The economic dispute has included U.S. tariffs, some up to 50%, on Canadian goods and retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada, adding to tensions between the longtime allies.Those tensions are visible plainly at the Aroostook Valley Country Club, which nearly entirely lies in Canada, but runs along the American border.On Wednesday, a parking lot on the American side of the border across from the clubhouse was empty and partially overgrown. A single small red sign reading, “No access beyond this point,” was the only indication that things have changed.Canadian retiree Leroy Turner, who stopped his golf cart to chat with the Scripps News Group Wednesday, shouted across the border that the club has seen a decline in members from Maine, “big time.”“It's gone from 150 to 175, [or] 200 down to 25 members from Maine,” he said Wednesday.Turner, who lives seven miles from the border, said making regular crossings is harder than they used to be, and Canadians along the border have changed their habits about crossing into neighboring Maine communities.“We used to cross and buy stuff because it was cheaper, you had more to choose from,” Turner said. “People aren't doing that now.”In northern Maine, it’s not clear if a change in which party controls Congress will be enough to de-escalate tensions between Washington and Ottawa.“Until your management changes, I think it's going to stay that way,” Turner said. “We used to go to Fort Fairfield, Maine, every week. Now, [we] go once in a while.”

entry.title: Semi-truck turns into path of SUV, killing Vero Beach driver, FHP says
entry.summary: A man was killed Thursday morning in a crash involving a semi-truck in unincorporated Indian River County, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash happened around 6:45 a.m. at the intersection of 66th Avenue and 49th Street. According to FHP, a Freightliner semi-truck was attempting to make a left turn from a stop sign at westbound 49th Street onto 66th Avenue. At the same time, a Dodge Durango was traveling north in the inside lane of 66th Avenue, which had no traffic controls at the intersection. Troopers said the Freightliner entered the path of the SUV, causing the front of the Durango to collide with the left side of the semi-trailer. Both vehicles came to rest in the area of the collision. The driver of the SUV, a 60-year-old Vero Beach man, was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead just after 8 a.m., according to FHP. The driver of the Freightliner, a 59-year-old Jacksonville man, was not injured. The crash remains under investigation.

entry.summary: Martin County airport committee to review overnight flights and noise concerns    WPEC
entry.article_text: Martin County’s Airport Noise Advisory Committee is scheduled to meet at 9 a.m. Thursday at Witham Field’s Airport Administration Building to review nighttime flight activity and noise concerns. The committee advises the county on airport noise and possible mitigation measures. The airport recorded 7,474 takeoffs and landings in September, including 1,224 jet operations. Of those, 258 took place during the voluntary curfew, which runs from 11 p.m. The airport reported a 96.55% compliance rate. The county also sent 20 letters to aircraft operators about nighttime activity; the report does not specify how many flights, if any, were considered violations. Residents say private jet traffic can increase when flight restrictions are imposed in Palm Beach County during President Donald Trump’s visits to Mar-a-Lago, affecting their quality of life. The committee is also scheduled to receive an update on the Residential Sound Insulation Program, which aims to reduce aircraft noise inside eligible homes near the airport. The agenda does not list a proposal to change the voluntary curfew or a vote on airport rules. If you would like to review the agenda for the meeting, CLICK HERE. This is a developing story.

Investigators said help from victims and witnesses, along with license plate reader cameras, led them to the suspects, and PBSO is now looking for potential additional victims. Investigators said the men demanded a passport or other documents proving the victim was a U.S. citizen. entry.title: Charges dropped against Indian River County school bus driver accused of child abuse - WPEC
entry.summary: Charges dropped against Indian River County school bus driver accused of child abuse    WPEC
entry.article_text: The child abuse case against an Indian River County school bus driver has ended after prosecutors declined to file formal charges. The State Attorney’s Office filed a no information in the case against Tracy Marie Alpy on Oct. 5, according to a court document. The filing listed the charge as child abuse intentional act, but did not explain why prosecutors decided not to proceed. Alpy, 65, of Sebastian, was arrested Sept. 10 after investigators reviewed surveillance video from a school bus. The allegations were described in an arrest affidavit. The alleged incident happened Aug. 24 as the bus was transporting students to after-school care. The video, recorded from 3:44 to 4:31 p.m., showed the bus waiting at Liberty Magnet School for another bus to exchange children headed to the Gifford Youth Aquatic Center and the Boys & Girls Club, according to the affidavit. Investigators said a student seated near the front of the bus repeatedly got out of the seat. Alpy was seen walking through the aisle and directing the student to sit down. The student also appeared to repeatedly raise a middle finger toward Alpy when her back was turned, the affidavit said. About 15 minutes into the video, Alpy sat on the edge of the student’s seat to keep the child from getting up, investigators said. After more children boarded and the bus began moving, the student again stood up and turned around to interact with other children. The affidavit said Alpy repeatedly told the student to sit down. When the child did not, she pulled the bus over, left the driver’s seat and approached the student. Investigators alleged she grabbed the child, forced the child back into the seat and fastened the seat belt. Both vehicles came to rest in the area of the collision. The driver of the Freightliner, a 59-year-old Jacksonville man, was not injured. The crash remains under investigation. entry.title: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday - WFLX
entry.summary: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday    WFLX
entry.article_text: Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation’s aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves’ final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.summary: A federal judge issued a ruling late Wednesday setting limits for ICE agents visiting homes of immigrants to investigate claims of voter fraud and make arrests. With early voting already underway, ICE has taken the unprecedented step of deploying agents into communities to knock on doors and follow up on data the agency has collected that suggests people at those addresses either voted or registered to vote even though they were ineligible to do so as non-U.S. citizens. But U.S. District Judge Araceli Martnez-Olgun said ICE is relying on data that is unreliable, some of it coming from unknown artificial intelligence tools. She pointed to the U.S. governments acknowledgement that the target list could be tainted by similar names, incomplete records or clerical errors. entry.summary: WPTV had the rare opportunity to go inside the St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant on Thursday. This year, the facility is celebrating 50 years of operation and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission just granted licenses for 20 more.   On Thursday, WPTV learned about operations inside the plant and spoke with people who keep the power on. 'My job is to calibrate and make sure all the equipment used to work on the equipment that controls the reactor itself meets all the government standards and accuracies.' We're here, but yet we're still invisible because what we do, we do it well, .Phillips said.   Alfreds son, Alfred Sinclair Phillips, followed his father's footsteps and works in the operations department. 'There's a pressure with it, but there's also a sense of pride, Phillips said. Knowing that my dad has worked his butt off and he's left an impact with the people here on his work to make this place better. WPTV learned from Carlos Santos, site vice president, how the plant generates power. 'The simplest way to put it is the reactor creates the heat,' Santos said. Santos said that heat comes from nuclear fission from uranium pellets stacked into rods inside the two units on site. The heat from the rods builds up and produces steam, which travels into a secondary closed system into a turbine, which then generates power and produces electricity for the grid. entry.title: Homeowner gets better news on insurance after contacting WPTV
entry.summary: A Delray Beach homeowner who got a new roof this year now is finding out her insurance will not go up. Betty Haygood contacted WPTV after finding out her insurance renewal was going up $300 even though she had a new roof installed in August. Her insurer, Universal, based in South Florida, told us they were looking over Haygood's policy and gave her a new quote of $3,087, which is $90 less than what she is paying now. 'Im OK with that,' the 76-year-old home healthcare worker told WPTV. 'You have helped by bringing it to attention because so many people and neighbors and people I didnt know reached out to me about that, because Im not the only one going through something like this,' Haygood said. Haygood says she does plan to shop around some other insurance companies, something insurance experts now recommend. Litigation reforms in Florida have led to more insurers, more competition and lower rates. But lower rates don't always mean lower premiums as inflation has made it more expensive to build and repair homes. Many insurers also focus on the age of a roof in assessing risk, and experts also advise checking with an agent first. Lee Wiglesworth of Wiglesworth-Rindom Insurance Agency in Stuart says one step can solve issues down the road. 'Call an agent who can shop multiple carriers and say what would it save me if I got a new roof,' Wiglesworth says.
entry.article_text: A Delray Beach homeowner who got a new roof this year now is finding out her insurance will not go up.Betty Haygood contacted WPTV after finding out her insurance renewal was going up $300 even though she had a new roof installed in August.Her insurer, Universal, based in South Florida, told us they were looking over Haygood's policy and gave her a new quote of $3,087, which is $90 less than what she is paying now."I’m OK with that," the 76-year-old home healthcare worker told WPTV."You have helped by bringing it to attention because so many people and neighbors and people I didn’t know reached out to me about that, because I’m not the only one going through something like this," Haygood said. entry.title: Supreme Court says New Hampshire can limit use of student IDs for voting
entry.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday allowed New Hampshire officials to limit when voters may use a student ID to receive a ballot, agreeing that a lower court ruling that blocked enforcement of the policy was too close to Election Day. The unsigned order was a win for New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, a Republican, and the Republican National Committee, which had supported Scanlan in the fight. The court did not provide a vote count, though it did provide a brief explanation, invoking the Purcell principle that warns against last-minute decisions from courts that change election rules. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a liberal, wrote a brief dissent questioning the application of the Purcell doctrine. New Hampshire voters will fill an open Senate seat in November to replace the retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. A recent CNN poll found that Democrats enjoy a 31 percentage point advantage over Republicans among younger adults. Lower federal courts allowed the state to enforce the central prohibition of a law enacted by the state legislature this spring. Under that law, student IDs on their own may no longer be used to verify a voters identity. But state law also includes a safety valve that allows voters to attempt to prove their identity through other means and the fight at the Supreme Court was about whether, in those circumstances, student IDs could be used as one factor, along with other evidence, to help officials identify people requesting a ballot. When New Hampshire officials interpreted the new state law as shutting off the ability to use student IDs even in those circumstances, a voting rights group called Coalition for Open Democracy sued. A federal district court blocked enforcement of that interpretation on October 2. New Hampshire filed an emergency appeal at the Supreme Court arguing that the Purcell opinion meant should decide the case in its favor. The RNC had warned that the lower courts order threatens to disrupt identity verification in New Hampshires looming elections. The Supreme Court has been called on to address several high-profile election disputes heading into next months midterms, most notably a decision in mid-September rejecting President Donald Trumps proposal to change how mail ballots are sent to voters across the country. entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire Chief Jeff Lee is speaking out after the fire board terminated his contract Wednesday, ending his tenure after months of turmoil surrounding a hazing investigation and growing criticism of district leadership.Lee did not attend Wednesday’s heated fire board meeting, where commissioners voted to terminate him without cause.In a statement to WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey following the vote, Lee pointed to his previous comments highlighting increases in staffing, pay and benefits he fought for during his time leading the district."During the 2023–2026 period, these efforts included approximately 19% average pay-plan growth, an increase of approximately 100 uniformed personnel, and improved minimum engine staffing from two to three firefighters," the Fire District wrote in a statement October 9. "The District also expanded employee benefits, increased retirement-health contributions, and invested in additional training opportunities, equipment, and facilities to better support personnel in carrying out their responsibilities." “That’s really all I have to say,” Lee told Hussey Thursday. Lee’s termination marks the latest fallout from a controversy that began after videos surfaced showing probationary firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. A third-party investigator concluded the conduct amounted to hazing.Three veteran firefighters were fired following the investigation, prompting significant public backlash from firefighters, their families and community members who argued the punishment went too far.“Not only have they lost their jobs, but they lost their reputation,” one speaker told the board Wednesday.Others said the controversy had damaged confidence in the district.“We need to restore faith in this fire district,” another speaker said.Lee’s departure also follows an overwhelming union vote of no confidence in district leadership.St Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board Member, Jamie Fowler, said the decision to remove Lee was not based solely on the vote of no confidence. “At the end of the day, it’s gotten very messy,” Fowler said. “It’s not about one single decision that he’s made. It’s about bringing peace and calm and respect.”Lee had already signaled that his time as chief could be nearing an end. 15 letter to the board, Lee wrote that “the position of fire chief requires confidence” and raised the possibility of a mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition.Deputy Chief Paul Langel has now been appointed interim fire chief as the district searches for Lee’s permanent replacement.Langel inherits a department facing questions about morale, trust and what some speakers Wednesday described as a broader “culture problem.”“Personally, I don’t think there is a culture problem,” Langel said. “But I’m going to do the due diligence and I’m going to evaluate whether that’s visiting fire stations, one-on-one conversations with employees, group settings to get the vibe, what's going on out there, where are we at as an organization, and then once I receive all that, process it, I'll correct the course and move this district forward." The board is now confronting several major issues left unresolved by Lee’s departure.Commissioners plan to hire a headhunter to conduct a search for a permanent chief inside and outside the district. "I'm sure we have a very talented pool right here, but we'll see how it plays out," said Fowler. The district and firefighters union are also expected to continue discussions over the possible reinstatement of the three firefighters fired following the hazing investigation.“I’m excited to see if we can just come back together and collectively work together,” union representative Ryan Sapp said.At the same time, the board is moving forward with an outside law firm to overhaul the district's complaint policies after a heated Sept. 30 meeting identified what board members called "a significant gap" in existing policy. Commissioner James Clasby has also called for reconsidering the terms offered in the next fire chief’s contract, as Lee’s existing contract could leave taxpayers responsible for more than $350,000 in severance following his termination.“That’s the consequences of firing somebody with those terms,” Clasby said. "The next chief — I'm going to be fighting very hard does not get those terms, and I think that could lead to more accountability." For the four board members who supported Lee’s removal, Wednesday’s vote represented an attempt to turn the page after months of controversy.“There was a large desire to have a change in leadership,” Clasby said, “and we delivered that today.”But Lee’s departure does not end the larger fight over the district’s future. Commissioners must now determine who will permanently lead the agency, whether the terminated firefighters will return and whether new leadership can rebuild trust among firefighters and the community.

entry.title: Florida Senate president opposes Amendment 3 months after lawmakers put it on ballot
entry.summary: The president of the Florida State Senate says he is voting 'No' on Amendment 3, just months after the State Senate approved putting the referendum on the November ballot. 'As a native of Florida's Heartland, our rural communities are near and dear to my heart,' Albritton said in a post on the Florida Sheriffs Association's Instagram page. 'Amendment 3 would eliminate up to 30% of resources for Florida's rural counties, gutting essential support for law enforcement, emergency response services and critical infrastructure.' WATCH BELOW: Florida Senate president opposes Amendment 3 Florida Senate president opposes Amendment 3 Albritton also stated the Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission presents: 'An ideal opportunity to design property tax reform and create a solution that is meaningful, reasonable and balanced.' Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It would also cut property taxes for homesteaded homeowners, excluding school taxes. Cities and counties stand to lose significant revenue and many local leaders say it will lead to budget cuts, reduced services and possibly creating other revenue streams. The referendum needs 60% approval on Election Day to become law in Florida.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County fire chief terminated after months of controversy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 to terminate fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause after months of controversy, hazing allegations, and a no-confidence vote. Interim Chief Paul Langel said, "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job. Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process." The decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced for allegedly turning a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and using it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three firefighters ultimately lost their jobs. One of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, said, "I think it was a step in the right direction. I don’t think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department." The disciplined firefighters have called the termination retaliation for previous complaints they filed against district leadership. When asked about the possibility of the terminated firefighters regaining their jobs, Langel said, "I believe that there’s always scenarios that would unfold and happen. I’ve got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics." The board voted to appoint Langel as interim chief. He is a familiar face in the district, with 30 years of experience. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early. entry.article_text: More than 100 cats were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, including deceased kittens, prompting a criminal investigation. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say 124 cats, both living and deceased, were recovered from a residence in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street. Animal Control personnel responded to concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions on October 13. They documented accumulated feces and deceased kittens inside the home. See also: Wellington speed camera ticket tossed over missing state approval Two of the three residents have been issued citations for hoarding and failing to provide medical attention to animals, police said. The investigation remains active, and police have not provided details about potential future arrests. All 124 cats have been surrendered and are receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas. Others have needed surgery or additional veterinary care, with some transported to Veterinary Medical Center for treatment. Many of the surviving cats are friendly and could become available for adoption once their medical needs are addressed, police said. The case required a coordinated response involving animal control personnel, police officers, veterinarians and animal welfare organizations. Police said additional information will be released as the investigation continues.

entry.title: From the fairway to housing: Golf event supports a new shelter model
entry.summary: WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. A celebrity golf tournament in Palm Beach County brought athletes, community leaders, and supporters together for a day on the course, but the larger goal stretched far beyond golf. Par for the Culture, presented by the Higher Learning Foundation, raised support for The Lords Place and its efforts to expand housing and early-intervention services for people experiencing homelessness in Palm Beach County. The need is significant. The Lords Place says the county has more than 500 shelter beds dedicated to people experiencing homelessness, while roughly 1,500 people currently need housing. Those existing beds are generally prioritized for people with the greatest needs, including those who have experienced homelessness for longer periods of time or face significant health and safety concerns. That can leave people who are newly unhoused waiting for help -a gap The Lords Place hopes to address with a new shelter model focused on early intervention. The goal is to provide intensive, short-term support before a temporary housing crisis becomes long-term homelessness. We would really love to shorten their experience in homelessness and get them bridged back and transitioned back into the community as quickly as possible, said Christine Frederick, CEO of The Lords Place. Outreach workers say intervening early can help people maintain jobs, stay in school, address health needs and preserve the support systems that can help them regain stability. Cristina Lucier with The Lords Place said the longer someone remains on the streets, the greater the risk of losing those connections. The longer people spend on the streets, they may lose some of those critical social connections that will help them get back on their feet and retain stability long term, Lucier said. For Devin Perry, that instability was once part of everyday life. The hardest part is knowing where youre gonna sleep at, where youre gonna wake up at, if your stuff is gonna be there when you come back, Perry said. Perry later entered The Lords Place culinary training program, secured housing and began moving toward employment. Having a place of his own has changed what he is able to think about each day. entry.title: Martin County parents win push for school zone outside Citrus Grove Elementary
entry.summary: Martin County parents are celebrating a victory in a long battle to improve safety around their children's school. Citrus Grove Elementary School parents say the 45 mph speed limit outside the school puts their children's safety in jeopardy. They say a recently approved school zone is the first step to making Newfield Parkway a safer place for children who walk to school. On Southwest Newfield Parkway, morning and afternoon traffic is an obstacle for young students. 'It scares me,' parent Kendall George said. 'These cars are driving 45 miles an hour plus.' Kendall is among the many families who live in the Canopy Creek community across the street from Citrus Grove Elementary, so their children walk to school. Kelly Ribaudo, the PTA president and Martin County PTA Advocacy Chair, told WPTV she's spent the last five years asking the county to put in a school zone. 'We've had so many near misses with the kids just from people not paying attention,' Ribaudo said. 'Everyone has a right to a free and public education and they should be safe getting there. Our main priority should be the kids not the traffic.' At the previous Martin County Commission meeting, commissioners unanimously answered their call. 'Whatever the number is there is no price to someone getting hurt,' Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi said. 'You will absolutely get a school zone.' School Principal Rose Rynca told WPTV the need is greater than ever, with enrollment growing as new communities pop up in the area. 'The amount of students crossing Newfield Parkway has definitely increased,' Rynca said. 'This speed zone is going to really really improve the safety of students.' 'It's letting drivers know that, hey there's a school here, there's children crossing, and we have to slow down,' George said. "This speed zone is going to really really improve the safety of students.""It's letting drivers know that, hey there's a school here, there's children crossing, and we have to slow down," George said.WPTV's Cassandra Garcia followed up with the county on Thursday to find out the timeline for adding a school zone on SW Newfield Parkway. entry.title: Conflict of interest? Palm Beach County reconsiders data center consultant

entry.article_text: WPTV is staying on top of the future of data centers in Palm Beach County as commissioners rethink who should help develop new regulations for an industry that has already generated significant concern among residents.County commissioners on Wednesday backed away from immediately moving forward with one consultant selected by staff, instead deciding they want to consider other options before making a final selection.At the same time, commissioners agreed to bring back plans for a formal community task force, giving the public a greater role as the county considers what its future data center regulations should look like.The discussion comes less than a month after commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers on Sept. 24.County staff told commissioners the clock is now running to establish regulations before that moratorium expires.The county staff had proposed hiring VHB (Vanasse Hangen Brustlin, Inc.), an engineering and planning firm, to work alongside staff on a framework designed to protect communities, establish clearer expectations and create standards the county could administer and enforce.It would cost $224,900 for VHB's services.But the proposal quickly drew questions from residents.“I have concerns today about the consultant who was chosen,” said Rachel Smith, an Acreage resident.Resident Ben Brown questioned how the firm had been selected and whether enough alternatives were considered.“I have many questions. When did you reach out to this consultant? Are you interviewing other ones?” Brown said. “They obviously work with data centers. You are putting the fox in the henhouse.”County staff said they issued a request for information and received six proposals that were incomplete. Staff initially told commissioners the proposals ranged from $200,000 for a portion of the needed support to $2 million.Later in the discussion, staff described the range as about $125,000 for an architect who would only be part of the process, requiring additional experts, to about $2.1 million.Those concerns put particular scrutiny on VHB and its existing work involving data centers.“Do you have clients that are a part of data centers?” Mayor Sara Baxter asked the consultant representative directly.“We work for clients that have data centers in Massachusetts and Virginia,” answered Curt Ostrodka a VHB representative responded. “We don't have any clients in Florida building data centers.”The firm's representative also told commissioners VHB had worked as a consultant for private clients providing civil engineering, utility studies and other technical services supporting data centers.When Commissioner Gregg Weiss asked whether the company had ever developed regulations specifically for data centers, the answer was direct.“Not for data centers," said Ostrodka.VHB maintained it could serve as an objective third party while researching how other communities are handling data centers and studying potential impacts including noise, energy and water.“We don't know the answers right now,” Ostrodka said. “We would do that collaboratively with staff, members of the public.”The company outlined a nine-month process that would also examine applicable state and federal laws and determine thresholds and regulatory mechanisms for potential impacts.Commissioner Maria Sachs was among those who wanted more information before committing to the firm.“This is one company standing here I know nothing about,” Sachs said.But county staff stressed that the push to hire a consultant isn't simply about getting another opinion. Staff told commissioners they need additional capacity and technical expertise to develop the rules.“We are asking for this assistance because we are limited in our capacity to do the work,” staff told commissioners. “We need the technical expertise to help support the staff get this done.”Commissioner Joel Flores asked what it might cost for the county to instead bring in its own people to handle the workload.Staff estimated a dedicated team could require two employees, with an average annual salary of about $125,000 each, or roughly $250,000.Flores said the need for specialized knowledge was part of the reason he supported hiring outside help.“I'm not an expert on data centers and this technology is evolving so quick,” Flores said.Flores said commissioners will ultimately decide what the county's rules look like, but expert information could help them determine what safeguards are necessary.“Having someone on our side who is going to say these are the things you want to watch out for, these are the guardrails you want to put in place, I would feel more comfortable,” Flores said.For some residents, the concern was less about whether the county hires a consultant and more about making sure it hires the right one.“For me, at least, it’s less of a money issue and more of, I want quality information, not just necessarily what people want to hear,” Wellington resident Elizabeth Pandich said. “I want to make sure we pick a consultant that is maybe in an environmental and scientific aspect of it, not someone that’s just good at moving data around.”The timeline also weighed heavily on the discussion.Staff told commissioners the moratorium lasts a year. If it expires before the county has new regulations in place, data center applications would be handled under the regulations in place at that time. County attorneys said extending the moratorium could be possible under certain circumstances, but any extension would be limited.Weiss put the urgency bluntly.“Time is of the essence. The clock is ticking,” Weiss said.What initially appeared to be a decision to move forward with VHB changed dramatically near the end of the discussion.Commissioners first voted to proceed with the consultant, with Baxter and Sachs opposed. But moments later, Commissioner Bobby Powell moved to reconsider the decision.Powell said he wanted commissioners to have choices before committing to a single company.“My motion is not to consider two consultants,” Powell said. “It would be for us to have an option to not only consider this consultant but more options. One consultant, maybe there is another person or another consultant company.”The motion to reconsider passed 3-2.Commissioners then voted 4-1 to give the county the opportunity to look at other available consultants rather than immediately settling on VHB.That doesn't necessarily mean VHB is out of consideration.“I'm sure this gentleman may win out in the end,” Sachs said. “But then at least we would know. Let's find out.”While commissioners debated which experts should advise them, there was considerably more agreement about giving residents a direct role in the process.Several speakers called for commissioners to revive the idea of a community task force, arguing that the two public outreach meetings outlined by staff would not provide enough community involvement.Baxter supported establishing a formal task force and suggested that because the regulations would apply countywide, each commissioner could appoint someone to represent their district.“This new ordinance, it would be countywide,” Commissioner Marci Woodward said earlier in the discussion. “This isn't about a specific parcel.”Baxter said the task force proposal could come back before commissioners at their Nov. 18 meeting.Smith welcomed the idea of combining expert input with residents who could be affected by whatever rules the county ultimately adopts.“I do appreciate that they are looking at expert opinions, although I do think that we have enough experts in this area who are actually affected that could be very beneficial,” Smith said.Pandich said she and others who became involved after Project Tango have already formed the National Data Impact Coalition and hope to participate.“I’m excited about the task force. A couple of friends of mine, after Project Tango, started a national data impact coalition, and we are doing that basically internally. So we are going to put our name in the hat and hopefully get a seat at the table,” Pandich said.For Smith, commissioners' decision to take another look at the consultant while moving toward giving residents a more formal role represented progress.“Yeah, I’d say it’s a victory for the residents,” Smith said. “Thank you to Sachs and Baxter for doing what they did, and Powell, who came in last minute and saved the day.”WPTV reached out to VHB to address concerns raised during the meeting about potential conflicts of interest but has not received a response.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire Chief Jeff Lee is speaking out after the fire board terminated his contract Wednesday, ending his tenure after months of turmoil surrounding a hazing investigation and growing criticism of district leadership.Lee did not attend Wednesday’s heated fire board meeting, where commissioners voted to terminate him without cause.In a statement to WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey following the vote, Lee pointed to his previous comments highlighting increases in staffing, pay and benefits he fought for during his time leading the district."During the 2023–2026 period, these efforts included approximately 19% average pay-plan growth, an increase of approximately 100 uniformed personnel, and improved minimum engine staffing from two to three firefighters," the Fire District wrote in a statement October 9. "The District also expanded employee benefits, increased retirement-health contributions, and invested in additional training opportunities, equipment, and facilities to better support personnel in carrying out their responsibilities." “That’s really all I have to say,” Lee told Hussey Thursday. Lee’s termination marks the latest fallout from a controversy that began after videos surfaced showing probationary firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. A third-party investigator concluded the conduct amounted to hazing.Three veteran firefighters were fired following the investigation, prompting significant public backlash from firefighters, their families and community members who argued the punishment went too far.“Not only have they lost their jobs, but they lost their reputation,” one speaker told the board Wednesday.Others said the controversy had damaged confidence in the district.“We need to restore faith in this fire district,” another speaker said.Lee’s departure also follows an overwhelming union vote of no confidence in district leadership.St Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board Member, Jamie Fowler, said the decision to remove Lee was not based solely on the vote of no confidence. “At the end of the day, it’s gotten very messy,” Fowler said. “It’s not about one single decision that he’s made. It’s about bringing peace and calm and respect.”Lee had already signaled that his time as chief could be nearing an end. 15 letter to the board, Lee wrote that “the position of fire chief requires confidence” and raised the possibility of a mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition.Deputy Chief Paul Langel has now been appointed interim fire chief as the district searches for Lee’s permanent replacement.Langel inherits a department facing questions about morale, trust and what some speakers Wednesday described as a broader “culture problem.”“Personally, I don’t think there is a culture problem,” Langel said. “But I’m going to do the due diligence and I’m going to evaluate whether that’s visiting fire stations, one-on-one conversations with employees, group settings to get the vibe, what's going on out there, where are we at as an organization, and then once I receive all that, process it, I'll correct the course and move this district forward." The board is now confronting several major issues left unresolved by Lee’s departure.Commissioners plan to hire a headhunter to conduct a search for a permanent chief inside and outside the district. "I'm sure we have a very talented pool right here, but we'll see how it plays out," said Fowler. The district and firefighters union are also expected to continue discussions over the possible reinstatement of the three firefighters fired following the hazing investigation.“I’m excited to see if we can just come back together and collectively work together,” union representative Ryan Sapp said.At the same time, the board is moving forward with an outside law firm to overhaul the district's complaint policies after a heated Sept. 30 meeting identified what board members called "a significant gap" in existing policy. Commissioner James Clasby has also called for reconsidering the terms offered in the next fire chief’s contract, as Lee’s existing contract could leave taxpayers responsible for more than $350,000 in severance following his termination.“That’s the consequences of firing somebody with those terms,” Clasby said. "The next chief — I'm going to be fighting very hard does not get those terms, and I think that could lead to more accountability." For the four board members who supported Lee’s removal, Wednesday’s vote represented an attempt to turn the page after months of controversy.“There was a large desire to have a change in leadership,” Clasby said, “and we delivered that today.”But Lee’s departure does not end the larger fight over the district’s future. Commissioners must now determine who will permanently lead the agency, whether the terminated firefighters will return and whether new leadership can rebuild trust among firefighters and the community.

entry.title: WHERE'S WALTER? Having a day of discovery at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast
entry.summary: This week, I visited a place where learning and fun go hand in hand: the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast. From the moment I walked in, I could tell this wasn't your typical museum. Instead of looking at exhibits from behind a rope or glass case, kids are encouraged to jump in, get involved and learn by doing. As I explored the museum, I discovered exhibits designed to teach important life skills in creative and engaging ways. From learning about money and budgeting to exploring different careers and practicing job skills, every corner of the museum offered a new opportunity to learn something useful. WATCH: WHERE'S WALTER? Discovering the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast One of my favorite stops, of course, involved the weather. As a meteorologist, I was excited to check out the museum's WPTV weather simulator and hurricane simulator. It was fascinating to see how children can experience weather concepts in a hands-on environment and gain a better understanding of the science behind storms and hurricanes. What impressed me most was how interactive everything was. Kids aren't just reading signs or watching demonstrations. They're solving problems, making decisions, using their imaginations and building confidence along the way. The museum creates an environment where learning feels more like an adventure than a lesson. Whether they're exploring future careers, practicing financial skills or learning about science and weather, children are gaining valuable experiences that can help them throughout their lives. My visit was a great reminder that some of the best learning happens when you're having fun. By rolling up their sleeves, asking questions and trying new things, kids can discover skills and interests they never knew they had. If you're looking for a family-friendly destination on the Treasure Coast that combines education, creativity and fun, the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast is definitely worth a visit. That's where I was!

PGA HOPE introduces veterans and active-duty service members to golf to support their physical, mental, social and emotional well-being. The tournament will be held at The Club at Lost Lake, 8300 SE Fazio Drive in Hobe Sound. Registration and event information are available through Tee It Up for the Troops.

entry.title: Riviera Beach leaders question city manager absence after crash
entry.summary: Questions about who is leading Riviera Beach and the future of City Manager William E. Wilkins took center stage during a contentious city council discussion Wednesday, as some elected leaders said they were unaware of the extent of his absence following an August car crash. Wilkins has been working remotely since the crash, according to city officials. While assistant city manager staff have handled many day-to-day operations inside city hall, some council members said they only recently learned key details about Wilkins' condition and work arrangements. The debate comes as Riviera Beach continues to navigate leadership challenges following the April 2026 firing of former City Manager Jonathan Evans, with residents and officials alike calling for stability at City Hall. WATCH: Riviera Beach leaders seek answers on city manager's future, status Riviera Beach leaders seek answers on city manager's future, status Council members question communication and leadership During Wednesday's meeting at Marina Village, some council members expressed frustration over what they described as a lack of communication regarding Wilkins' status. Councilwoman Shirley D. Lanier said she had not spoken with Wilkins since August and was unaware he had been injured in a crash. 'I didn't know he was in a car wreck. I didn't know he was on TV and I haven't heard from him since then,' Lanier said. Lanier and Councilwoman Kashamba Miller-Anderson questioned whether the city's leadership structure is sustainable if the city manager remains out of the office for an extended period. 'I understand he has health issues. I understand that. But someone has to run the business of the city,' Lanier said during the discussion. Miller-Anderson argued that city leaders need clarity on Wilkins' plans moving forward. Miller-Anderson also questioned whether Wilkins' remote work arrangement aligns with the terms of his employment agreement. 'Either take leave, resign, or come back. And I think that's only right and that's only fair to ask,' Miller-Anderson said. Other officials say city operations continue Not everyone on the dais agreed with the criticism. Dr. Glen Spiritis, chair pro tem, said he has maintained communication with Wilkins and believes the city manager continues to oversee city operations while working remotely. entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates fire chief after union vote - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates fire chief after union vote    cw34.com
entry.article_text: After months of controversy, the St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire longtime Chief Jeff Lee, following an emotional meeting filled with calls for change and coming less than two weeks after the firefighters' union released the results of a no-confidence vote in the district's top leaders. The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many urged the board to change the district's leadership. Among them was Taylor Baldwin, who pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." The decision marks the latest development in a controversy that began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others . The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated . The issue later escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants voting they no longer had confidence in his leadership. Several speakers criticized both district leadership and the board's handling of the controversy. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," another resident Katie told the board. Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether Lee should be fired with or without cause. Ultimately, the board voted to terminate him without cause, triggering the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Those who supported Lee's removal said the district needs a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Commissioner Jamie Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." Following Lee's termination, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search for a permanent replacement begins. The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing the process for selecting the district's next chief. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract.
