entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - WPEC
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    WPEC
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

entry.summary: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides flooded streets and reached homes across Palm Beach County on Monday, while beach and road closures were reported as more high tides were expected through Wednesday. In Palm City, flooding made SW Dyer Point Road impassable. Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies brought in three high-water vehicles to help reach anyone stranded in a vehicle or home. Flooding also was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. One driver told CBS12 the water was about waist-deep in part of the area. Resident Terresa Baldwin said water came up around both the front and back of her home, and that Monday’s flooding was the worst she had seen in eight years. Baldwin also raised concerns about the water’s source and smell. This is not only runoff water, it’s sewage and it’s bad and you can smell it, she said. Deputies urged people to avoid flooded areas and not to drive through standing water. These vehicles can travel through several feet of water safely, Martin County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Flooding also reached Flagler Drive in downtown West Palm Beach and Sunset Avenue on Palm Beach Island, where water covered parts of the roadway and disrupted pedestrians and cyclists. In Boynton Beach, flooding led to road closures, including at Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. The Ocean Inlet Marina also closed because of high tides. In Boca Raton, water reached a Cub Scout pack’s campsite at Spanish River Park, prompting campers to move supplies to higher ground. Elsewhere, Midtown Beach was temporarily closed because of large surf and high tides. The northbound lane of South Ocean Boulevard between Chilean and Australian avenues was scheduled to close from 10 a.m. to noon while crews moved a lifeguard tower. Delray Beach officials raised red flags because of high surf and flooding, and the Juno Beach Pier remained closed because of damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf. See also: 15-year-old FAMU shooting suspect ordered to be held as prosecutors seek adult charges A coastal flood warning covers low-lying areas near the water in Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The National Weather Service said the warning runs through 8 p.m. Wednesday in coastal Palm Beach County and 2 a.m. Thursday in coastal Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The forecast high tides were: Monday: 9:06 p.m. The sheriff’s office advised residents not to drive through floodwater and to call 911 if they need emergency assistance.

entry.title: Strong winds, king tides flood parts of Martin County as officials warn of more high water
entry.summary: WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday. In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater. WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong winds King tides, strong winds flood areas of Martin County Terresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated. 'You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad,' Baldwin said. 'There were dead copperheads, so the snakes are coming out. They're getting flushed out with the water.' Baldwin said she was also dealing with flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals. She showed WPTV the water over her dock and in her new patio. 'The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that,' Baldwin said. Despite the water going down, she is still worried about what could happen in the next few days. 'The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see,' Baldwin said.  With high tide later Monday night, the sheriffs office told WPTV the situation could get worse. Lt. Dave Rosko said they have three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged neighbors to think twice before driving through the water. 'Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters,' Rosko said. 'If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety.' Rosko said neighbors living in coastal communities should be aware of future tides before traveling.

entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WFLX
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WFLX
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. "I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette. WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college football While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. "I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar. "I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette. And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. "Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it. "It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.

entry.title: Delray Beach students engineer AI-themed haunted house for a cause
entry.summary: Students at Space of Mind in downtown Delray Beach are putting math, engineering, technology and storytelling to work by creating their own Halloween haunted house, called SOMething Scary, to raise money for educational programs and scholarships. This year's theme puts a decidedly 2026 spin on Halloween: 'Error 404: Humanity Not Found.' Delray Beach students create SOMething Scary Halloween experience Kimberly Allegro, director of business development at Space of Mind, said students are incorporating robotics, electronics, audio and video into an experience built around artificial intelligence. 'The haunted house this year is themed error 404. Humanity not found,' Allegro said during an interview with WPTV. 'So the students are actually working on a bunch of themes in the haunted house that have to do with AI and the takeover that's impending on us in the future.' Students engineer their own scares The haunted house isn't simply a collection of Halloween decorations. Digital media coach Todd Belanca said students have incorporated core academic skills into the attraction, including mathematics and engineering, along with sound design, music and storytelling. 'We've been impressed, absolutely impressed with what they've done,' Belanca said. 'The amount of time, energy, the creativity, utilizing everything from core skills, mathematics to engineering, their sound design and music is incredible.' Belanca said storytelling is an important part of the students' work. 'So the whole idea of this is to build a story, not just have scares, build a storyline,' he said. That gives students an opportunity to take lessons beyond a traditional classroom setting and turn them into something thousands of drivers and pedestrians passing through downtown Delray Beach can immediately recognize: a Halloween attraction. Student Dieter said the young creators have put significant work into the project. 'All the students did lots of hard work to put together a haunted house,' he said. A haunted house with a larger purpose Behind the scares is a fundraising mission. Space of Mind works with Community Classroom Project, a nonprofit organization that supports educational opportunities in the community. entry.article_text: Students at Space of Mind in downtown Delray Beach are putting math, engineering, technology and storytelling to work by creating their own Halloween haunted house, called SOMething Scary, to raise money for educational programs and scholarships.This year's theme puts a decidedly 2026 spin on Halloween: "Error 404: Humanity Not Found."Kimberly Allegro, director of business development at Space of Mind, said students are incorporating robotics, electronics, audio and video into an experience built around artificial intelligence."The haunted house this year is themed error 404. Humanity not found," Allegro said during an interview with WPTV. "So the students are actually working on a bunch of themes in the haunted house that have to do with AI and the takeover that's impending on us in the future."The haunted house isn't simply a collection of Halloween decorations.Digital media coach Todd Belanca said students have incorporated core academic skills into the attraction, including mathematics and engineering, along with sound design, music and storytelling."We've been impressed, absolutely impressed with what they've done," Belanca said. "The amount of time, energy, the creativity, utilizing everything from core skills, mathematics to engineering, their sound design and music is incredible."Belanca said storytelling is an important part of the students' work."So the whole idea of this is to build a story, not just have scares, build a storyline," he said.That gives students an opportunity to take lessons beyond a traditional classroom setting and turn them into something thousands of drivers and pedestrians passing through downtown Delray Beach can immediately recognize: a Halloween attraction.Student Dieter said the young creators have put significant work into the project."All the students did lots of hard work to put together a haunted house," he said.Behind the scares is a fundraising mission.Space of Mind works with Community Classroom Project, a nonprofit organization that supports educational opportunities in the community.Allegro described Space of Mind as a homeschool schoolhouse community serving students from kindergarten through 12th grade. She said Community Classroom Project supports student and culinary scholarships."We are also putting on this haunted house in support of building and fundraising those scholarships throughout the year," Allegro said.Jack Feldman, marketing manager at Space of Mind, said Community Classroom Project has a mission of reducing school-related stress and that its initiatives include scholarships and workplace readiness training."It funds scholarships and also workplace readiness training as well," Feldman said.According to Feldman, building SOMething Scary also gives Space of Mind students an opportunity to pursue their individual interests and passions.SOMething Scary is scheduled for Friday, Oct. to 10 p.m.The haunted house will be at Space of Mind, 102 N. Swinton Ave., near Old School Square in downtown Delray Beach. entry.title: LagoonFest brings free family fun to West Palm Beach waterfront
entry.summary: LagoonFest returns to the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront Saturday with free boat tours, wildlife encounters, children's activities and opportunities to learn about the Lake Worth Lagoon. The free festival runs from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. near the West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Benji Studt of Palm Beach County Environmental Resources Management said the event is designed to help residents and visitors connect with the lagoon. 'It's all about connecting people with the lagoon,' Studt said. Shell hunts, wildlife and more at LagoonFest Boat tours offer a closer look at the lagoon Visitors can explore the Lake Worth Lagoon aboard the Hakuna Matata or through Aqua Adventure tours, according to Studt. The boat tours provide a chance to experience the lagoon from the water while learning more about the natural area and the work being done around it. Wildlife encounters and hands-on activities Studt said participating organizations include the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Busch Wildlife Sanctuary and Manatee Lagoon. The festival will feature touch tanks, wildlife experiences and a live python capture demonstration from FWC. Throughout the morning, families can also meet Laguna, the spotted eagle ray mascot representing Lake Worth Lagoon. Shell hunts and fishing lessons for children Studt said this year's children's zone includes a shell hunt, giveaways and calendars featuring work from local artists. Volunteers from the West Palm Beach Fishing Foundation will teach children how to cast and fish. Participating children will also get to take home a rod and reel, according to Studt. 'The kids can come, and they can do a little shell hunt, look for their shell treasures,' Studt said. Why LagoonFest matters now LagoonFest gives South Florida families a free way to spend time together while learning about a waterway that is part of Palm Beach County's environmental identity. Its location also allows visitors to pair the festival with a stop at the nearby West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Studt said the variety of activities makes the event accessible to visitors with different interests. 'There's something for everybody at LagoonFest,' Studt said. 'It's going to be an awesome time.' LagoonFest takes place Saturday from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. along the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront. entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department.The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away.WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty"Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day."Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time."We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge, 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025.The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

Ashley Moody's Palm Beach Gardens office to deliver a message, urging her to support Senate Bill 4814, which would extend Temporary Protected Status for Haitians living in the U.S. for three years. Since 2010, that status has allowed Haitian immigrants to legally live and work in the U.S. because of dangerous conditions in their country. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Advocates urge Sen. Moody to back Haitian TPS extension Homeland Security revoked Haitian TPS in July following a Supreme Court decision allowing it to do so. entry.title: New $17 million Boys & Girls Club opens in West Palm Beach, offering opportunities for hundreds of kids
entry.summary: A new Boys Girls Club officially opened its doors Tuesday in West Palm Beach, bringing a new place for hundreds of children and teens to learn, explore their interests and prepare for their futures. The Julie Mike Connors Boys Girls Club, located at 1150 Southern Blvd., celebrated its grand opening after years of planning. WATCH REPORT BELOW: New Boys Girls Club opens in West Palm Beach 'To have this come to fruition is more beautiful than I ever thought it could be,' Julie Connors said during the celebration. The $17 million, 31,000-square-foot facility is the 21st location for the Boys Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County and is expected to serve approximately 800 children and teens each year, with about 220 attending daily. The club will serve kids ages 6 to 18. For the Connors, however, the bigger story is the need they say exists in the surrounding community. 'People don't realize how big a need there is in West Palm Beach,' Mike Connors said. 'There are a lot of single families that need a lot of help, especially to get kids off the streets.' Inside the new facility are spaces designed for academics, recreation, the arts and career exploration. The club includes a gym and stage, academic center, cultural arts center, computer labs, dance studio, cafeteria, commercial kitchen, sound and recording studio, maker space and outdoor playground. Students will also have access to daily homework help and tutoring programs with certified teachers, along with STEM education, sports, health and fitness programs, cultural arts and leadership programs. For teens, the opportunities extend into career exploration and workforce readiness. They can get hands-on experience in areas such as robotics, health care, content creation, design and culinary arts while being introduced to potential college and career pathways. 'I can be a journalist, a content creator; I can do anything that's possible because we provide essential tools, systems and environment to help them grow,' said Pablo Tejada, Chief Impact Officer for the Boys Girls Club. entry.article_text: A new Boys & Girls Club officially opened its doors Tuesday in West Palm Beach, bringing a new place for hundreds of children and teens to learn, explore their interests and prepare for their futures.The Julie & Mike Connors Boys & Girls Club, located at 1150 Southern Blvd., celebrated its grand opening after years of planning.WATCH REPORT BELOW:"To have this come to fruition is more beautiful than I ever thought it could be," Julie Connors said during the celebration.The $17 million, 31,000-square-foot facility is the 21st location for the Boys & Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County and is expected to serve approximately 800 children and teens each year, with about 220 attending daily. Children will receive a snack and hot dinner after school. On full days, the club will provide breakfast, lunch and a snack.Membership costs $30 for a child to attend throughout the school year and summer, and scholarships are available to families who need financial assistance.

entry.title: Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team
entry.summary: The Indian River State College Board of Trustees has delayed taking action on a recommendation to eliminate the college's swimming and diving team. During a meeting held in Okeechobee, the board voted Tuesday to table the president's recommendation to eliminate the program. PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: IRSC swimmers react to possible elimination of program Swimmers rally to save IRSC swim and dive teams Instead, trustees asked the college administration to prepare a comprehensive report on the swimming and diving program. The board requested that the report include input from the community. The administration is expected to present the report at the Board of Trustees Nov. 17 meeting, when recommendations on how to move forward will be considered. This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. Former swimmer Ella Smith started a petition last week to save the program, which has more than 12,500 signatures.

entry.title: 15-year-old seriously injured after wrong-way crash following police pursuit in Stuart
entry.summary: A 15-year-old driver and another motorist were seriously injured early Tuesday after a police pursuit ended in a wrong-way crash on U.S. Highway 1, according to the Stuart Police Department. Police said officers were conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent at about 3:45 a.m. when they spotted a vehicle traveling north at what officers described as an extremely high rate of speed. An officer attempted to make a traffic stop, but police said the driver refused to stop and fled. The pursuit eventually continued onto U.S. 1, where police said the driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger posed to other motorists, according to the department. Police said officers also attempted to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway. The fleeing vehicle eventually collided with a vehicle traveling south at the Mall South Entrance intersection, police said. After the crash, officers learned the driver of the fleeing vehicle was 15 years old. Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce with serious injuries. The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident, while the Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash. Police said no additional information would be released at this time because the investigation remains ongoing.

entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - WPEC
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    WPEC
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own,” the district said in a statement. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. “Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves,” the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge’s family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge’s family be given privacy during this time. “We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss,” the district said. “Today and always, we stand together.” The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge , 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025. The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

entry.title: St. Lucie County honors firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge after line-of-duty death
entry.summary: St. Lucie County firefighters and community members gathered to honor firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, escorting him through the community he served after the fire district said he died Saturday and is being honored with a line-of-duty death designation. WATCH: St. Lucie County Honors Firefighter-Paramedic Austin Hodge St. Lucie County Honors Firefighter-Paramedic Austin Hodge | WPTV Hodge served the St. Lucie County Fire District for more than nine years. According to the district, he was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse during shift change. Firefighters escorted Hodge from the medical examiner's office to the funeral home as colleagues and community members paid their respects along his final journey through Fort Pierce. 'A bright light' Dr. Aleta Paschal, who worked alongside Hodge outside the fire district, described him as someone whose personality made an impression on those around him. 'Austin is just a bright light,' Paschal said. 'He always made me smile. He had the biggest bear hugs. Everybody loved him.' Paschal said Hodge had a way of making the people around him feel welcomed. 'Anybody he interacted with, he made you feel like family for sure,' she said. His service extended beyond the firehouse Hodge's work caring for people extended beyond his role as a firefighter-paramedic. Paschal said Hodge also worked as a respiratory therapist, where the two cared for critically ill patients together. 'Everybody loved him,' Paschal said. 'He was a critical part of our team. He's going to be very missed at the hospital.' Within the St. Lucie County Fire District, Hodge also served on the Honor Guard and the district's Firefighter Challenge Team. Those roles added to a legacy of service that spanned more than nine years with the district. Community says goodbye As Hodge's colleagues escorted him through Fort Pierce, Paschal said she hopes people remember the qualities that made him special to those who knew him. 'Remember his smile. entry.title: Seminole Ridge flag football eyes third straight state title
entry.summary: Greatness doesn't happen overnight; it takes countless hours and endless repetition. Over the past two years, the girls' flag football team at Seminole Ridge High School has won 37 games and lost only four, while winning two straight championships. WATCH BELOW: Seminole Ridge flag football eyes 3rd straight state title Seminole Ridge flag football eyes 3rd straight state title 'It's an amazing feeling that the girls are so hungry and into flag football. They love what they do and work so hard. It's really a joy to be the coach,' head coach Scott O'Hara said. His joy as a coach comes from having the best team in Florida. The girls are sure-handed, disciplined, and have fun while doing it. 'If we're too serious with the team, then it's going to be a lot of tension with the team, but adding the jokes and the calmness helps keep the balance between everything,' said Samantha Musgrave, the team captain. She knows the girls have a chance to win three straight titles, but takes it day by day. 'This upcoming season I expect for us to win some games. It's all about who puts in the most work, and I think our team puts in even more work than we need to, for sure,' said Musgrave. One reason the girls can let their hair down and be free is thanks to Chachi Saunders, but on the field she's a playmaker. From game-winning catches in the championship to leading the team in almost every statistical category, 17 interceptions last season, and even earning First Team All-Defensive honors. To cap it all off, she's the first flag footballer in Palm Beach County to commit to a Division I school for flag football. 'I didn't know this would ever happen, but I'm so proud and so happy to have all of my coaches to help me and my team being on my back,' said Saunders.

entry.article_text: WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday.In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater.WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong windsTerresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated."You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad," Baldwin said. "There were dead copperheads, so the snakes are coming out. They're getting flushed out with the water."Baldwin said she was also dealing with flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals.She showed WPTV the water over her dock and in her new patio."The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that," Baldwin said.Despite the water going down, she is still worried about what could happen in the next few days."The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see," Baldwin said. With high tide later Monday night, the sheriff’s office told WPTV the situation could get worse.Lt. Dave Rosko said they have three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged neighbors to think twice before driving through the water."Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters," Rosko said. "If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety."Rosko said neighbors living in coastal communities should be aware of future tides before traveling.

entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WPTV
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WPTV
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County."I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette.WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college footballWhile football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins."I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette.While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him."Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette.He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits."One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette.Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas.Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar."I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette.Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach."I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette.And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns.With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech."Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette.At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work."I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette.He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period.So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it."It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.

entry.title: Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team
entry.summary: The Indian River State College Board of Trustees has delayed taking action on a recommendation to eliminate the college's swimming and diving team. During a meeting held in Okeechobee, the board voted Tuesday to table the president's recommendation to eliminate the program. WATCH REPORT BELOW: IRSC trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming, diving team Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team Instead, trustees asked the college administration to prepare a comprehensive report on the swimming and diving program. The board requested that the report include input from the community. President Timothy Moore said at Tuesday's meeting that the proposal to cut the programs comes down to money. 'It's a tremendous opportunity to leave this college with that kind of skill, resource and talent here, but it comes at a price,' Moore said. The school president said the program currently costs around $1.4 to $2 million, money that isn't coming in through donations. 'What's required to maintain it as it sits today? We will require $15 to $20 million of an endowment to throw off enough revenue per year to sustain the program as it sits today,' Moore said. There's also a proposal to transition the remaining sports to Division II, resulting in potential savings of around $500,000. But if the swimming and diving program stays, Moore said the school may be forced to cut 50 percent for sports across the board. 'It's elimination of one or impose a penalty across all, and I would imagine that our championships will suffer because of that decision,' Moore said. entry.title: Frankel, Adeimy outline affordability priorities in race for Florida's redrawn 23rd congressional district
entry.summary: With just a week left until the General Election, the candidates vying for the newly redrawn 23rd congressional district in Florida sat down with WPTV morning anchor Hollani Davis to talk about their priorities for voters here at home if they're elected. U.S. Rep. Louis Frankel, D-Fla., is fighting to continue representing South Florida. She says affordability is at the top of her list to tackle. WATCH REPORT BELOW: District 23 candidates focus on affordability Candidates vying to represent Florida's 23rd District lay out priorities to tackle affordability 'When I'm at the supermarket, and people can't afford their food, that's a pretty big message,' says Frankel. Frankel, who is seeking an eighth term in Congress, says Democrats must seek to end the war with Iran and rein in the Trump administration's tariffs to help bring costs under control. She also says there is another glaring issue that can't be ignored. '(There's) probably nothing more important for the people of Palm Beach County, where we have a big senior population, is (the need) to protect Social Security and Medicare,' Frankel said. Challenging Frankel in the race is Deborah Adeimy. The Republican, is a native of Palm Beach County who's worked as a financial adviser to companies like Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan Chase. She says she'd use her financial acumen to help solve South Florida's affordable housing problem by rewriting the playbook. 'Currently in Palm Beach County, there are real estate developers who are taking advantage of antiquated tax incentives, tax breaks that are driving up costs here in Palm Beach County (including) rent,' says Adeimy. Florida's 23rd congressional district previously straddled the Palm Beach-Broward County line with a heavy focus on Broward County. After the districts were redrawn this year, it now covers a portion of West Palm Beach and extends south to include Boynton Beach.

entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - cw34.com
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County deputy accused of DUI in Vero Beach crash that injured woman and child    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff's deputy has been charged with DUI following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that left a woman seriously injured and her son hospitalized. The crash happened at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach. Investigators said Tyler Horstman, an off-duty St. Lucie County sheriff's detective, was driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV carrying a woman and her son. According to investigators, the SUV's driver ran a red light, while Horstman had a green light. All three individuals involved in the crash were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal. "Given the nature of the vehicles at a decent rate of speed, I mean, I don't want to say it worked out in its best. I mean, obviously injuries were still sustained, possibly long-lasting injuries, but at the end of the day, it's very feasible that a fatality could have occurred," Lt. Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, Horstman stated during his assessment that he had "a few beers" earlier in the evening. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Police also said the truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash. Horstman turned himself in on Monday. Police explained that the investigation took several months to complete. "It was a matter of investigators going through search warrants, subpoenas, and obtaining all different records," Kerensky said. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro, Horstman subsequently turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail and was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy. Sheriff Del Toro released this statement: "Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process," said Sheriff Richard R. "The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires." Horstman faces several charges, including DUI, and his arraignment is scheduled for Dec. "Our job is to investigate no matter who's involved, and we're going to do the due diligence to make sure what we do is right. At the end of the day, it happens to be a warrant was issued for Tyler Horstman," Kerensky said. entry.title: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff’s deputy turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued in connection with an off-duty crash in Vero Beach, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Read also: Road Ranger killed, hit at crash scene on I-95 near Lantana Road Deputy Tyler Horstman was driving an agency vehicle when he was involved in the crash on March 1, the sheriff’s office said. On September 9, the Sheriff’s Office received Horstman’s blood-test results. They showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit. According to the arrest report, March 1 at about 11:25pm at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach, Horstman was off-duty driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he hit a Chevy Equinox with a woman and an infant inside. The arrest report says: "Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening." It says Horstman had a "faint odor or alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and later posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WFLX
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WFLX
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. “I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan,” said Burnette. While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. “I wasn’t zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion,” said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. “Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do,” said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn’t receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. “One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited,” said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn’t on any other college football program’s radar. “I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team,” said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. “I spoke with the coach there and told him, ‘You guys offered me in high school,’ and he said, ‘I don’t really remember. Send me your film.’ He saw my film and said, ‘Hey, bring it,’” said Burnette. And he did “bring it.” In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. “Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out,” said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. “I called my dad and told him, ‘Hey, I need to do something. I can’t just sit here,’ so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan,” said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he’s making the most of it. “It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it’s a blessing,” said Burnette.

entry.article_text: WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday.In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater.WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong windsTerresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated."You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad," Baldwin said. entry.title: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County - WPEC
entry.summary: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County’s sea turtles broke a record. The county documented 14,083 nests as of Thursday, its highest total ever recorded. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen credits decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. This is actually a really big deal because what we’re seeing is decades of conservation paying off, Whalen said. But the record season is facing a rough finish. Powerful waves and high tides are eroding beaches, threatening some remaining nests. Loggerheads lead the record season The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. The total surpassed the previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Whalen. Loggerheads drove much of that increase. They’re dominating with 10,000 nests across our entire coastline, which is an insane number, Whalen said. The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests along its 22.4-mile coastline. If we mark 14,000 nests you wouldn’t have anywhere to sit on the beach, Whalen said. And like seriously it would be a sea of orange. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting turtles and their nesting beaches. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices. Rough surf threatens remaining nests A nor’easter and king tides have brought challenging conditions as nesting season winds down. Waves strip away sand, potentially exposing eggs buried beneath the beach. Unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. A lot of them have already hatched out, a lot of them have made it to the water safely, Whalen said. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween. Some nests may continue incubating beyond that date. Nesting numbers across the Treasure Coast Other counties also provided nesting figures. The totals cover different reporting dates and monitoring areas. Indian River County : As of Oct. 22, the county recorded 14,083 nests: 10,045 loggerhead, 3,970 green turtle and 68 leatherback nests. Lucie County : As of Sept. 30, the county recorded 10,239 nests: 9,111 loggerhead, 956 green turtle and 172 leatherback nests. Martin County: As of Sept. 28, its Hutchinson Island monitoring area recorded 4,874 nests: 4,532 loggerhead, 161 green turtle and 181 leatherback nests. Martin County’s figures cover approximately 7.5 miles of Hutchinson Island shoreline. That area stretches from the north side of St. Lucie Inlet to the Martin St. CBS12 News has requested Palm Beach County’s latest countywide figures from FWC and is awaiting those numbers. Boca Raton sees high nest counts, lower hatch success In Boca Raton, a strong nesting season did not translate into equally strong hatching results. David Anderson, sea turtle conservation coordinator at Gumbo Limbo Nature Center, reported the city’s third-highest nesting season. That included record counts of 1,118 loggerhead nests and 43 leatherback nests. But an average of only about 50% of the eggs in inventoried nests hatched. Anderson said a typical hatch rate would be 70% to 80% or more. He attributed some losses to prolonged hot, dry conditions during peak incubation. High sand temperatures can prevent embryos from continuing to develop. Storms and high tides also washed out approximately 185 nests, Anderson said. Predators affected another 13 nests. Artificial lighting created additional problems after hatching. Anderson said hatchlings from at least 85 nests became disoriented and headed into the dunes. Staff plan to evaluate beachfront lighting and work with nearby properties before next season. So sure, it’s sad to see so many hatchlings and eggs not fully developed, but once again, we had a great nesting season, Anderson said. So as long as the nesting numbers continue to climb, it gives us hope. What to do if you find eggs or hatchlings The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season. That strategy helps some nests survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may find exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC says to leave exposed eggs in place. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive, and people should not collect or rebury them. Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. Do not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches clean, flat and dark. Remove beach gear, fill holes, flatten sandcastles and keep lights off the beach at night.

entry.title: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff’s deputy turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued in connection with an off-duty crash in Vero Beach, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Read also: Road Ranger killed, hit at crash scene on I-95 near Lantana Road Deputy Tyler Horstman was driving an agency vehicle when he was involved in the crash on March 1, the sheriff’s office said. On September 9, the Sheriff’s Office received Horstman’s blood-test results. They showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit. According to the arrest report, March 1 at about 11:25pm at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach, Horstman was off-duty driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he hit a Chevy Equinox with a woman and an infant inside. Vero Beach police say Horstman was driving at 63 mph in a posted 35 mph zone and entered the intersection on a green light. The other driver entered the intersection against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital, and the infant was not injured. The arrest report says: "Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening." It says Horstman had a "faint odor of alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and later posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

entry.title: 15-year-old seriously injured after wrong-way crash following police pursuit in Stuart
entry.summary: A 15-year-old driver and another motorist were seriously injured early Tuesday after a police pursuit ended in a wrong-way crash on U.S. Highway 1, according to the Stuart Police Department. Police said officers were conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent at about 3:45 a.m. when they spotted a vehicle traveling north at what officers described as an extremely high rate of speed. An officer attempted to make a traffic stop, but police said the driver refused to stop and fled. The pursuit eventually continued onto U.S. 1, where police said the driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger posed to other motorists, according to the department. Police said officers also attempted to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway. The fleeing vehicle eventually collided with a vehicle traveling south at the Mall South Entrance intersection, police said. After the crash, officers learned the driver of the fleeing vehicle was 15 years old. Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce with serious injuries. The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident, while the Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash. Police said no additional information would be released at this time because the investigation remains ongoing.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County commissioners unanimously voted during a second public hearing to implement a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications, giving staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. During the hearing, every resident who spoke during public comment opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," said Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades. "I don’t want to spend another year or longer where somebody that I know is trying to do me great bodily harm. Folks, it’s in your hands. These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," said resident Richard Miller. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed there is an applicant for a data center. "One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. The application for the Florida Gateway Project was submitted on Oct. 12, with the first public hearing held the following day. "We got the information late on the Monday before the 13th ... so, I didn't have the information in advance of the 13th. At the meeting on the 13th, I disclosed to everybody that I had just found out about it. I'm sorry, Commissioner, we did alert the commission as soon as we could," said County Attorney Elysse A. "I understand, but somebody took the money on this date is what I'm trying to say. Doesn't anybody talk to anybody here?" Vargas said. The application will go through the development review process, which staff said is expected to take a year. Aside from this application, there are currently no other large-scale data center applications pending. entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - cw34.com
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - WPEC
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    WPEC
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.
