entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District is honoring the life and service of firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died Saturday while on duty. On Monday afternoon, firefighters escorted Hodge’s body from the medical examiner’s office to a funeral home in Fort Pierce. Tears, respect and a sense of loss were visible on the faces of those gathered to pay tribute. FIREFIGHTER MOURNED: Family honors late St. Lucie County firefighter’s birthday with cookout and balloon release His fellow firefighters, friends and members of the community came together to honor Hodge’s more than nine years of service. Diana Harrison, who has known Hodge’s mother since the early 1990s, shared her memories of him. “So, we actually homeschooled our kids together. Austin was just a little bitty guy back then,” Harrison said. Friends and coworkers expressed the heartbreak of losing Hodge, especially as his brother, Jarius Hodge, also a firefighter-paramedic with the St. Lucie County Fire District, died last year after falling ill while on duty. “I have no words, there’s no words, and the brokenness, the sadness — you can’t imagine losing not one son but two sons,” Harrison said. The fire district reported that Austin Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse during a shift change Saturday. Crews immediately began life-saving measures, but Hodge later died at the hospital. Lucie County Fire District holds procession for firefighter Austin Hodge Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Hodge joined the district’s firefighter challenge team in 2018 and helped the team win a world championship in 2021. "He was always a giver, even from a little bitty kid, you know. And if I remember right, even when he was a little kid, he wanted to be a firefighter, and then that's what he became," Harrison said. Howard Dunn Jr., founder of the Howard Dunn Jr. Foundation, which supports first responders, shared his personal connection to Hodge. “A couple of years ago I had a close call, and when the rescue came to me, I met Austin. I had an emergency; they transported me to the hospital. He made me feel better — I forgot what I was going for,” Dunn said. Retired lieutenant and former fire district chaplain Thomas Neiman reflected on the Hodge family’s impact on the community. “Knowing that we saw those kids as grade school kids in the library for our homeschool co-op meetings,” Neiman said. “And of course, we can’t begin to imagine what the family and mom and dad are going through, but we’re holding on to them as best we can, and they know we love them." entry.title: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County - WPEC
entry.summary: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County’s sea turtles broke a record. The county documented 14,083 nests as of Thursday, its highest total ever recorded. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen credits decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. This is actually a really big deal because what we’re seeing is decades of conservation paying off, Whalen said. But the record season is facing a rough finish. Powerful waves and high tides are eroding beaches, threatening some remaining nests. Loggerheads lead the record season The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. The total surpassed the previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Whalen. Loggerheads drove much of that increase. They’re dominating with 10,000 nests across our entire coastline, which is an insane number, Whalen said. The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests along its 22.4-mile coastline. If we mark 14,000 nests you wouldn’t have anywhere to sit on the beach, Whalen said. And like seriously it would be a sea of orange. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting turtles and their nesting beaches. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices. Rough surf threatens remaining nests A nor’easter and king tides have brought challenging conditions as nesting season winds down. Waves strip away sand, potentially exposing eggs buried beneath the beach. Unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. A lot of them have already hatched out, a lot of them have made it to the water safely, Whalen said. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween. Some nests may continue incubating beyond that date. Nesting numbers across the Treasure Coast Other counties also provided nesting figures. The totals cover different reporting dates and monitoring areas. Indian River County : As of Oct. 22, the county recorded 14,083 nests: 10,045 loggerhead, 3,970 green turtle and 68 leatherback nests. Lucie County : As of Sept. 30, the county recorded 10,239 nests: 9,111 loggerhead, 956 green turtle and 172 leatherback nests. Martin County: As of Sept. 28, its Hutchinson Island monitoring area recorded 4,874 nests: 4,532 loggerhead, 161 green turtle and 181 leatherback nests. Martin County’s figures cover approximately 7.5 miles of Hutchinson Island shoreline. That area stretches from the north side of St. Lucie Inlet to the Martin St. CBS12 News has requested Palm Beach County’s latest countywide figures from FWC and is awaiting those numbers. Boca Raton sees high nest counts, lower hatch success In Boca Raton, a strong nesting season did not translate into equally strong hatching results. David Anderson, sea turtle conservation coordinator at Gumbo Limbo Nature Center, reported the city’s third-highest nesting season. That included record counts of 1,118 loggerhead nests and 43 leatherback nests. But an average of only about 50% of the eggs in inventoried nests hatched. Anderson said a typical hatch rate would be 70% to 80% or more. He attributed some losses to prolonged hot, dry conditions during peak incubation. High sand temperatures can prevent embryos from continuing to develop. Storms and high tides also washed out approximately 185 nests, Anderson said. Predators affected another 13 nests. Artificial lighting created additional problems after hatching. Anderson said hatchlings from at least 85 nests became disoriented and headed into the dunes. Staff plan to evaluate beachfront lighting and work with nearby properties before next season. So sure, it’s sad to see so many hatchlings and eggs not fully developed, but once again, we had a great nesting season, Anderson said. So as long as the nesting numbers continue to climb, it gives us hope. What to do if you find eggs or hatchlings The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season. That strategy helps some nests survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may find exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC says to leave exposed eggs in place. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive, and people should not collect or rebury them. Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. Do not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches clean, flat and dark. Remove beach gear, fill holes, flatten sandcastles and keep lights off the beach at night.

Trump International Airport and Mar-a-Lago. The North American Aerospace Defense Command has said the deployment was made at the request of the U.S. Secret Service. What are the air defense systems? 'What you see here are three trailer-mounted anti-aircraft, anti-drone, actually even anti-vehicle defense systems,' Ingram told Hoffman. Ingram said the weapons are surface-to-air missile systems, commonly known as SAMs, and described them as a final layer of protection. 'This is the last line of defense that will eliminate the threat to the president of the United States,' Ingram said. entry.title: St. Lucie County deputy accused of DUI in Vero Beach crash that injured woman and child - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County deputy accused of DUI in Vero Beach crash that injured woman and child    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff's deputy has been charged with DUI following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that left a woman seriously injured and her son hospitalized. The crash happened at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach. Investigators said Tyler Horstman, an off-duty St. Lucie County sheriff's detective, was driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV carrying a woman and her son. According to investigators, the SUV's driver ran a red light, while Horstman had a green light. All three individuals involved in the crash were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal. "Given the nature of the vehicles at a decent rate of speed, I mean, I don't want to say it worked out in its best. I mean, obviously injuries were still sustained, possibly long-lasting injuries, but at the end of the day, it's very feasible that a fatality could have occurred," Lt. Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, Horstman stated during his assessment that he had "a few beers" earlier in the evening. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Police also said the truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash. Horstman turned himself in on Monday. Police explained that the investigation took several months to complete. "It was a matter of investigators going through search warrants, subpoenas, and obtaining all different records," Kerensky said. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro, Horstman subsequently turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail and was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy. Sheriff Del Toro released this statement: "Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process," said Sheriff Richard R. "The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires." Horstman faces several charges, including DUI, and his arraignment is scheduled for Dec. "Our job is to investigate no matter who's involved, and we're going to do the due diligence to make sure what we do is right. At the end of the day, it happens to be a warrant was issued for Tyler Horstman," Kerensky said. entry.title: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff’s deputy turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued in connection with an off-duty crash in Vero Beach, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Read also: Road Ranger killed, hit at crash scene on I-95 near Lantana Road Deputy Tyler Horstman was driving an agency vehicle when he was involved in the crash on March 1, the sheriff’s office said. On September 9, the Sheriff’s Office received Horstman’s blood-test results. They showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit. According to the arrest report, March 1 at about 11:25pm at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach, Horstman was off-duty driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he hit a Chevy Equinox with a woman and an infant inside. Vero Beach police say Horstman was driving at 63 mph in a posted 35 mph zone and entered the intersection on a green light. The other driver entered the intersection against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital, and the infant was not injured. The arrest report says: "Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening." It says Horstman had a "faint odor of alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and later posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

entry.summary: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides flooded streets and reached homes across Palm Beach County on Monday, while beach and road closures were reported as more high tides were expected through Wednesday. In Palm City, flooding made SW Dyer Point Road impassable. Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies brought in three high-water vehicles to help reach anyone stranded in a vehicle or home. Flooding also was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. One driver told CBS12 the water was about waist-deep in part of the area. Resident Terresa Baldwin said water came up around both the front and back of her home, and that Monday’s flooding was the worst she had seen in eight years. Baldwin also raised concerns about the water’s source and smell. This is not only runoff water, it’s sewage and it’s bad and you can smell it, she said. Deputies urged people to avoid flooded areas and not to drive through standing water. These vehicles can travel through several feet of water safely, Martin County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Flooding also reached Flagler Drive in downtown West Palm Beach and Sunset Avenue on Palm Beach Island, where water covered parts of the roadway and disrupted pedestrians and cyclists. In Boynton Beach, flooding led to road closures, including at Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. The Ocean Inlet Marina also closed because of high tides. In Boca Raton, water reached a Cub Scout pack’s campsite at Spanish River Park, prompting campers to move supplies to higher ground. Elsewhere, Midtown Beach was temporarily closed because of large surf and high tides. The northbound lane of South Ocean Boulevard between Chilean and Australian avenues was scheduled to close from 10 a.m. to noon while crews moved a lifeguard tower. Delray Beach officials raised red flags because of high surf and flooding, and the Juno Beach Pier remained closed because of damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf. See also: 15-year-old FAMU shooting suspect ordered to be held as prosecutors seek adult charges A coastal flood warning covers low-lying areas near the water in Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The National Weather Service said the warning runs through 8 p.m. Wednesday in coastal Palm Beach County and 2 a.m. Thursday in coastal Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The forecast high tides were: Monday: 9:06 p.m. The sheriff’s office advised residents not to drive through floodwater and to call 911 if they need emergency assistance.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County commissioners unanimously voted during a second public hearing to implement a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications, giving staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. During the hearing, every resident who spoke during public comment opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," said Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades. "I don’t want to spend another year or longer where somebody that I know is trying to do me great bodily harm. Folks, it’s in your hands. These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," said resident Richard Miller. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed there is an applicant for a data center. "One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. The application for the Florida Gateway Project was submitted on Oct. 12, with the first public hearing held the following day. "We got the information late on the Monday before the 13th ... so, I didn't have the information in advance of the 13th. At the meeting on the 13th, I disclosed to everybody that I had just found out about it. I'm sorry, Commissioner, we did alert the commission as soon as we could," said County Attorney Elysse A. "I understand, but somebody took the money on this date is what I'm trying to say. Doesn't anybody talk to anybody here?" Vargas said. The application will go through the development review process, which staff said is expected to take a year. Aside from this application, there are currently no other large-scale data center applications pending. Austin Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse early Saturday and was taken to a hospital, according to information provided to his family. He later died. His family told WPTV they do not yet know what happened. The feeling is unbearable, his sister, Alexis Hodge, told WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache during an exclusive interview. Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austins home as they remembered a brother they described as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Hes strong. Hes fun. Hes caring. Hes smart. Its so much, Alexis said. Family says Austin appeared normal hours before his death Alexis said the family has been told Austin appeared to be himself in the hours before he was found unresponsive. It’s so much,” Alexis said.Family says Austin appeared normal hours before his deathAlexis said the family has been told Austin appeared to be himself in the hours before he was found unresponsive. entry.title: Interactive: How the midterms could shape the future of Social Security
entry.summary: Social Security faces a funding deadline in 2032. The senators elected this year could help decide what happens next. See why your midterm vote matters in our interactive story.
entry.article_text: Verdict: false Former Social Security Commissioner Martin O Malley was explicit: every current beneficiary could face a 20% reduction in benefits if Congress doesn t act. The cut applies across the board — retirees, disabled recipients, and survivors. Verdict: true O Malley cited polling showing that eliminating or altering the Social Security tax cap is supported by over 80% of people — making it one of the rare proposals with genuine cross-partisan backing. Verdict: false The 1980s presented a similar moment, and Congress ultimately reached a deal — though not until the deadline was just months away. That precedent cuts both ways: a fix is possible, but it may not come early. A report from the Trump administration found that lower fertility rates, higher deportations, and tax changes have contributed to fewer dollars flowing into Social Security. The finding is notable because it ties specific policy decisions — not just demographic trends — to the program s funding pressures.

entry.title: Trump jokes about Ted Cruz Supreme Court nomination on campaign trail
entry.summary: President Donald Trump is crisscrossing the campaign trail in the final days before the midterm elections, making stops in Texas, Ohio and South Carolina as Republicans fight to hold key seats. Trump campaigned in Texas on Tuesday, where Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton is locked in a competitive race against Democrat James Talarico. While there, Trump also took time to talk about another prominent Texas Republican, Sen. Ted Cruz. Trump joked that Cruz would be an easy choice to confirm if a seat opened on the U.S. Supreme Court. I would pick Ted Cruz to be the next Supreme Court justice, Trump said. And I wouldnt have to worry about, I wouldnt even have to make a phone call. Trump went on to joke that Cruz would receive unanimous support for an unusual reason. RELATED STORY | Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challenges The Democrats will 100% vote for it because they hate the guy and they want to get rid of him, Trump said. And the Republicans would 100% vote for it because they cant stand him. They would like to get rid of him. So Id get 100% of the vote. Trumps Texas appearance was part of a late campaign push aimed at turning out Republican voters ahead of Election Day. He also focused on energy policy, announcing a move to loosen methane rules for oil and gas producers. Trump said the change would save consumers and energy producers $45 billion and unlock an additional 210 million barrels of oil. The president is scheduled to campaign Wednesday in Chillicothe, Ohio, marking his third visit to the state this month. Republicans are trying to defend a Senate seat against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is seeking a return to Washington. Trump is then expected to turn his attention to South Carolina, where he plans to campaign Thursday in Rock Hill. The traditionally Republican state has drawn increased attention after a New York Times poll showed the Senate race tied at 48% between Democrat Annie Andrews and Republican Sen. Darlene Graham. entry.title: The new renter is getting older
entry.summary: Renting a place to live isn't just for the young anymore. According to a 2026 analysis by Realtor.com , the typical family renter household is headed by a 42-year-old. The data also shows today's long-term renter is 55 years old, with a median household income of $48,500. Experts say for some households, staying in the same rental property is more about affordability and not just preference. However, the dream of homeownership hasn't disappeared. The same research shows around 65% of renters would like to own a home if they had the financial means. WATCH: The new renter is getting older The new renter is getting older Home warranty specialists 'Cinch Home Services' released a list this month of the states where it takes the longest to save for a home down payment. Florida ranks number 5 behind Hawaii, California, Montana and New York. In Florida, the study found it takes about 3.5 years to save up for a 15% down payment of $56,320 for a home valued around the median price of $375,470. Based on these figures, a potential homeowner in Florida would need to save about $1,341 a month. The analysis accounted for household earnings, factoring in the state's median income and the earnings that remain after paying rent, groceries, health care costs and transportation. Across the country, the estimated time to save for a home down payment is around two years and nine months, based on monthly savings of approximately $1,692. Cinch Services asked for a credit. There is nothing that ties directly to this study, but here is their website that was provided in the press release.

entry.title: Heart Walk aims to spread an important message on heart health
entry.summary: WTPV is the proud media sponsor of the American Heart Association 2026 Palm Beach Heart Walk, and we'd like to invite everyone to join the important community gathering! WPTV morning anchor Ashley Glass is glad to emcee the Heart Walk for a second year. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Heart Walk aims to spread an important message on heart health Glass spoke with one of the event's co-chairs, Marilyn Spunar, CFO of TBC Corporation, and asked whether sharing her personal journey with heart health could impact others. 'Yes,' Spunar said. 'Its opening your heart. People are inspired, and I think more people than we know have a personal history with heart disease.' Another co-chair, Bill Schafer, Chief Revenue Officer at TBC Corporation, echoed the Heart Walk's importance. 'It helps the entire community,' he said. 'When you think of nine out of ten people who suffer a cardiac incident outside the hospital dont survive, the ability for us to have the funding to train people for CPR so that we can, one, take care of the community but also take care of ourselves and our loved ones is essential.' The Heart Walk is Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, at Meyer Amphitheater in West Palm Beach. To donate, register with an existing team or sign up a new one, visit here .

entry.title: Murray Middle School breaks ground on $33 million rebuild after Hurricane Milton damage
entry.summary: Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million phase of its campus rebuild after Hurricane Milton spawned a tornado that damaged three main buildings , forcing students and school programs into portable classrooms, according to Martin County school officials. District leaders said improvements to Murray Middle School were already planned, but the hurricane damage added urgency to the project. The new construction will include learning and performing arts spaces, while the school's gym will also be renovated. WATCH: Murray Middle is rebuilding after Hurricane Milton. Murray Middle Begins $33M Rebuild After Hurricane Milton | WPTV Students and staff gathered for a groundbreaking marking the next step in a rebuilding process that has required them to adapt while parts of their campus remain unavailable. Students adapt after hurricane damage For Murray Middle student Nicholas Lowe, the transition meant adjusting to a different learning environment. 'It was a big change, but also I had to adapt to it to, like, be better for the choir,' Lowe said. Choir was among the programs that lost permanent space following Hurricane Milton. Dr. Anita Caswell, Murray Middle School's choir and drama director, said the storm destroyed decades of materials used by her programs. 'It was 60 years of drama props,' Caswell said. 'Our dresses were in that, the boys' vest that we used to sing in, and just to see it all mangled and stuck up on the wall, it just hurt.' Despite losing their old space, Caswell said her students continued singing in a portable classroom. 'Is it the best place to sing in? No, but we adapt,' Caswell said, adding that the choir received straight superior ratings that year 'even in the small portable.' entry.title: Surface-to-air missile systems deployed near Trump airport, Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach
entry.summary: New surface-to-air missile systems have been deployed in Palm Beach as part of expanded security around President Donald Trump, with air defense assets visible near Donald J. Trump International Airport and Mar-a-Lago. The North American Aerospace Defense Command has said the deployment was made at the request of the U.S. Secret Service. WATCH: Surface-to-air missiles deployed in Palm Beach Surface-to-air missile systems deployed near Trump airport, Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach The new equipment is attracting attention from people traveling around the airport and near the president's private club. WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman spoke with aviation experts Dewitt Ingram and Matthew 'Whiz' Buckley about what the systems are designed to do and the types of threats they can counter. What are the air defense systems? 'What you see here are three trailer-mounted anti-aircraft, anti-drone, actually even anti-vehicle defense systems,' Ingram told Hoffman. Ingram said the weapons are surface-to-air missile systems, commonly known as SAMs, and described them as a final layer of protection. 'This is the last line of defense that will eliminate the threat to the president of the United States,' Ingram said. Hoffman also sat down with Buckley, a decorated former U.S. Navy fighter pilot and graduate of the Navy's elite TOPGUN flight school. 'I'm surprised those SAMs haven't been there longer,' Buckley said. Buckley said the systems are capable of defending against more than conventional aircraft. 'It's anti-aircraft, anti-drone, anti-anything that's a potential threat,' he said. Buckley identified some of the equipment visible near the airport as Avenger systems carrying Stinger missiles. WPTV's independent reporting has also identified Avenger short-range air defense systems among the equipment deployed in the area. 'It looks like there are a couple Avenger batteries, which are Stinger missiles, and there's four on each side, so a total of eight,' Buckley told Hoffman. 'I think they might have .50-caliber machine guns on those weapons too.' The developments come amid heightened airspace security around Palm Beach when Trump is in the area.NORAD conducted a planned air defense exercise over Palm Beach on Oct. 14 involving F-16s and Civil Air Patrol aircraft. The command said it routinely uses exercises involving scenarios such as airspace violations, hijackings and unknown aircraft to test its responses, systems and equipment. NORAD also reported an F-16 intercept of an aircraft that violated temporary flight restrictions near Palm Beach on Oct. The latest deployment comes months after WPTV spoke with Buckley about an anti-drone laser defense system at the airport.Buckley told Hoffman then, and maintains now, that one threat deserves particular attention: drone swarms."Most people have seen the movie 'Miracle on the Hudson' with (Capt. Chesley 'Sully' Sullenberger) landing the U.S. "That's what a flock of birds did to a couple of engines. What do you think a flock of drones — inexpensive, cheap drones — are going to do in front of an airliner?""I'm shocked that we haven't lost an airliner yet due to a drone swarm," he added.For Buckley, the type of technology being deployed is less important than having defenses capable of responding to potential threats."Whether it's directed-energy weapons, laser or an Avenger missile battery, I think, you know, the president's safety is pretty important," Buckley said.The military has not publicly disclosed how long the air defense systems will remain deployed around Mar-a-Lago. entry.title: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development
entry.summary: By a 4-0 vote, commissioners in Martin County on Tuesday unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities. This was the second reading after commissioners moved forward with the moratorium during a meeting held Oct. 13. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development Tuesday's vote comes after Martin County recently received an application to build its first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. That application is for the construction of a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. However, because the application was submitted before the moratorium, it will not be affected by Tuesday's vote. The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development.

entry.title: Palm Beach Co. voters to decide whether to renew school tax funding teacher pay, safety and student programs
entry.summary: Palm Beach County voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to renew an existing 1-mill property tax for public schools for four more years, continuing funding for teacher pay, school safety, mental health services and student programs through June 30, 2031. The referendum is a renewal, not a new tax. According to the School District of Palm Beach County, the 1-mill levy has supported local schools since 2019. Voters approved the levy in 2018 and renewed it in 2022. If approved again, the measure would take effect July 1, 2027, after the current authorization expires, and automatically end June 30, 2031. What would the Palm Beach County school referendum fund? The ballot language says money from the tax would be dedicated to school safety, school police, mental health services, arts, music, physical education, career and choice program teachers, and improved teacher pay. An independent committee of citizens and experts would oversee the funds. According to the district, half of the funding currently supports teacher salary supplements, while 25% supports more than 900 career and choice, arts, music and other specialized teaching positions. The remaining 25% supports mental health services, school police and security staff. Students speak out in support Some students who are too young to cast ballots are speaking in support of the referendum and highlighting the impact they believe the measure has on their schools. 'Teacher issues are everybody's issues,' referendum supporter Sawyer Tinsley told WPTV. Tinsley said the issue extends beyond what students experience inside the classroom. 'It goes much further than just high school and high school education. It really impacts our future and the future of our country,' Tinsley said. What happens if the referendum fails? The School District of Palm Beach County says the local funding currently provides teachers salary supplements averaging about $8,000 annually. The money also funds more than 900 teaching positions in areas including art, music and physical education. According to the district, those teaching positions and programs would face cuts without the funding. The League of Women Voters of Palm Beach County's referendum synopsis also states that if voters reject the measure, teachers would face an average $8,000 annual reduction in pay and more than 900 teaching positions in the arts, physical education and choice programs would be eliminated. The remaining 25% supports mental health services, school police and security staff. Some students who are too young to cast ballots are speaking in support of the referendum and highlighting the impact they believe the measure has on their schools."Teacher issues are everybody's issues," referendum supporter Sawyer Tinsley told WPTV.Tinsley said the issue extends beyond what students experience inside the classroom."It goes much further than just high school and high school education. It really impacts our future and the future of our country," Tinsley said.The School District of Palm Beach County says the local funding currently provides teachers salary supplements averaging about $8,000 annually. The money also funds more than 900 teaching positions in areas including art, music and physical education. According to the district, those teaching positions and programs would face cuts without the funding. The League of Women Voters of Palm Beach County's referendum synopsis also states that if voters reject the measure, teachers would face an average $8,000 annual reduction in pay and more than 900 teaching positions in the arts, physical education and choice programs would be eliminated.Ultimately, Palm Beach County voters will determine whether the existing levy continues for another four years when they cast their ballots Nov. 3.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: USAA auto insurance rates dropping for nearly 500,000 Florida policies
entry.summary: Nearly half a million USAA auto insurance policies in Florida are set to see lower rates after state regulators approved a series of reductions, according to the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation. Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky approved several auto insurance program rate decreases for USAA Group that average 7%. The changes affect more than 498,000 policies across the state. Individual policyholders could see different savings depending on their program. According to the state, average rate changes range from a decrease of 0.4% to as much as 11.2%. USAA has its highest concentration of Florida business in Brevard, Escambia and Okaloosa counties. Average decreases in those counties are 5.8% in Brevard, 8% in Escambia and 8.4% in Okaloosa. 'The Office of Insurance Regulation is constantly reaching out to insurers to inquire about rate relief, and USAA is always stepping up to the plate and looking out for their consumers,' Yaworsky said in the release. He encouraged other insurers to consider additional rate reductions. Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia pointed to the reductions as another sign of improvement in the state's insurance market and credited Florida's tort reforms. 'These auto insurance rate decreases will help Florida families keep more of their hard-earned money in their pockets, especially our military families,' Ingoglia said. The latest reductions follow other savings announced by USAA over the past year. According to the release, the company provided nearly $1 billion in rate reductions and direct member returns to Florida members between December 2025 and July 2026. That included a $500 million dividend distributed to approximately 830,000 members. State regulators also said Florida's five largest auto insurance groups are showing a combined indicated rate change of negative 12.6% for 2026. Those companies represent 81% of Florida's auto insurance market, according to the release. The state also reported that Florida had the nation's lowest personal auto liability loss ratio in 2025 at 52.5%, its lowest level in 15 years.

entry.title: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving?
entry.summary: If you're traveling for Thanksgiving, one question could significantly affect your holiday budget: Is it cheaper to fly or drive? The answer can depend on where you're going, how many people are traveling, and when you plan to leave and return. Travelers we spoke with were divided. WATCH: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving? Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving? 'It depends where you're going,' Leticia Rivera said. 'But I would say fly right now.' Others would rather stay on the road. 'For the preference, regardless of pricing, drive,' Erik Eliassen said. 'Oh, definitely drive,' Calvin Landau added. Carol Baxter, meanwhile, has already made her decision: 'I'm flying.' Airfare can add up quickly for families According to Hopper data provided for this story, the average domestic round-trip flight for Thanksgiving is currently about $402 per person, compared with $307 last year. For a family of four, four tickets at the $402 average would total about $1,608 in airfare alone, before adding other potential travel expenses. Driving can look very different because everyone in the vehicle shares expenses such as fuel. Using the example in our comparison, the driving cost is about $160. That means families should consider the total cost of the trip rather than simply comparing the price of one plane ticket with one tank of gas. Your return date could make a big difference For people planning to fly, choosing a different return date could also affect the cost. Hopper data provided for this story shows a round trip with a return on the Sunday after Thanksgiving averaging about $604. Returning on Monday or Tuesday, however, could bring that average down to around $350. That's a difference of roughly $254 per ticket. For a family of four, that difference could potentially add up to more than $1,000. The bottom line There isn't one answer that works for every Thanksgiving traveler. Flying may save time on a long-distance trip, while driving can make the cost easier to spread across several people traveling together. Before booking, compare the total cost for everyone traveling, including airfare or fuel and any additional expenses associated with the trip. Also consider whether changing your travel dates could bring down the price. For families in particular, doing the math on the entire trip could make a significant difference in the Thanksgiving travel budget.

And then we’re going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”Both Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would "be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of U.S. military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. While saying the Trump administration wants to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the U.S. could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.Moments after Trump spoke at the rally, Rubio posted on social media that “now is the time” for action on Cuba, addressing his post “to those who seek to create positive change” and urging them “to seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.”Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a Sept. 29 interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. entry.title: A pumpkin wonderland in the Florida sunshine: Inside the fall fun at Bedner's Farm
entry.summary: Just outside Boynton Beach, Bedner's Farm offers a little bit of country, a whole lot of fall fun and a reminder that autumn magic doesn't require chilly weather. Fall fun in the Florida sunshine: Inside Bedner's Farm near Boynton Beach At the family-owned South Florida staple tucked away in west Boynton Beach, even the goats get in on the hospitality. According to Judi Brooker, who has been sharing the farm's charm with visitors for more than a decade, they're a crowd favorite. 'They're so soft, and everybody loves the goats,' Brooker said. I mentioned that the little kids probably love them. 'And by little kids, everybody under the age of 100,' Brooker joked. Bedner's is one of South Florida's last family-owned markets, with a farming legacy that stretches back generations. 'A lot of people don't realize there is life in west Boynton off 441,' Brooker said. 'I know I live here!' More than 50 years ago, Arthur and Henrietta Bedner brought their Pennsylvania farming roots to South Florida, trading harsh winters for a warmer climate and new opportunities. 'They came from farming families in Pennsylvania, but they'd had enough of the winter,' Brooker said. The family began farming in the area in the mid-20th century before purchasing the property that would become home to the farm visitors know today. Their mission remains simple: grow fresh, flavorful produce that's affordable, too. And there's plenty growing here. The farm grows about 60 crops, including tomatoes, corn, strawberries, broccoli, kale, lettuce, cauliflower, peppers and zucchini. The farm also grows sunflowers, adding a splash of color to the agricultural landscape. October is one of the best months to visit. Fall at Bedner's means family outings, festive photo opportunities and plenty of seasonal fun. 'It's a day full of fun. Bring the family, cousins, aunties, grandmas it's great,' Brooker said. One of the biggest attractions is finding the perfect pumpkin. 'We have this beautiful greenery and all the pumpkins on top,' Brooker said. 'It's just a pumpkin wonderland.' Pumpkins aren't the only seasonal stars. Visitors can also spot an assortment of colorful gourds, adding even more variety to the fall display from the popping orange of the pumpkins to the golden glow of the sunflower fields. Those cheerful blooms also play an important role in the farm's ecosystem. Bedner's keeps beehives on the property, recognizing the essential role pollinators play in agriculture. entry.article_text: Fall at Bedner's means family outings, festive photo opportunities and plenty of seasonal fun."It's a day full of fun. Bring the family, cousins, aunties, grandmas — it's great," Brooker said.One of the biggest attractions is finding the perfect pumpkin."We have this beautiful greenery and all the pumpkins on top," Brooker said. "It's just a pumpkin wonderland."Pumpkins aren't the only seasonal stars. Visitors can also spot an assortment of colorful gourds, adding even more variety to the fall display — from the popping orange of the pumpkins to the golden glow of the sunflower fields.Those cheerful blooms also play an important role in the farm's ecosystem. Bedner's keeps beehives on the property, recognizing the essential role pollinators play in agriculture."We do have hives on the farm because the honeybee is the farmer's best friend," Brooker said.It's a reminder that behind the colorful fields and family-friendly attractions, there's a working farm where growing food and caring for the land go hand in hand.For a closer look at the operation, visitors can climb aboard one of the farm's tractor rides, which take you around all 80 acres of Bedner's. The ride offers more than a scenic tour. It's a glimpse into the technology and planning that keep the farm productive in South Florida's challenging climate.Tall crops help protect other plants from the wind, while drip irrigation delivers water directly where it's needed — helping keep the fields hydrated through changing weather conditions.The farm has a long agricultural history to match its modern techniques."Palm Beach County was once known as the winter produce capital of the United States," Brooker said.That legacy is still visible in the fields, where agriculture remains at the heart of the experience.Of course, no fall adventure would be complete without a corn maze — and at Bedner's, finding the exit is easier said than done. Each year brings a new maze to explore, with twists, turns and a few surprises along the way.The maze comes with its own cast of characters, including the occasional zombie and a few strategically placed scarecrows."Sometimes we have some zombie friends along the way," Brooker said.There may be a few spooky sights, but the experience is designed to be more playful than frightening. Still, the maze comes with its share of wrong turns and dead ends, but after plenty of backtracking, the exit finally comes into view.After all that walking, exploring and navigating the maze, there's only one thing left to do: cool off with a sweet treat.At Bedner's, the fall experience is about more than pumpkins and photo ops. It's about spending time outdoors, learning a little about where food comes from, and making memories with family and friends.And the best part? You can soak up all those autumn vibes without bundling up for cold weather. Because at Bedner's Farm, fall magic comes with sunshine, fresh air and just a little bit of Florida flair.Watch "Finding Florida" each Sunday at 10 a.m.

entry.title: Martin County parents win push for school zone outside Citrus Grove Elementary
entry.summary: Martin County parents are celebrating a victory in a long battle to improve safety around their children's school. Citrus Grove Elementary School parents say the 45 mph speed limit outside the school puts their children's safety in jeopardy. They say a recently approved school zone is the first step to making Newfield Parkway a safer place for children who walk to school. On Southwest Newfield Parkway, morning and afternoon traffic is an obstacle for young students. 'It scares me,' parent Kendall George said. 'These cars are driving 45 miles an hour plus.' Kendall is among the many families who live in the Canopy Creek community across the street from Citrus Grove Elementary, so their children walk to school. Kelly Ribaudo, the PTA president and Martin County PTA Advocacy Chair, told WPTV she's spent the last five years asking the county to put in a school zone. 'We've had so many near misses with the kids just from people not paying attention,' Ribaudo said. 'Everyone has a right to a free and public education and they should be safe getting there. Our main priority should be the kids not the traffic.' At the previous Martin County Commission meeting, commissioners unanimously answered their call. 'Whatever the number is there is no price to someone getting hurt,' Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi said. 'You will absolutely get a school zone.' School Principal Rose Rynca told WPTV the need is greater than ever, with enrollment growing as new communities pop up in the area. 'The amount of students crossing Newfield Parkway has definitely increased,' Rynca said. 'This speed zone is going to really really improve the safety of students.' entry.title: WHERE'S WALTER? Having a day of discovery at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast
entry.summary: This week, I visited a place where learning and fun go hand in hand: the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast. From the moment I walked in, I could tell this wasn't your typical museum. Instead of looking at exhibits from behind a rope or glass case, kids are encouraged to jump in, get involved and learn by doing. As I explored the museum, I discovered exhibits designed to teach important life skills in creative and engaging ways. From learning about money and budgeting to exploring different careers and practicing job skills, every corner of the museum offered a new opportunity to learn something useful. WATCH: WHERE'S WALTER? Discovering the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast One of my favorite stops, of course, involved the weather. As a meteorologist, I was excited to check out the museum's WPTV weather simulator and hurricane simulator. entry.title: Year-long bridge closure in southern Martin County forces drivers onto detour, adds minutes to commutes
entry.summary: A major road closure is now in effect in southern Martin County, where the bridge at Southeast County Line Road is closed for a year-long reconstruction project. The detour could add several minutes to daily drives, so officials are urging commuters to plan ahead or find an alternate route. George May lives just off Southeast County Line Road, where a road block is now notifying drivers to turn around. 'It'll be inconvenient, for sure. People commuting to work and people that live in little club,' May said. May said the road closure is going to take some getting used to. 'I already drive over an hour to work everyday. It'll probably add about 20 minutes to my commute,' May said. Martin County says the bridge will be closed for a year, with a lot of work ahead. 'There are a lot of utilities ther,' Mark Aveni, Martin County public works deputy director, said. 'There's a lot of coordination that needs to occur. We're removing a pedestrian bridge and we're going to repurpose that somewhere else and unfortunately these things just take time.' Despite the closure, residents say they're glad to see the investment. 'There were large cracks under the bridge. It was deteriorating,' May said. 'It's a little bit of an inconvenience but I'm happy for that to have a new bridge and have better infrastructure in the area,' Daniel Von said. Six of the project's $7 million price tag is covered by state and federal grants. The new bridge will be two feet higher and built to be safer and more resilient. 'We're replacing it with a very resilient type of rebar that's going to be safer. There is a very sharp curve before that bridge, we're going to totally eliminate that and soften the curve. It'll also be much safer for pedestrians,' Aveni said. Residents are now hoping the project will go on without delays. 'I'm fine with it as long as they keep the project on schedule,' May said. entry.title: Man exercising at night critically injured in hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie, man arrested, police say
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie police (PSLPD) said it has arrested a person in connection with an Oct. 9 hit-and-run crash that injured a 63-year-old man. The crash happened at around 12:56 a.m. near NW University Boulevard and NW California Boulevard. 'Our officers that work night we're used to seeing him out exercising in the evening and he was known to jog, walk in the street medians,' Chief Leo Niemczyk said. The victim was identified through information on his Garmin watch and traced back to his home. PSLPD said the man was found unconscious in the roadway with severe head injuries, was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, and remains in critical condition.' Watch report: Man exercising at night critically injured in hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie, man arrested: Officials Detectives reviewed surveillance video and additional evidence, identified Eric Saint Aude, 60, as a suspect, and arrested him, PSLPD said. He was arrested for leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury.

entry.summary: WPTV had the rare opportunity to go inside the St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant on Thursday. This year, the facility is celebrating 50 years of operation and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission just granted licenses for 20 more.   On Thursday, WPTV learned about operations inside the plant and spoke with people who keep the power on. 'My job is to calibrate and make sure all the equipment used to work on the equipment that controls the reactor itself meets all the government standards and accuracies.' Phillips said hes been working at the plant for nearly 20 years. 'You have million-dollar homes right down the street. We're here, but yet we're still invisible because what we do, we do it well, .Phillips said.   Alfreds son, Alfred Sinclair Phillips, followed his father's footsteps and works in the operations department. 'There's a pressure with it, but there's also a sense of pride, Phillips said. Knowing that my dad has worked his butt off and he's left an impact with the people here on his work to make this place better. WPTV learned from Carlos Santos, site vice president, how the plant generates power. 'The simplest way to put it is the reactor creates the heat,' Santos said. Santos said that heat comes from nuclear fission from uranium pellets stacked into rods inside the two units on site. The heat from the rods builds up and produces steam, which travels into a secondary closed system into a turbine, which then generates power and produces electricity for the grid. entry.title: 2 vehicles sought in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run investigation, police say
entry.summary: The Port St. Lucie Police Department has released new information in its investigation of a hit-and-run crash that left a 63-year-old man seriously injured earlier this month on Oct. 9. Detectives now believe the victim may have been hit by two separate vehicles near the intersection of Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard. According to police, one vehicle was traveling northbound while the other was traveling southbound at the time of the incident. The crash occurred at approximately 12:56 a.m and the victim, a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, was found unconscious in the roadway suffering from severe head injuries. In a previous update, police said surveillance video from a nearby business captured the incident and showed what investigators believed to be a white four-door sedan striking the man before leaving the scene without stopping. As detectives continued reviewing evidence and surveillance footage, investigators developed information indicating a second vehicle may also have been involved in the crash. Police are now working to identify both vehicles and their drivers. Investigators have released images of the vehicles and are asking for the public's help. Anyone who recognizes either vehicle, was in the area around the time of the crash, witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or surveillance video from the area is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

entry.title: High surf and red flag warnings put St. Lucie County beaches under high hazard advisory this week
entry.summary: A red flag warning was cautioning swimmers about dangerous surf at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park, where waves between four and six feet we're crashing along the shoreline Wednesday. Fort Pierce Inlet State Park was among several beaches in St. Lucie County under a red flag high hazard warning. The conditions are tied to a low pressure system off the eastern U.S. coast in the mid-Atlantic. 'The sea was angry today my friends,' Fort Pierce resident Lee Bertucelli said. St. Lucie County Ocean Rescue says conditions like these make it more important than ever to swim at a lifeguarded beach. There are two in St. Lucie County, at Pepper Park and Waveland Beach. Officials say both will likely be flying red or double red flags for the next few days. 'It was very windy and very choppy and it's really challenging because you have to negotiate all of the chop,' foil surfer Lisa Rose said. 'I went in, not with my surfboard, but like, to my waist and it's just, it's rough and it's just not super safe for like I'm sort of a beginner so not safe for me, but like, some of the other surfers have definitely been out,' surfer Jodi Riley said. 'I went in, you know, not too far. The waves were fun, but again not too far, didn't want to deal with rip tides or anything else,' Bertucelli said. The county says rip currents are possible in these conditions. If you find yourself stuck in one, Ocean Rescue says don't panic and swim parallel with the shoreline. entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board votes to terminate Chief Jeff Lee after hazing fallout
entry.summary: In a 4-3 vote, the St. Lucie County Fire Board voted Wednesday to terminate Chief Jeff Lee's contract without cause. 'At the end of the day, it's gotten very messy. It's not about one single decision that he's made. It's about bringing peace and calm and respect back to the district and the men and women that serve this community every day, and it just got to a point where he was not effective anymore,' said St. Lucie County Commissioner and Board Member Jamie Fowler. WATCH KATE HUSSEY'S REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie Fire District chief fired in 4-3 vote This is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation brought to light earlier this year. WPTV reported last week that more than 74% of firefighters who participated in a union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said they had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, while 97% said the same about District Attorney Kim Sabol. entry.title: Indian River State College trustees to consider eliminating men's, women's swimming and diving programs
entry.summary: Indian River State College trustees are expected to consider a major restructuring of the college's athletic programs next week that would eliminate men's and women's swimming and diving and move several remaining sports to Division II competition. The recommendations are included on the agenda for the college's Governance Legislative Affairs Committee meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at the Dixon Hendry Campus in Okeechobee. The committee meetings begin at 9:30 a.m., followed by the full District Board of Trustees meeting at 1 p.m. WATCH TYLER HATFIELD'S REPORT BELOW: Swimmers rally to save IRSC swim and dive teams Under the proposed athletic restructuring plan, both the men's and women's swimming and diving programs would be eliminated beginning with the fall 2027-28 academic year. The proposal would also transition baseball, softball and men's basketball to Division II competition beginning that same academic year. Volleyball already competes at the Division 2 level, according to the agenda. College administrators would also be directed to evaluate whether the women's basketball program could be reinstated for the 2028-29 season. The agenda says that possibility would depend on the availability of resources. The recommendations come from the college president and cabinet and are scheduled to be presented to the Governance Legislative Affairs Committee for approval. The agenda itself does not provide a reason for the proposed elimination of swimming and diving or detail the financial impact of the restructuring. All of this comes after Indian River State College's men's swim and dive team in March captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, with the women's team also claiming its 48th national title. The meeting will take place at the Williamson Conference Center Auditorium on Indian River State College's Dixon Hendry Campus at 2229 NW 9th Avenue in Okeechobee.

William Reaves , 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. entry.article_text: Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6 p.m. execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, "No, I do not."The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves — an Army veteran — as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: Palm Beach County families face a youth mental health gap. A new FAU program aims to fill it.
entry.summary: For years, Palm Beach County has faced a shortage of mental health resources for children, leaving families vulnerable. Now, members of the community are stepping up to fill the need. Florida Atlantic University is launching a new program to provide that support for free. The program, called 'OWLS-FLY' (short for Opportunity, Wellness, Leadership Strength with Families Leading Youth), is being spearheaded by researchers Kelly Emelianchik-Key and Alex Fields inside the education building at FAU. It was made possible by a $1.2 million grant from the Children's Services Council of Palm Beach County. The program will provide free mental health counseling for kids ages 6 through 17 and their families. 'We provide group counseling, individual counseling, family counseling, and we'll have some different parental supports that are going to take place,' Emelianchik-Key said. The space is still coming together with different rooms for family and individual therapy. There's also a room set up to provide care via telehealth. Emelianchik-Key said she anticipates the first clients to be served in January. Fields said the stakes for young people are high. 'If you don't have solid mental health support, you can't build the foundation for a really healthy and high quality of life down the road,' Fields said. The program serves two needs: it helps families who need services, and it provides work experience for the people who are learning to provide them. 'We've worked with clinicians in the community, specifically for youth with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and I've heard how long their wait lists are, and that they're not able to provide services for months and on out,' Fields said. Master's students and graduates will get work experience through the program. Michelle Abarca of the Children's Services Council hopes to take what's learned through FAU's program and scale it in the future. 'Working with FAU is particularly exciting for us because we are a data-driven organization, and with the research that's going to be taking place at FAU, we hope to learn. We hope to be able to replicate some of this at one point,' Abarca said. The program is funded for three years, but Emelianchik-Key and Fields hope to continue it for years to come. 'To be able to do this is a really great honor,' Emelianchik-Key said. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting

entry.title: Black women on the ballot in the midterms could make history across the country
entry.summary: From the U.S. Senate to the governors mansion, dozens of Black women are on the ballot across the country. Dr. Ndidiamaka Okpareke, a pharmacist and Republican newcomer seeking a New Mexico congressional seat, is one of them. We need adequate representation at the table so that we can pull our communities forward, Okpareke told Scripps News. The daughter of Nigerian immigrants and a mother of three, Okpareke would be the first Black woman to represent New Mexico in Congress if she wins her long-shot bid against a three-term incumbent. The Gen Z Democrat is running in South Carolinas 4th Congressional District in the Upstate, one of the states most conservative districts. She is seeking to become the first Black woman the state has sent to Congress. McClain told Scripps News that many people doubted her candidacy at the start. Now that we are so close to the finish line and with the support that weve been able to get people now realize that we can win this race, McClain said. entry.article_text: Senate to the governor’s mansion, dozens of Black women are on the ballot across the country.Dr. Ndidiamaka Okpareke, a pharmacist and Republican newcomer seeking a New Mexico congressional seat, is one of them.“We need adequate representation at the table so that we can pull our communities forward,” Okpareke told Scripps News.The daughter of Nigerian immigrants and a mother of three, Okpareke would be the first Black woman to represent New Mexico in Congress if she wins her long-shot bid against a three-term incumbent.RELATED STORY | Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challengesSome 1,500 miles away, 25-year-old Courtney McClain is making a similar bid. The Gen Z Democrat is running in South Carolina’s 4th Congressional District in the Upstate, one of the state’s most conservative districts. She is seeking to become the first Black woman the state has sent to Congress.McClain told Scripps News that many people doubted her candidacy at the start.“Now that we are so close to the finish line and with the support that we’ve been able to get people now realize that we can win this race,” McClain said.“STILL CONTINUING TO RUN”Okpareke and McClain are part of a larger group challenging assumptions about Black women’s electability. There are 72 Black women on the midterm ballot, according to data from Rutgers University’s Center for American Women and Politics and Higher Heights. Near majority are Democrats.Four Black women are running for the Senate while 40 Black women nominees are in the running for the lower chamber, two are in the running for governor and 26 are running for other statewide offices.University of Florida professor Sharon Austin told Scripps News these were once officer that women didn't tend to run for, especially women of color.“Now it seems the sky's the limit and more women of color are seeking all offices at all levels,” Austin said.Austin, who has studied Black women in politics, said Black women candidates know the climb to the ballot, let alone victory, is steep.“These are women who know that when they decide to run for office it isn’t going to be easy. They’re going to have to deal with a lot of biases and a lot of bigotry. But many of them are able to overcome it, and they’re still continuing to run,” she said.“There definitely has been progress. There always is going to be bigotry, unfortunately, and there’s always going to be barriers,” Austin added. “But I think there are people in today’s society who are a lot more willing to look beyond race and gender when they cast their votes.”“TAKE YOURSELF OUT OF THE BOX”McClain said she doesn’t want her campaign defined by history-making alone.“Representation isn’t just about what the person looks like, but it’s about what that person can actually bring and do for the community,” McClain added.For Okpareke, a medical professional who says she’s bringing firsthand experience to policy that impacts different communities, representation goes beyond race or gender.“There are boxes that are built for us on both sides of the aisle,” Okpareke said. “We've seen that so often where you align yourself with a certain ideology or a certain way to think and you get boxed in and you can never come out of that.”“So take yourself out of the box, be true to who you are, and stand for the people,” she added.INTERACTIVE | How the midterms could shape the future of Social SecurityKelly Dittmar, director of research at CWAP, told Scripps News the election story this year goes beyond the firsts. Some Black women are leaving Congress, so the overall number may not rise sharply, she said. But the new candidates include younger women and those from different backgrounds who clear new paths and bring complex perspectives to office."We found in our own research that what that means is they're often bringing not only their own voices but also voices from their communities,” Dittmar said. “They’re diversifying the representation among the Black women who are serving.”She said voters are also looking for something new, and women can use the fact that they haven’t been part of the status quo to their advantage.“I think this year we will see a number of cases of success to further prove the case that women can and do win some of the toughest races, that Black women can and do win in majority-white electorates, which has been a bias in a lot of the discussions around when and where Black women should run,” Dittmar said.McClain said that’s the message she is carrying into Election Day.“That excitement. That want for change,” she said. "Not just on being the first Black woman but running on being a candidate that is truly going to represent the Upstate and is truly going to bring change.”“I hope to see a version of America that works for all people, and a version of America that is truly going to be representative of the least of us,” McClain said.Win or lose Tuesday, Okpareke said she hopes to change the conversation about where and when Black women can run for office.“I would just want to inspire anyone from different backgrounds to let them know you can do it,” she said. “You too can stand for and guard and protect and nurture the American dream because it's not going to end with you.”

entry.title: Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team
entry.summary: The Indian River State College Board of Trustees has delayed taking action on a recommendation to eliminate the college's swimming and diving team. During a meeting held in Okeechobee, the board voted Tuesday to table the president's recommendation to eliminate the program. WATCH REPORT BELOW: IRSC trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming, diving team Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team Instead, trustees asked the college administration to prepare a comprehensive report on the swimming and diving program. The board requested that the report include input from the community. President Timothy Moore said at Tuesday's meeting that the proposal to cut the programs comes down to money. 'It's a tremendous opportunity to leave this college with that kind of skill, resource and talent here, but it comes at a price,' Moore said. The school president said the program currently costs around $1.4 to $2 million, money that isn't coming in through donations. 'What's required to maintain it as it sits today? We will require $15 to $20 million of an endowment to throw off enough revenue per year to sustain the program as it sits today,' Moore said. There's also a proposal to transition the remaining sports to Division II, resulting in potential savings of around $500,000. But if the swimming and diving program stays, Moore said the school may be forced to cut 50 percent for sports across the board. 'It's elimination of one or impose a penalty across all, and I would imagine that our championships will suffer because of that decision,' Moore said. The administration is expected to present the report at the Board of Trustees Nov. 17 meeting, when recommendations on how to move forward will be considered. This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. Former swimmer Ella Smith started a petition last week to save the program, which has more than 12,500 signatures.

entry.title: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development
entry.summary: By a 4-0 vote, commissioners in Martin County on Tuesday unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities. This was the second reading after commissioners moved forward with the moratorium during a meeting held Oct. 13. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development Tuesday's vote comes after Martin County recently received an application to build its first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. That application is for the construction of a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. However, because the application was submitted before the moratorium, it will not be affected by Tuesday's vote. The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development.
