entry.title: Women's hockey growing in South Florida as University of Miami club gains momentum
entry.summary: Women's hockey is growing in South Florida, from the pee-wee level all the way up to the college level, and the University of Miami Women's Hockey Club team is part of that surge. Head coach Justina Holland, a former player, rebooted the women's hockey club program at the University of Miami in 2021. She rebuilt it from the ground up, taking on every task herself as a college student. WATCH BELOW: Women's hockey growing at University of Miami Women's hockey growing at University of Miami 'Yes, all by myself. I did. I had to find some girls that wanted to play. I had to find a league. I did buy jerseys, get ice time, like everything. Every single little thing you can think of, I had to do myself,' Holland said. At first, the team had only six players and no subs, and they competed in a women's league. 'We didn't even have any colleges to play against. You're playing against grown women, and that was a little bit humbling, but we had a lot of fun, and that was kind of the start of your year. So from there, it kind of picked up. The year after, we had UT Tampa, USF; they joined. Then we got it going, and you get teams like Georgia, Alabama, Auburn, and we're slowly building up the South to what it is right now,' Holland said. This year, the Canes have 14 players, and Holland credits social media for helping to spread the word and getting more students on skates. 'It's everything we gained almost 7,000 followers within like a month,' Holland said. With more people seeing the pictures and videos they post on Instagram, the more support they see. Co-captain Alex Meola wants the team to become a flagship club on campus and says the camaraderie is what makes it special. 'We just have such a good time with each other. It's like it's hard not to. And that's the beautiful thing about club sports is like it brings you back to that first initial reason why you started playing hockey, right?' Meola said. With more and more interest in skating the club's way, Holland says anyone can gear up. 'You don't have to be the best player ever. We have girls from all different levels. So it's more of like if you know how to play, you want to play, like come join. That's kind of the vibe: to have fun,' Holland said.

It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport.Argentina's migration authority said Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and his daughters Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro crossed into the country at 10:50 p.m. They entered via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a primary border checkpoint linking Brazil to Argentina's northeastern province of Misiones."Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country," the Argentine migration authority said on X.The authority said that at 11:30 p.m. local time, shortly after clearing immigration control, the four boarded a private charter flight operated by aviation company Baires Fly S.A. According to the filed flight plan, the aircraft departed for Guayaquil, Ecuador.The move is almost certain to cause a big diplomatic rift between Lula and Argentine President Javier Milei, a Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to take part in Bolsonaro's campaign.Bolsonaro lands in MiamiFlight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed that a plane fitting the description of Bolsonaro's landed in Guayaquil at about 4 a.m. local time, before taking off minutes later for Miami-Opa locka Executive Airport. The plane carrying Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami at around 9:30 a.m. EST.Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, told several dozen supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia before the plane landed that he didn't have precise information about Bolsonaro's whereabouts, but said he had left Brazil."I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true," Lula said. entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

entry.article_text: Early voting ends Saturday, Oct. Lucie, Indian River and Okeechobee counties. Palm Beach County voters have one more day to vote early, with sites open through Sunday, Nov. See also: Sand crews mobilize as king tides, gale-force winds erode Jupiter Civic Center beach On Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, polls will be open from 7 a.m. Voters must cast their ballots at their assigned polling place. Check your location and sample ballot with your county Supervisor of Elections before heading out. Early voting hours Hours vary by county: Palm Beach County: Through Nov. Martin County: Through Oct. Lucie County: Through Oct. Indian River County: Through Oct. to 4 p.m., with extended hours Thursdays. Okeechobee County: Through Oct. During early voting, voters may use any open early voting site in their county. 3, they must go to their assigned polling place. What’s on the ballot Voters across the region will decide races for governor, U.S. The statewide contests include Republican Byron Donalds against Democrat David Jolly for governor, Republican Ashley Moody against Democrat Angie Nixon for U.S. Senate, and Republican James Uthmeier against Democrat Jose Javier Rodriguez for attorney general. Congressional and state legislative races also will appear on ballots. Local races and ballot questions depend on a voter’s address. Palm Beach County voters also should check their congressional district and polling place after recent redistricting. One statewide ballot question is Amendment 3, which would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes and lower the annual cap on assessment increases for certain non-homestead properties. It also would limit how local governments can use property tax revenue. Supporters say it would provide tax relief; local governments and public agencies have warned it could reduce funding for services. A proposed constitutional amendment needs at least 60% voter approval to pass. Vote-by-mail deadline The deadline to request a vote-by-mail ballot was Oct. Returned ballots must reach the local elections office by 7 p.m. on Election Day to be counted. In Palm Beach County, ballots delivered to branch offices must arrive by 5 p.m. Voters can check their sample ballot, polling place and county-specific voting information through their Supervisor of Elections office: Palm Beach County Martin County St. Lucie County Indian River County Okeechobee County

entry.title: Florida's U.S. Senate Race: What voters need to know before Election Day
entry.summary: With Election Day just a week away, Florida voters will decide a high-profile race for the U.S. Senate. The special election pits incumbent Republican Ashley Moody against Democratic challenger Angie Nixon, with independent candidate Neil Gillespie also on the ballot. Marco Rubio's term. Rubio left the Senate after becoming U.S. Secretary of State, and Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed Ashley Moody to the seat in January 2025. The winner will serve the final two years of Rubio's term, meaning the seat will be on the ballot again in 2028. Ashley Moody's Campaign Moody, a former two-term Florida attorney general from Plant City, is running as the incumbent Republican. Angie Nixon's Campaign Democratic challenger Angie Nixon is a state representative and labor organizer from Jacksonville. Nixon emerged from a competitive Democratic primary, defeating a more centrist opponent who significantly outraised her campaign. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America, Nixon has campaigned alongside U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and supports policies including a $25 minimum wage and Medicare for All. Throughout her campaign, Nixon has focused on affordability and economic issues, arguing working families are struggling with rising costs while politicians benefit from the current system. entry.title: Cracked: In South Texas, new Congressional lines divide neighbors
entry.summary: On the north end of Corpus Christi, Texas, Craig Street is a new dividing line. Diane Gudmanson and Carol Lowe live on one side. Matilda Rodriguez lives on the other. In January, they will have different representatives in Congress because Republicans redrew Congressional maps. We cant even go and talk to our neighbors across the street and say, 'Lets work together and talk to our representative together,' because we have different representatives in Congress, Lowe said. I hate that map, said Gudmanson. In redrawing District 34, the strategy used cracking, a method that divides communities among districts to dilute their electoral influence. In addition to carving out a section of Corpus Christi, which predominantly votes Democrat, the Republican-led Texas Legislature also split parts of the Rio Grande Valley into separate districts, leaving some farmers and ranchers with land and business interests in both. You're going to have people going in there pulling that damn lever, and they don't have any idea who's who they're voting for, or who's actually going to be representing them, said rancher Mike England, who is from Mercedes, a town on the district line. Brian Jones, a farmer who lives nearby, said even though the new district is anchored by urban centers Corpus Christi to the north and Brownsville in the south, theres still a lot of ranching and farming that happens in between. He says whoever wins in the midterms will have to represent agricultural interests as well. The redrawing was done on the political assumption that Latino voters, who voted for Donald Trump in record numbers in Texas in 2024, would vote Republican in 2026. Itll backfire, said Rodriguez.

Baxter is seeking another term representing District 6, while Waldron is looking to bring her previous experience at the Port of Palm Beach and in the Florida House to the County Commission.Hoffman has been following the District 6 contest for months. As the race enters its final stretch, he pressed both candidates on how their experience would shape their approach to some of the district's most contentious issues.Baxter is the Republican incumbent. Her time representing District 6 is her first elected political office. She has also been endorsed by President Donald Trump."We're putting in a lot of hard work," Baxter told WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman.Waldron, a Democrat, previously served as a Port of Palm Beach commissioner before serving one term as a state representative."We're out there every day," Waldron told Hoffman.That difference in experience has become part of the choice before voters. Baxter points to her record on the County Commission, while Waldron points to her experience in multiple elected offices.Hoffman asked both candidates about affordability, traffic and development, issues affecting residents across District 6.Waldron argued that transparency has been lacking and said she has heard from residents who don't believe their concerns are being heard."My general sense when I've been out there talking to voters in my district and beyond is that they feel like they're not being heard. They feel like there's not transparency," Waldron told Hoffman.She also questioned whether enough is being done to mitigate the effects of development on surrounding communities."They're not really looking into or trying to mitigate the impact that it will have on the constituents, on schools, on traffic, on quality of life," Waldron said.Baxter pointed voters to her record on the commission, telling Hoffman she has tried to fight for residents while navigating competing opinions within the district."I have always tried to do what's best for the residents and fight for them. And sometimes I have residents on different sides of issues," Baxter said.Baxter said residents can look at her previous votes and commission meetings when deciding whether she has effectively represented them."I think, in my seat particularly, I have a record. People can see what I have fought for. They can watch past commission meetings and know that you'll not find a better fighter for, you know, our district," Baxter said.Baxter also noted that decisions before the County Commission involve seven commissioners, each bringing their own opinions to the table.On one of the most controversial development issues in western Palm Beach County, Baxter and Waldron find themselves on the same side.Both candidates have opposed Project Tango, the proposal for a massive AI data center near the Arden community and a new elementary school.The issue has become part of a broader conversation over data center development in Palm Beach County and what that development could mean for surrounding communities.For Waldron, the Project Tango debate also connects to her broader argument about transparency and how development decisions affect residents.For Baxter, the issue is part of the record she is asking voters to consider as she seeks another term representing District 6.After discussing their differences, Hoffman closed each interview with a different question: What is one thing each candidate respects about her opponent?"I respect anybody who wants to serve the public and represent the public," Waldron told Hoffman.Waldron said she believes elected officials can sometimes face criticism without people appreciating the challenges that come with serving in public office."A lot of times people bash politicians or leaders and stuff like that. And a lot of times, I don't think it's really fair," Waldron said."You can have tough days, and I imagine she's probably had some," Waldron added.Baxter expressed a similar view about the difficulty of representing residents with different opinions."It's definitely not as easy as people might think," Baxter told Hoffman. "You have people with different opinions, as we should. So you're always going to have somebody who's upset because they don't like that, and your people are going to be happy because they like what you stand for.""At the end of the day, we do our best to represent the residents," Baxter said.Despite their differences over how District 6 should be represented, Baxter and Waldron agree on one thing as the race nears its end: They want residents to get out and vote.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Report: Peltola campaign linked to effort to recruit second Dan Sullivan in Alaska Senate race
entry.summary: The Democratic campaign for Alaska's U.S. Senate seat was involved in efforts to place on the ballot a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a bid to confuse voters in a race that could determine which party controls the chamber, The New York Times reported Wednesday. The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican their candidate was running against. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. Sullivan. He made it through the state's August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday's general election. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola's campaign: Zero, none, zilch, he said in June after announcing his run. He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press. A top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the ballot after he declared his candidacy, claiming it was filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballots fairness or neutrality. The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. The U.S. Constitution sets out only age, citizenship and residency requirements to run for the Senate. President Donald Trump, who directed his Department of Justice to file a lawsuit last week pre-emptively contesting a Peltola win due to the presence of the second Dan Sullivan, called for legal penalties against Democrats over the situation: Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done, Trump wrote on his social media site on Wednesday. entry.article_text: The Democratic campaign for Alaska's U.S. Senate seat was involved in efforts to place on the ballot a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a bid to confuse voters in a race that could determine which party controls the chamber, The New York Times reported Wednesday.The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican their candidate was running against. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. He made it through the state's August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday's general election.Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola's campaign: “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press.A top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the ballot after he declared his candidacy, claiming it was “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Constitution sets out only age, citizenship and residency requirements to run for the Senate.President Donald Trump, who directed his Department of Justice to file a lawsuit last week pre-emptively contesting a Peltola win due to the presence of the second Dan Sullivan, called for legal penalties against Democrats over the situation: “Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done,” Trump wrote on his social media site on Wednesday.He added that he didn't think Peltola should be able to run, calling her campaign's alleged act, "ELECTION FRAUD.""The Democrats cheated! They found a man named Dan Sullivan, put him on the Ballot, then lied to the Court, and said they didn’t know anything about it. That’s perjury," Trump stated. "She shouldn’t be allowed to run, and neither should the FAKE Dan Sullivan."“Alaskans deserve the truth,” said Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. “Mary Peltola, her campaign and her senior advisers colluded with the DSCC, national Democrat lawyers and Alaska Democrat operatives to recruit candidates to deliberately confuse and deceive voters.”Peltola's campaign, in a statement Wednesday, said it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” They issued a similar statement in June after Sen. Sullivan questioned the other Sullivan's candidacy.Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick.“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan," the organization said in a statement Wednesday. The Times report said DSCC staffers were on texts with the Peltola campaign discussing the second Sullivan.Legal experts said the report about Democrats appearing to recruit Dan J. Sullivan as a way to potentially confuse voters will have no impact on a lawsuit filed recently by the U.S. President Donald Trump directed the department to file the lawsuit, which seeks to halt certification of a possible Peltola win, citing the presence of the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.“It’s a dirty campaign trick, and it’s good reason the Alaska Supreme Court should have permitted the candidate to have been removed from the ballot,” said Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor. “But now it’s in the hands of the voters, not litigation.”It's not the first time a candidate's appearance on the Alaska ballot has been questioned. In 2024, the state Democratic Party sued to keep off the U.S. House ballot a man with no apparent ties to the state who is serving time in a federal prison in New York. A divided state Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot. The man is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election ballot.The Times story about the recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan is based partly on interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August amid a campaign shake-up. The newspaper said she tried to retract her comments last week. Efforts by the AP to reach Rios were not immediately successful.As of Monday, 46,204 ballots had already been cast in Alaska, according to AP data. Sullivan is listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.

entry.title: North Palm Beach Fire Rescue first in Florida to equip crews with Ben's Blue Bags for autism emergencies
entry.summary: What looks like an ordinary blue backpack is giving first responders in North Palm Beach a new way to connect with people with autism during an emergency. North Palm Beach Fire Rescue has equipped its fire trucks with Ben's Blue Bags, backpacks filled with sensory and communication tools designed to help first responders interact with people experiencing sensory overstimulation. WATCH REPORT BELOW: North Palm Beach firefighters add sensory bags for autism calls Backpacks for Autism The bags can include items such as fidget toys, noise-canceling headphones, dry-erase boards, and communication tools that can help someone express what they need or how they are feeling. 'Fidget toys, fidget spinners, Rubik's Cubes,' firefighter Noah Denker said while showing WPTV reporter Christy Waite what is inside one of the bags. 'The special thing about these bags is they have communication devices. There's a blank white board they can write on, there's a keyboard so they can type it out, and a how are you feeling chart.' For Denker, bringing the bags to North Palm Beach started with a connection close to home. His wife is a fifth-grade teacher who works with children with autism. Seeing how she uses sensory tools with her students inspired Denker to find a way to give first responders similar resources in the field. 'My wife is a fifth-grade teacher for kids with autism, and she gave me the idea,' Denker said. 'She has things in her classroom to help with overstimulation before they hit that meltdown stage.' That idea led Denker to research Ben's Blue Bags. Ben's Blue Bags is a nonprofit that was founded in 2019 by Matt Kodicek, a captain and paramedic with the Crown Point Fire Department in Indiana and the father of a child on the autism spectrum. The idea was inspired by his son, Ben, after Kodicek saw a need for first responders to have additional tools and training to help people experiencing sensory overstimulation. The organization has distributed more than 700 bags, and they are being used by more than 3,000 first responders across seven states and Canada. Now, some of those bags are riding along on North Palm Beach fire trucks, giving crews immediate access to sensory and communication tools when they respond to a call. entry.title: Who's watching the vote? A guide to poll watchers, observers and monitors in 2026
entry.summary: On Election Day, around 100,000 precincts will be up and running, filled with election officials, volunteer poll workers, and potentially some election monitors or observers. Election monitoring has long been part of the US electoral system. Avery Davis-Roberts, the director of the Democracy Program at the Carter Center said, 'It's a great way for people to get engaged in the process, right? To understand how elections work, to really sort of learn the nuts and bolts of what goes into running an election. For 2026, there are a few different types of observers voters could see at their polling site. People there to observe or monitor the election will largely fall a handful camps partisan poll watchers, nonpartisan observers, volunteers, DOJ election monitors and congressional observers. RELATED STORY | Federal agents are ending up at polling places for reasons unrelated to the election In every state except West Virginia, political parties or candidates are allowed to send poll watchers to voting sites. This does mean ensuring the integrity of elections... but it also means ensuring that their own supporters can vote and from time to time, challenge challenging the eligibility of potential opposition supporters, explained Mollie Cohen, an associate professor of political science at Purdue University. What exactly partisan poll watchers can do depends on the state. But in 32 states, they can challenge the eligibility of a voter. As Cohen explains, the requirements for those challenges vary by state: 'For example, in North Carolina, poll watchers who challenge the eligible eligibility of a voter have to submit an oath under threat of perjury and perjury to an election official in the state of North Carolina is a felony offense. In a place like Nevada, Election Day challenges of voters have are only considered valid if they're based on direct personal knowledge. Advocacy groups and nonprofits, like the Carter Center, also organize and train poll watchers. entry.article_text: On Election Day, around 100,000 precincts will be up and running, filled with election officials, volunteer poll workers, and potentially some election monitors or observers.Election monitoring has long been part of the US electoral system. Avery Davis-Roberts, the director of the Democracy Program at the Carter Center said, "It's a great way for people to get engaged in the process, right? To understand how elections work, to really sort of learn the nuts and bolts of what goes into running an election.”For 2026, there are a few different types of observers voters could see at their polling site. People there to observe or monitor the election will largely fall a handful camps – partisan poll watchers, nonpartisan observers, volunteers, DOJ election monitors and congressional observers.RELATED STORY | Federal agents are ending up at polling places for reasons unrelated to the electionIn every state except West Virginia, political parties or candidates are allowed to send poll watchers to voting sites.“This does mean ensuring the integrity of elections... but it also means ensuring that their own supporters can vote and from time to time, challenge challenging the eligibility of potential opposition supporters,” explained Mollie Cohen, an associate professor of political science at Purdue University.What exactly partisan poll watchers can do depends on the state. But in 32 states, they can challenge the eligibility of a voter. As Cohen explains, the requirements for those challenges vary by state: "For example, in North Carolina, poll watchers who challenge the eligible eligibility of a voter have to submit an oath under threat of perjury and perjury to an election official in the state of North Carolina is a felony offense. In a place like Nevada, Election Day challenges of voters have are only considered valid if they're based on direct personal knowledge.”Advocacy groups and nonprofits, like the Carter Center, also organize and train poll watchers. Depending on state rules, they could be inside or outside the polling place, but they're there purely to observe and help improve transparency.“All of the observers that you might see have to abide by state law. They shouldn't be interfering in the process. There shouldn't be anything that makes voters feel unsafe or intimidated,” said Davis-Roberts.Also, the Department of Justice is deploying about 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states. It’s a notable increase from the last midterm election, where the department deployed only 388 election monitors in 2022. In a statement to Scripps News, the DOJ said: “Every monitor will merely observe and report any potential violations of federal law to the Department, which will be reviewed after Election Day.”MORE ELECTION NEWS | Why Social Security could become a major issue for the senators elected in 2026Two other types of people voters might see. Volunteers might be outside the ‘electioneering line’ providing sample ballots, information on issues or assisting voters stuck in a long line. You also could see congressional election observers. They are allowed to see every part of the voting process and their observations could even come into play if a race is contested.And election observation will extend beyond November 3. In many states, observers can watch the ballot counting and the procedures for processing mail-in ballot, which is officially called canvassing.

entry.title: Palm Beach County families face a youth mental health gap. A new FAU program aims to fill it.
entry.summary: For years, Palm Beach County has faced a shortage of mental health resources for children, leaving families vulnerable. Now, members of the community are stepping up to fill the need. Florida Atlantic University is launching a new program to provide that support for free. WATCH REPORT BELOW: FAU launches free mental health program for children FAU launches free mental health program for children The program, called 'OWLS-FLY' (short for Opportunity, Wellness, Leadership Strength with Families Leading Youth), is being spearheaded by researchers Kelly Emelianchik-Key and Alex Fields inside the education building at FAU. It was made possible by a $1.2 million grant from the Children's Services Council of Palm Beach County. The program will provide free mental health counseling for kids ages 6 through 17 and their families. 'We provide group counseling, individual counseling, family counseling, and we'll have some different parental supports that are going to take place,' Emelianchik-Key said. The space is still coming together with different rooms for family and individual therapy. There's also a room set up to provide care via telehealth. Emelianchik-Key said she anticipates the first clients to be served in January. Fields said the stakes for young people are high. 'If you don't have solid mental health support, you can't build the foundation for a really healthy and high quality of life down the road,' Fields said. The program serves two needs: it helps families who need services, and it provides work experience for the people who are learning to provide them. 'We've worked with clinicians in the community, specifically for youth with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and I've heard how long their wait lists are, and that they're not able to provide services for months and on out,' Fields said. Master's students and graduates will get work experience through the program. Michelle Abarca of the Children's Services Council hopes to take what's learned through FAU's program and scale it in the future. 'Working with FAU is particularly exciting for us because we are a data-driven organization, and with the research that's going to be taking place at FAU, we hope to learn. We hope to be able to replicate some of this at one point,' Abarca said. The program is funded for three years, but Emelianchik-Key and Fields hope to continue it for years to come. 'To be able to do this is a really great honor,' Emelianchik-Key said. This story was reported on-ai

WPTV's independent reporting has also identified Avenger short-range air defense systems among the equipment deployed in the area."It looks like there are a couple Avenger batteries, which are Stinger missiles, and there's four on each side, so a total of eight," Buckley told Hoffman. "I think they might have .50-caliber machine guns on those weapons too."Hoffman previously reported that NORAD and U.S. Northern Command confirmed defense assets had been placed in and around Mar-a-Lago at the Secret Service's request. NORAD declined to provide specific operational information, citing security considerations.The military has not publicly said whether a specific threat prompted the deployment. The developments come amid heightened airspace security around Palm Beach when Trump is in the area.NORAD conducted a planned air defense exercise over Palm Beach on Oct. 14 involving F-16s and Civil Air Patrol aircraft. The command said it routinely uses exercises involving scenarios such as airspace violations, hijackings and unknown aircraft to test its responses, systems and equipment. NORAD also reported an F-16 intercept of an aircraft that violated temporary flight restrictions near Palm Beach on Oct. The latest deployment comes months after WPTV spoke with Buckley about an anti-drone laser defense system at the airport.Buckley told Hoffman then, and maintains now, that one threat deserves particular attention: drone swarms."Most people have seen the movie 'Miracle on the Hudson' with (Capt. Chesley 'Sully' Sullenberger) landing the U.S. "That's what a flock of birds did to a couple of engines. What do you think a flock of drones — inexpensive, cheap drones — are going to do in front of an airliner?""I'm shocked that we haven't lost an airliner yet due to a drone swarm," he added.For Buckley, the type of technology being deployed is less important than having defenses capable of responding to potential threats."Whether it's directed-energy weapons, laser or an Avenger missile battery, I think, you know, the president's safety is pretty important," Buckley said.The military has not publicly disclosed how long the air defense systems will remain deployed around Mar-a-Lago. entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - WPEC
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    WPEC
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

entry.summary: Developer Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County in support of restoring the St. Lucie River. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Mattamy Homes donating portion of development to aid in future St. Lucie River clean-up   James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the land will have the capacity to host large amounts of muck that will need to be dredged out of the St. Lucie River to improve water quality.   Fitzgerald said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres.   Combined, Fitzgerald said the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck from the river. WPTV asked Fitzgerald what happens to the muck after the removal project. 'The muck will dry out, and we're hoping at some point in the future that land can be used as a recreational project,' Fitzgerald said. 'Or perhaps, depending on the needs of the county, in some other future environmental restoration projects.' Fitzgerald said the project to remove the muck will begin once federal funding is authorized.

entry.title: Strong surf damages historic Jupiter Civic Center, forcing closure as crews work to protect building
entry.summary: Strong surf pounding Palm Beach Countys coastline has damaged the historic Jupiter Civic Center at Carlin Park, forcing the building to close as crews take emergency measures to protect the nearly 100-year-old structure. The impact is hard to miss. The front of the Civic Center is blocked off by caution tape. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Strong surf damages historic Jupiter Civic Center King tides damage Jupiter Civic Center, emergency work underway Behind the building, much of the beach has been washed away, leaving broken branches, eroded sand and steps exposed or damaged along the shoreline. entry.title: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

entry.title: Delray Beach homeowner faces higher costs after new roof, new insurance company
entry.summary: A Delray Beach homeowner says a new roof and a new insurance company resulted in a new worry over money. 'My finances are very limited,' says 83-year-old Doris Fiorenza. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Delray Beach homeowner seeks solutions for higher insurance 'I only have Social Security, I'm low income, and with all these bills I'm getting hit with, I'm going to run out of money.' Doris says that after she got a new roof on her villa, which cost $14,000, she was dropped by Citizens Insurance. She found a private insurer, but her premium of around $3,300 is far higher than the $1,800 she was paying to Citizens. Part of the problem was a $900 surcharge on her policy for a lapse in coverage between her Citizens policy and her new policy. It's a mistake homeowners need to know can be costly. Homeowners also need to know that improvements like a new roof do trigger insurance discounts. 'It's happening to a lot of people,' says Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana. 'That's what we tell everybody: when you get upgrades that get you credits, always, always turn them into your current company, make sure those get processed.' Norberg also says homeowners are saving money by shopping around to find better premiums. 'A lot of our clients are able to get either a better rate,' he says. 'It's very competitive; rates are changing a lot, they all seem to be going down, and the other companies are getting really aggressive.'

entry.summary: Boynton Beach city leaders are considering potential changes to the city's parking ordinance after residents raised concerns about limited parking options and challenges enforcing the rules in different neighborhoods. The ordinance, which took effect in February , restricts parking on public streets, swales and sidewalks. Violations can result in a $25 fine. And sometimes I have residents on different sides of issues," Baxter said.Baxter said residents can look at her previous votes and commission meetings when deciding whether she has effectively represented them."I think, in my seat particularly, I have a record. People can see what I have fought for. They can watch past commission meetings and know that you'll not find a better fighter for, you know, our district," Baxter said.Baxter also noted that decisions before the County Commission involve seven commissioners, each bringing their own opinions to the table.On one of the most controversial development issues in western Palm Beach County, Baxter and Waldron find themselves on the same side.Both candidates have opposed Project Tango, the proposal for a massive AI data center near the Arden community and a new elementary school.The issue has become part of a broader conversation over data center development in Palm Beach County and what that development could mean for surrounding communities.For Waldron, the Project Tango debate also connects to her broader argument about transparency and how development decisions affect residents.For Baxter, the issue is part of the record she is asking voters to consider as she seeks another term representing District 6.After discussing their differences, Hoffman closed each interview with a different question: What is one thing each candidate respects about her opponent?"I respect anybody who wants to serve the public and represent the public," Waldron told Hoffman.Waldron said she believes elected officials can sometimes face criticism without people appreciating the challenges that come with serving in public office."A lot of times people bash politicians or leaders and stuff like that. entry.title: Report: Peltola campaign linked to effort to recruit second Dan Sullivan in Alaska Senate race
entry.summary: The Democratic campaign for Alaska's U.S. Senate seat was involved in efforts to place on the ballot a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a bid to confuse voters in a race that could determine which party controls the chamber, The New York Times reported Wednesday. The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican their candidate was running against. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. Sullivan. He made it through the state's August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday's general election. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola's campaign: Zero, none, zilch, he said in June after announcing his run. He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press. A top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the ballot after he declared his candidacy, claiming it was filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballots fairness or neutrality. entry.article_text: The Democratic campaign for Alaska's U.S. Senate seat was involved in efforts to place on the ballot a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a bid to confuse voters in a race that could determine which party controls the chamber, The New York Times reported Wednesday.The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican their candidate was running against. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. He made it through the state's August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday's general election.Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola's campaign: “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press.A top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the ballot after he declared his candidacy, claiming it was “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Constitution sets out only age, citizenship and residency requirements to run for the Senate.President Donald Trump, who directed his Department of Justice to file a lawsuit last week pre-emptively contesting a Peltola win due to the presence of the second Dan Sullivan, called for legal penalties against Democrats over the situation: “Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done,” Trump wrote on his social media site on Wednesday.He added that he didn't think Peltola should be able to run, calling her campaign's alleged act, "ELECTION FRAUD.""The Democrats cheated! They found a man named Dan Sullivan, put him on the Ballot, then lied to the Court, and said they didn’t know anything about it. That’s perjury," Trump stated. "She shouldn’t be allowed to run, and neither should the FAKE Dan Sullivan."“Alaskans deserve the truth,” said Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. “Mary Peltola, her campaign and her senior advisers colluded with the DSCC, national Democrat lawyers and Alaska Democrat operatives to recruit candidates to deliberately confuse and deceive voters.”Peltola's campaign, in a statement Wednesday, said it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” They issued a similar statement in June after Sen. Sullivan questioned the other Sullivan's candidacy.Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick.“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan," the organization said in a statement Wednesday. The Times report said DSCC staffers were on texts with the Peltola campaign discussing the second Sullivan.Legal experts said the report about Democrats appearing to recruit Dan J. Sullivan as a way to potentially confuse voters will have no impact on a lawsuit filed recently by the U.S. President Donald Trump directed the department to file the lawsuit, which seeks to halt certification of a possible Peltola win, citing the presence of the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.“It’s a dirty campaign trick, and it’s good reason the Alaska Supreme Court should have permitted the candidate to have been removed from the ballot,” said Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor. “But now it’s in the hands of the voters, not litigation.”It's not the first time a candidate's appearance on the Alaska ballot has been questioned. In 2024, the state Democratic Party sued to keep off the U.S. House ballot a man with no apparent ties to the state who is serving time in a federal prison in New York. A divided state Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot. The man is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election ballot.The Times story about the recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan is based partly on interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August amid a campaign shake-up. The newspaper said she tried to retract her comments last week. Efforts by the AP to reach Rios were not immediately successful.As of Monday, 46,204 ballots had already been cast in Alaska, according to AP data. Sullivan is listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.

entry.title: King tides swamp Treasure Coast roads as coastal flood warning stretches into Friday - WPEC
entry.summary: King tides swamp Treasure Coast roads as coastal flood warning stretches into Friday    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. Martin County has taken some of the worst of it. In Sewall’s Point , floodwater has covered streets and made driving dangerous. Indian River Drive is also underwater for long stretches. Martin County officials say flooding has been reported on Southeast MacArthur Boulevard on Hutchinson Island, in Old Palm City and along South Sewall’s Point. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding in Palm City, including Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Drivers should not go around barricades or through water of unknown depth.

entry.title: Martin County puts brakes on new large data centers for one year - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County puts brakes on new large data centers for one year    WPEC
entry.article_text: Martin County commissioners voted to temporarily halt new applications for large data centers in unincorporated areas of the county for one year on Tuesday. The vote passed 4-0 among Martin County commissioners. The decision gives county officials time to develop regulations governing large data centers, which have raised concerns about electricity consumption and environmental impacts. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana The vote follows an earlier commission meeting in which officials advanced the proposed moratorium for further consideration. The temporary pause applies to new applications for large data centers in areas outside city limits, not throughout the entire county. County officials plan to use the one-year period to review and develop rules for future large data center proposals.

entry.title: Murray Middle School breaks ground on $33 million rebuild after Hurricane Milton damage
entry.summary: Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million phase of its campus rebuild after Hurricane Milton spawned a tornado that damaged three main buildings , forcing students and school programs into portable classrooms, according to Martin County school officials. District leaders said improvements to Murray Middle School were already planned, but the hurricane damage added urgency to the project. The new construction will include learning and performing arts spaces, while the school's gym will also be renovated. WATCH: Murray Middle is rebuilding after Hurricane Milton. Students adapt after hurricane damage For Murray Middle student Nicholas Lowe, the transition meant adjusting to a different learning environment. entry.title: Dolphins look to build on first win as they prepare for tough test against Patriots
entry.summary: After securing their first win against the New York Jets last Sunday , the Miami Dolphins locker room has new energy. 'I think we did a good job celebrating as a team in the locker room. That's when you have the most excitement and the most joy from going out there and putting it all on the line,' said starting quarterback Malik Willis. While the win is a breath of fresh air, the guys know things won't get easier as they prepare to face the New England Patriots on Sunday. 'Division games are important. All these guys watched them play in the Super Bowl last year. I mean, we have 15 rookies, and I hope they all watched the Super Bowl last year, but you never know these days. I'd assume that they all know that the team just went to the Super Bowl,' said head coach Jeff Hafley. The players said they watched the Super Bowl last year, and they're ready for arguably their toughest test of the season. 'It starts today; you know we have to bring our juice today in practice. During the whole week, we have to up our level from last week and just come out and attack them, boys,' said defensive lineman Kenneth Grant. If the intensity on the practice field is any indication, the Dolphins are set to fight and claw against the Pats. The defense looked sharp in their drills, special teams executed well, and Willis and the offense looked poised; speaking of poise, third-year running back Ollie Gordon has been just that since taking over the starting role after De'Von Achane tore his ACL. Gordon has rushed for a touchdown in four straight games and gained 100 yards twice. 'I would say it's huge. I can't do it without my teammates, though; without the line blocking how they are, the tight ends playing how they are, and without our quarterback playing how he is. I come out here and play for my teammates,' Gordon said.

entry.title: Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team
entry.summary: The Indian River State College Board of Trustees has delayed taking action on a recommendation to eliminate the college's swimming and diving team. During a meeting held in Okeechobee, the board voted Tuesday to table the president's recommendation to eliminate the program. WATCH REPORT BELOW: IRSC trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming, diving team Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team Instead, trustees asked the college administration to prepare a comprehensive report on the swimming and diving program. The board requested that the report include input from the community. President Timothy Moore said at Tuesday's meeting that the proposal to cut the programs comes down to money. 'It's a tremendous opportunity to leave this college with that kind of skill, resource and talent here, but it comes at a price,' Moore said. The school president said the program currently costs around $1.4 to $2 million, money that isn't coming in through donations. 'What's required to maintain it as it sits today? We will require $15 to $20 million of an endowment to throw off enough revenue per year to sustain the program as it sits today,' Moore said. There's also a proposal to transition the remaining sports to Division II, resulting in potential savings of around $500,000. But if the swimming and diving program stays, Moore said the school may be forced to cut 50 percent for sports across the board. 'It's elimination of one or impose a penalty across all, and I would imagine that our championships will suffer because of that decision,' Moore said. The administration is expected to present the report at the Board of Trustees Nov. 17 meeting, when recommendations on how to move forward will be considered. This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. Former swimmer Ella Smith started a petition last week to save the program, which has more than 12,500 signatures.

entry.title: Florida teen struck by lightning during soccer game reunites with the first responders who saved him
entry.summary: A 14-year-old boy who went into cardiac arrest after being struck by lightning while playing soccer at a park is now back on the field. Kevin Sosa reunited Wednesday at Delray Medical Center with the first responders, doctors and nurses who helped save his life after the August lightning strike. The crews were honored for their role in Kevin's survival. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Teen survives lightning strike while playing soccer Doctors say CPR and fast emergency care made a critical difference. 'This is not a common thing. I can say that in Palm Beach County Fire Rescue we've put a lot of work in for the men and women who are sitting up here today,' Peter Antevi said. Kevin spent about a month in the hospital, followed by rehabilitation. Doctors say his recovery continues. His family and care team say his story shows the impact of quick action during an emergency.

entry.title: Mattamy Homes donates 125 acres in Martin County to support St. Lucie River restoration - WFLX
entry.summary: Mattamy Homes donates 125 acres in Martin County to support St. Lucie River restoration    WFLX
entry.article_text: Developer Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County in support of restoring the St. The developer said the parcel was donated from the northern section of the Newfield development to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect, and preserve South Florida's water resources. WATCH REPORT BELOW: James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the land will have the capacity to host large amounts of muck that will need to be dredged out of the St. Lucie River to improve water quality. Fitzgerald said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres. Combined, Fitzgerald said the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck from the river. WPTV asked Fitzgerald what happens to the muck after the removal project. "The muck will dry out, and we're hoping at some point in the future that land can be used as a recreational project," Fitzgerald said. "Or perhaps, depending on the needs of the county, in some other future environmental restoration projects." Fitzgerald said the project to remove the muck will begin once federal funding is authorized.

entry.summary: King tides swamp Treasure Coast roads as coastal flood warning stretches into Friday    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. Martin County has taken some of the worst of it. In Sewall’s Point , floodwater has covered streets and made driving dangerous. Indian River Drive is also underwater for long stretches. Martin County officials say flooding has been reported on Southeast MacArthur Boulevard on Hutchinson Island, in Old Palm City and along South Sewall’s Point. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding in Palm City, including Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Drivers should not go around barricades or through water of unknown depth.

entry.title: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County - WPEC
entry.summary: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County’s sea turtles broke a record. The county documented 14,083 nests as of Thursday, its highest total ever recorded. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen credits decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. This is actually a really big deal because what we’re seeing is decades of conservation paying off, Whalen said. But the record season is facing a rough finish. Powerful waves and high tides are eroding beaches, threatening some remaining nests. Loggerheads lead the record season The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. The total surpassed the previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Whalen. Loggerheads drove much of that increase. They’re dominating with 10,000 nests across our entire coastline, which is an insane number, Whalen said. The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests along its 22.4-mile coastline. If we mark 14,000 nests you wouldn’t have anywhere to sit on the beach, Whalen said. And like seriously it would be a sea of orange. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting turtles and their nesting beaches. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices. Rough surf threatens remaining nests A nor’easter and king tides have brought challenging conditions as nesting season winds down. Waves strip away sand, potentially exposing eggs buried beneath the beach. Unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. A lot of them have already hatched out, a lot of them have made it to the water safely, Whalen said. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween. Some nests may continue incubating beyond that date. Nesting numbers across the Treasure Coast Other counties also provided nesting figures. The totals cover different reporting dates and monitoring areas. Indian River County : As of Oct. 22, the county recorded 14,083 nests: 10,045 loggerhead, 3,970 green turtle and 68 leatherback nests. Lucie County : As of Sept. 30, the county recorded 10,239 nests: 9,111 loggerhead, 956 green turtle and 172 leatherback nests. Martin County: As of Sept. 28, its Hutchinson Island monitoring area recorded 4,874 nests: 4,532 loggerhead, 161 green turtle and 181 leatherback nests. Martin County’s figures cover approximately 7.5 miles of Hutchinson Island shoreline. That area stretches from the north side of St. Lucie Inlet to the Martin St. CBS12 News has requested Palm Beach County’s latest countywide figures from FWC and is awaiting those numbers. Boca Raton sees high nest counts, lower hatch success In Boca Raton, a strong nesting season did not translate into equally strong hatching results. David Anderson, sea turtle conservation coordinator at Gumbo Limbo Nature Center, reported the city’s third-highest nesting season. That included record counts of 1,118 loggerhead nests and 43 leatherback nests. But an average of only about 50% of the eggs in inventoried nests hatched. Anderson said a typical hatch rate would be 70% to 80% or more. He attributed some losses to prolonged hot, dry conditions during peak incubation. High sand temperatures can prevent embryos from continuing to develop. Storms and high tides also washed out approximately 185 nests, Anderson said. Predators affected another 13 nests. Artificial lighting created additional problems after hatching. Anderson said hatchlings from at least 85 nests became disoriented and headed into the dunes. Staff plan to evaluate beachfront lighting and work with nearby properties before next season. So sure, it’s sad to see so many hatchlings and eggs not fully developed, but once again, we had a great nesting season, Anderson said. So as long as the nesting numbers continue to climb, it gives us hope. What to do if you find eggs or hatchlings The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season. That strategy helps some nests survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may find exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC says to leave exposed eggs in place. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive, and people should not collect or rebury them. Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. Do not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches clean, flat and dark. Remove beach gear, fill holes, flatten sandcastles and keep lights off the beach at night.
