entry.title: Health Department takes another look at St. Lucie County glioblastoma cases - WPTV
entry.summary: Health Department takes another look at St. Lucie County glioblastoma cases    WPTV
entry.article_text: Nearly eight years after WPTV first investigated concerns about a possible cluster of glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County, health officials have reviewed the numbers again.The latest findings show the number of cases remains in line with what would be expected based on the county's population, but families who lost loved ones to the deadly brain cancer say important questions remain unanswered.WATCH THE REPORT BELOW: The latest review by the Florida Department of Health follows years of WPTV reporting into concerns raised by patients and families who discovered they lived near others diagnosed with the same aggressive form of brain cancer.While health officials say the data does not show a statistically significant increase in cases, the review does not examine whether patients were concentrated on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.For families who have spent years searching for answers, that distinction matters.READ THE FULL STATE REPORT BELOW: A young man's death helped spark an investigationFor Deb Johnston, the loss of her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., is still painful."It's been eight years since Lenny passed," she said.Lenny was just 33 years old when he died from glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer.He was healthy, active and loved fishing. He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis."Everybody loved Lenny. He just had this charm about him," his mother recalled.Lenny's story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18.After WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories.Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns.Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families.But it wasn't just their ages that raised questions.As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018.Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health.What did the original 2019 investigation find?The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County."You brought it to my attention. It was alarming; it was nerve-wracking," Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, told WPTV's Meghan McRoberts.Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida's cancer registry."I asked for assistance from our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss," he said. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. "We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county."According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year.The report also shows that from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected.Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations.Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns.What questions remain?Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families.Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.That means the review's broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families, determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging.Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source."I wish there was an answer," Sperber said. "I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma."As St. Lucie County's population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well.But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story.A mother's call for a closer look at her hometownFor Johnston, hearing that the state's findings have not changed was difficult."I was deflated when you told me that. I was like, oh my God," she told McRoberts.She remains grateful that health officials are continuing to review the numbers.When asked whether she was glad the state was still looking into the issue, she responded, "Yes … it gives you hope for the others that come behind us."But she wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, rather than relying on broader geographic data.When McRoberts asked where she would like additional testing conducted, her answer was immediate."In the White City area," she said.Nearly eight years after losing her son, Deb says the search for answers has taken an emotional toll."I haven't given up; it's just you get tired," she said.Millions invested in glioblastoma researchSince WPTV's initial reporting, the Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research.Deb has also worked to support research in her son's memory.Each year, she hosts a fishing tournament honoring Lenny, who loved spending time on the water.The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research.Another tournament is approaching, continuing her efforts to help other families facing the same devastating diagnosis.For Deb, the hope is that continued research and closer examination of local cases will eventually provide answers."I'm just glad you have followed through the way that you have," she told McRoberts.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Beachgoers in Martin County urged to stay out of water after high levels of fecal bacteria found: Officials
entry.summary: Martin County health officials are urging beachgoers to stay out of the water this weekend after water quality tested poor in several areas of the county. The Department of Health in Martin County put a health advisory in place after water samples taken Monday came back with unsafe levels of fecal bacteria at 10 locations across the county, including: Sandsprit Park Bathtub Beach Charlie Leighton Park Stuart Sandbar Jensen Beach Causeway Stuart Causeway Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge Jensen Beach Bob Graham Beach Hobe Sound Beach Beach conditions Friday were less than ideal with choppy waters, a red flag flying and water quality concerns. For some beachgoers, the rough surf was reason enough to stay dry. 'You know, it's not safe to swim in the water, especially at this time of year when you want to be in the water,' beachgoer Dan Casamento said. Valentin Kapranoe, a snowbird, just learned that the health department is urging the public to avoid contact with the water. 'Very good waves. Very good waves. It's rough sea, but you told me something is wrong,' Kapranoe said. Once he heard about the advisory, his tone changed. 'I would be a little bit concerned for sure,' Kapranoe said. The health department says exposure could increase the risk of illness in swimmers. Officials say the poor water quality is likely tied to the recent wind, king tides and stormwater runoff from heavy rain. For beachgoer Charlene Cook, the situation was disappointing. 'What a shame especially if you're vacationing,' Cook said. She added that the broader environmental impact concerns her most. 'What bothers me the most is the runoff from the lawns and the lawn treatments and what it does to the environment,' Cook said. The health department plans to resample the water on Monday if conditions allow. Officials told us they expect water quality to stabilize as the weather clears up. entry.title: Woman, 66, charged with 29 counts of animal cruelty after 124 cats removed from Port St. Lucie home
entry.summary: A 66-year-old woman has been arrested on dozens of animal cruelty charges following an investigation that resulted in 124 cats being removed from a Port St. Lucie home , according to police. The Port St. Lucie Police Department said Kimberly K. Robinson was arrested Friday by members of the Marshals Task Force after detectives obtained a warrant charging her with 29 counts of felony animal cruelty. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Woman arrested after more than 120 cats removed from home Port St. Lucie woman arrested after more than 120 cats removed from home The investigation began Oct. 13, when Animal Control responded to a home in the 2500 block of Southwest Warwick Street over concerns about the animals' welfare and unsanitary conditions, police said. Officers initially found more than 60 cats inside the home, according to police. Investigators said there were extensive accumulations of animal feces and urine, a strong ammonia odor and numerous cats that appeared to have untreated medical conditions. Authorities ultimately removed 124 cats, including newborn kittens, juvenile cats and adult cats. The animals were divided between Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County. Police said many required veterinary treatment for conditions including respiratory and eye infections, elevated temperatures, fleas and ear mites. Some cats also had open and infected wounds. Investigators reviewed Animal Control reports, veterinary records and other evidence as part of the case. Police said the 29 felony charges against Robinson are based on veterinary findings involving the first 29 cats that were evaluated. The investigation remains ongoing as authorities review medical findings involving the remaining animals. Police said additional charges could be considered.

entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman, 67, arrested in hoarding of more than 100 cats    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie woman was arrested Friday after 124 cats and kittens were rescued from a hoarding situation in her home. Marshals Service arrested Kimberly K. Lucie Police Department detectives obtained an arrest warrant charging her with 29 counts of cruelty to animals, a third-degree felony. Robinson was arrested in Indian River County on the outstanding warrant. The arrest stems from an investigation that began on Oct. Lucie Animal Control responded to a residence in the 2500 block of Southwest Warwick Street, east of Florida's Turnpike, after concerns about the welfare of animals and unsanitary living conditions. Animal Control officers discovered more than 60 cats inside the residence. Officers observed extensive accumulations of animal feces and urine, an overwhelming ammonia odor, and numerous cats suffering from apparent untreated medical conditions. Officers then made multiple visits to the residence and ultimately removed 124 cats, including newborn kittens, juveniles up to 1 year old and adult cats. Animal Control removed the animals over three days. The animals were divided between Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County after Animal Control reached capacity. PSLPD detectives reviewed Animal Control reports, veterinary medical records and other investigative documentation. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory," Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, earlier told WPBF. "The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues." Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. The Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens.

entry.title: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicated its new regional operations center in Fort Pierce Thursday morning, bringing its work under one roof and expanding its capacity to serve people across four counties. The 132,000-square-foot facility at 401 Loop Road supports the organization’s food storage and fresh food programs, prepared meals, nutrition education, benefits assistance and workforce training. The food bank, which began in 1988, is the only food bank serving Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. It reaches about 250,000 people each week and works with hundreds of nonprofit partners. The center’s production kitchen has more than doubled in size, growing from 7,000 to 15,000 square feet. It can produce up to 25,000 meals a day during a disaster, while also preparing nutritious meals for the community. The new freezer area alone could fit one and a half of the food bank’s former facilities. The center is designed to help people build stability for the future as well as meet immediate needs. Adults and children can take nutrition education classes on site, and nutrition information is sent with food boxes delivered to seniors. Its three job-training programs focus on culinary, hospitality and barista skills. Students learn skills such as knife safety, food safety and making pasta from scratch. The programs offer certifications in stages, and some courses are free. See also: Project Thanksgiving: Ruth & Norman Rales Jewish Family Services helps families in need During the dedication, 10 community members took part in a ceremonial First Box packing to represent the network behind the food bank’s work. Robin Safley of Feeding Florida added fresh vegetables on behalf of the statewide hunger-relief network. Donor Dee Locke added fresh fruit, and volunteer Tatiana Rousseau added peanut butter. The food bank’s capital campaign is continuing. To donate, visit the Feed Unite Flourish capital campaign page . Project Thanksgiving The Treasure Coast Food Bank is also a recipient of donations through CBS12 News' Project Thanksgiving . Drop off non-perishable food items at Treasure Coast iTHINK Financial bank branches to help the food bank feed families this holiday season. Treasure Coast Branches Fellsmere: 56 N. entry.title: Still no cancer cluster? Florida updates Treasure Coast brain cancer review - cw34.com
entry.summary: Still no cancer cluster? Florida updates Treasure Coast brain cancer review    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Florida health officials released an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review Thursday, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. But families who have spent years tracking brain tumor diagnoses say the review still does not answer all of their questions particularly about patients living on the same streets or just doors apart. This upsets me, said Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. I see family after family, and when is it enough? Like, when do we actually look into this problem? The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. I am hopeful that, after reviewing the website and the available documents, you will find reassurance in the thorough work conducted by our public health scientists, Sperber wrote. What the state found The updated assessment examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties, along with three St. Officials compared recorded diagnoses with the number expected based on statewide cancer rates, accounting for age. Lucie County, the state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, the ZIP code analysis found: 34952: 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected. 34983: 21 diagnoses, compared with approximately 20 expected. 34982: 12 diagnoses, compared with approximately 13 expected. None showed a statistically significant excess. Officials said small case numbers can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without an increase in underlying risk. The report does not determine what caused individual patients’ cancers. Questions beyond glioblastoma Ankiel said she was not surprised by the state’s conclusion. Earlier this month, she drove I-Team reporter Katie Bente through Fort Pierce neighborhoods, pointing out homes where she said brain tumor patients had lived in some cases, only doors apart. Her questions are also personal. Ankiel’s husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma in 2012. Ankiel said his cancer was later diagnosed as glioblastoma. Now, Ankiel is helping another patient with the same initial diagnosis. Amber Lee, 37, is living with oligodendroglioma, a brain tumor that is distinct from glioblastoma. The first thing I remember thinking of when they told me I had cancer was, I have a daughter, Lee said. Lee also grew up in the same Fort Pierce neighborhood as Ankiel’s husband. I realized that a lot of those people were family members of people that I grew up with, people that my family, my parents grew up with, Lee said. The shared diagnosis and neighborhood history do not establish a common cause or prove a cancer cluster. But Ankiel believes the geographic patterns deserve a closer examination. The state analyzed entire ZIP codes, not individual streets. Maybe the ZIP codes are a little bit too broad, Ankiel said. Let’s actually, let’s look at some of the streets. Why oligodendroglioma was not counted The updated review focuses specifically on glioblastoma. It excludes oligodendroglioma the tumor Lee is living with and the tumor Ankiel said her husband was initially diagnosed with. The report shows two tumor classification codes included in the state’s 2019 analysis 9450 and 9451 were excluded from the new review. The department said medical classifications have evolved and those oligodendroglioma codes are no longer included in the current glioblastoma definition. The I-Team previously asked health officials how their analysis handles patients whose diagnoses change and whether other brain cancers were examined separately. The report does not explain how a case initially classified as oligodendroglioma and later diagnosed as glioblastoma would be counted. Recent diagnoses fall outside the review The assessment does not include diagnoses from 2024 through 2026. An accompanying FAQ says 2023 was the latest finalized cancer registry year available. Officials said the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy. Lee’s diagnosis falls outside the period examined. Her tumor also would not be included in the glioblastoma analysis because it is classified as oligodendroglioma. Lee said she wants officials to continue studying brain tumor diagnoses in the area. She is especially concerned about her younger sister, who grew up in the same home. I want to know if my sister can get tested somehow before it’s too late for her, Lee said. The review also does not capture more recent glioblastoma diagnoses previously covered by the I-Team. Lucie resident Laura Cooper told CBS12 News in June that she was diagnosed with glioblastoma in November 2025, years after losing her best friend to the disease. At the time of the interview, she was undergoing treatment and participating in a clinical trial. Street-level limitations The report acknowledges limitations in the Florida Cancer Data System. The registry generally records a patient’s address at the time of diagnosis. It does not contain a complete residential history or detailed information about possible environmental exposures. That means a patient’s address at diagnosis may not reflect where that person lived years earlier or where a potentially relevant exposure occurred. The report also does not analyze whether cases are concentrated on individual streets or within smaller sections of the ZIP codes examined. Environmental records reviewed Health officials reviewed public drinking-water records, available private-well data and radiation monitoring around the St. Lucie nuclear power plant. The department reported that its water review did not identify contamination involving chemicals linked by the Environmental Protection Agency to glioblastoma or other brain-related health concerns. It also reported no increase in monitored environmental radiation levels around the plant. The documents describe reviews of existing records and monitoring data. They do not specify whether new environmental samples were collected specifically for this assessment. In Thursday’s email, Sperber highlighted the department’s conclusion that no environmental hazard in the Treasure Coast region has been shown to cause glioblastoma. The scientific journal article provided by the department is a broader review of existing research into environmental hazards and brain tumors. It is not a study of Treasure Coast patients, neighborhoods or environmental conditions. The department said it will continue monitoring cancer incidence and working with state and local partners. Ankiel said she is not trying to work against health officials and wants to work with them. But for the families she has met, the state’s statistical conclusion does not resolve the questions raised by patients living in the same neighborhoods or sometimes only a few houses apart.

entry.title: Florida man receives life sentence for using AI to create child pornography of neighborhood children
entry.summary: A Martin County judge has ordered a sentence equal to life in prison for a man who used artificial intelligence to create child pornography, a case the Martin County Sheriff's Office said it had never seen at that time. Daniel Warren was charged with 75 felony counts of possession of child pornography and seven felony counts of video voyeurism for using AI to create child pornography. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida man receives life sentence for using AI to create child pornography of neighborhood children 'His innocent neighbors, whose parents trusted him to be appropriate with their children, he was taking covert photos of them and then asking for those children to be transformed into some sexualized image which he shared with others,' prosecutor Kristen Chase said. Warren was arrested for these crimes in 2024. At the time, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said it was their first case involving AI and child exploitation. A man who identified himself as an extended family member testified before the judge Wednesday. 'That would be a detriment to the children to have this man even anywhere near a child,' the extended family member said. Before sentencing, Warren showed some remorse. entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie woman, 67, arrested in hoarding of 124 kittens, cats - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman, 67, arrested in hoarding of 124 kittens, cats    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie woman was arrested Friday after 124 cats and kittens were rescued from a hoarding situation in her home. Marshals Service arrested Kimberly K. Lucie Police Department detectives obtained an arrest warrant charging her with 29 counts of cruelty to animals, a third-degree felony. Robinson was arrested in Indian River County on the outstanding warrant. The arrest stems from an investigation that began on Oct. Lucie Animal Control responded to a residence in the 2500 block of Southwest Warwick Street, east of Florida's Turnpike, after concerns about the welfare of animals and unsanitary living conditions. Animal Control officers discovered more than 60 cats inside the residence. Officers observed extensive accumulations of animal feces and urine, an overwhelming ammonia odor, and numerous cats suffering from apparent untreated medical conditions. Officers then made multiple visits to the residence and ultimately removed 124 cats, including newborn kittens, juveniles up to 1 year old and adult cats. Animal Control removed the animals over three days. The animals were divided between Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County after Animal Control reached capacity. PSLPD detectives reviewed Animal Control reports, veterinary medical records and other investigative documentation. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory," Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, earlier told WPBF. "The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues." Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. The Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens.

entry.article_text: Daniel Clark Warren was sentenced to more than 84 years in prison after being found guilty on 82 counts, including possessing child sexual abuse material and video voyeurism involving a minor, according to court records. Warren was adjudicated guilty on all counts Wednesday in Martin County . The court sentenced him to 1,013.1 months in Florida Department of Corrections custody, with credit for 1,002 days already served. That sentence is about 84 years and five months. The charges included 75 counts of possessing 10 or more images of child pornography and seven counts of video voyeurism involving a victim younger than 16 and an offender 24 or older, court records show. See also: 'Did he actually point the gun?' Family questions fatal Boca Raton deputy shooting The court denied a request for a downward departure from the sentence and designated Warren a sexual offender, according to handwritten court notes. Warren was arrested in 2024 after investigators accused him of using artificial intelligence to create child sexual abuse images from real photos. He takes the face of a child and then he sexualizes that, removes the clothing and poses the child, and engages them in certain sexual activity, and that’s the images he’s making with this AI," Det. Brian Broughton of the Special Victims Unit at the Martin County Sheriff's Office said at the time of Warren's arrest in 2024. "He was very friendly to many of the neighborhood children, as well as the other families, and so it was an activity that happened in the shadows, and the other families were unaware, Broughton told CBS12 News at the time.

entry.article_text: Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Their conclusion remains largely unchanged. “The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today,” Sperber told WPTV. “We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county.” According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year. The report also shows that from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected. Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations. Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.

entry.article_text: Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.The dueling developments came days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate.Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.”Separately, the Justice Department — as part of a lawsuit it filed last week — asked a judge to order that state elections officials isolate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan to investigate potential voter “confusion” with the senator. The owner of a boat dealership in the candidate's hometown of Petersburg who had donated to his campaign told The Associated Press that an FBI agent visited the business and wanted to know whether he had been misled by Dan J. He said he had not and that “Everybody knows who the incumbent is.”Alaska Assistant U.S. Bryan Wilson, in a filing, said the government “seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary.”The Department of Justice also filed with the court a list of proposed questions it seeks to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer as part of the civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he told the department to file the case.State elections officials made efforts to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballotPeltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot: “I am not interested in tricking voters,” she said.RELATED STORY | Peltola denies involvement as DOJ expands Alaska election investigationDemocrats, including the DSCC, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest.The request to segregate the ballots in Alaska comes after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department’s request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election sent to some 20,000 people the administration contends may not be U.S. California officials argued the list is highly unreliable and most likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.Justice Department attorneys in the Alaska case said there is a “substantial risk” that Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy “will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity.”“To guard against this danger, the United States seeks an order directing Defendants to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary,” the filing states. It requests a decision by Monday.Attorneys for the state in response questioned how segregation would be possible, writing that voters' ballots are commingled in the ballot box on Election Day and that election workers couldn't segregate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan without violating ballot secrecy protections. Ballots segregated or not wouldn't reveal any voter's reason for voting for Dan J. Sullivan, they said.They have asked a judge to dismiss the case and said Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, while the challenger is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. That's also how they appeared on the August open primary ballot.Attorneys for the state also have argued that Alaska’s ranked voting system further addresses concerns about potential confusion by allowing voters to rank both Sullivans.Timing of Justice Department announcements unusualHeyman on Friday would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but asked members of the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.RELATED STORY | Alaska governor orders investigation into ‘Dan Sullivan’ ballot controversyIt’s highly unusual for Justice Department officials to publicly discuss a criminal investigation or even confirm its existence. The timing of the press conference is particularly notable given the Justice Department has had a longstanding practice of avoiding taking public steps in the weeks leading up to an election that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.Trump during a rally late Friday in Florida said Peltola and Dan J. Sullivan should be prosecuted. Attorney General Todd Blanche was in attendance and said, “He’s going to make his own decision.”Trump, then addressing Blanche directly, said of decisions regarding the case, “Todd, please make your own,” and watched Blanche’s response.Trump added: “OK, he said ‘yes.’”Peltola, at a campaign rally in Anchorage late Friday, said she is “so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else’s candidacy.” She said she doesn't need any help in winning the race outside of the support of voters.She was asked before the rally if it was possible that someone on her campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan: “I have no idea,” she told KTUU. “I honestly have no idea.”The Times story revealing the potential recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan was based partly on interviews with a former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired before the August primary. Asked about Rios by the station, Peltola said certain people are “gone for a good reason. If I could fire them again, I’d be happy to fire them again.”Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said, following The New York Times' reporting, that he'd ordered an investigation into whether any violations took place.Meanwhile, the Alaska Democratic Party has sued state elections officials, alleging absentee in-person voting sites did not open as advertised in some rural communities. The director of the Division of Elections in a letter dated Monday said the agency signs agreements with local or tribal offices to operate the sites and that most of the 18 highlighted had opened. A message seeking comment from the state Department of Law was not immediately returned.

entry.summary: Woman, 66, charged with 29 counts of animal cruelty after 124 cats removed from Port St. Lucie home    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 66-year-old woman has been arrested on dozens of animal cruelty charges following an investigation that resulted in 124 cats being removed from a Port St. Lucie home , according to police. Lucie Police Department said Kimberly K. Robinson was arrested Friday by members of the Marshals Task Force after detectives obtained a warrant charging her with 29 counts of felony animal cruelty. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Woman arrested after more than 120 cats removed from home The investigation began Oct. 13, when Animal Control responded to a home in the 2500 block of Southwest Warwick Street over concerns about the animals' welfare and unsanitary conditions, police said. Officers initially found more than 60 cats inside the home, according to police. Investigators said there were extensive accumulations of animal feces and urine, a strong ammonia odor and numerous cats that appeared to have untreated medical conditions. Authorities ultimately removed 124 cats, including newborn kittens, juvenile cats and adult cats. The animals were divided between Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Police said many required veterinary treatment for conditions including respiratory and eye infections, elevated temperatures, fleas and ear mites. Some cats also had open and infected wounds. Investigators reviewed Animal Control reports, veterinary records and other evidence as part of the case. Police said the 29 felony charges against Robinson are based on veterinary findings involving the first 29 cats that were evaluated. The investigation remains ongoing as authorities review medical findings involving the remaining animals. Police said additional charges could be considered.

entry.title: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center - cw34.com
entry.summary: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicated its new regional operations center in Fort Pierce Thursday morning, bringing its work under one roof and expanding its capacity to serve people across four counties. The 132,000-square-foot facility at 401 Loop Road supports the organization’s food storage and fresh food programs, prepared meals, nutrition education, benefits assistance and workforce training. The food bank, which began in 1988, is the only food bank serving Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. It reaches about 250,000 people each week and works with hundreds of nonprofit partners. The center’s production kitchen has more than doubled in size, growing from 7,000 to 15,000 square feet. It can produce up to 25,000 meals a day during a disaster, while also preparing nutritious meals for the community. The new freezer area alone could fit one and a half of the food bank’s former facilities. The center is designed to help people build stability for the future as well as meet immediate needs. Adults and children can take nutrition education classes on site, and nutrition information is sent with food boxes delivered to seniors. Its three job-training programs focus on culinary, hospitality and barista skills. Students learn skills such as knife safety, food safety and making pasta from scratch. The programs offer certifications in stages, and some courses are free. See also: Project Thanksgiving: Ruth & Norman Rales Jewish Family Services helps families in need During the dedication, 10 community members took part in a ceremonial First Box packing to represent the network behind the food bank’s work. Robin Safley of Feeding Florida added fresh vegetables on behalf of the statewide hunger-relief network. Donor Dee Locke added fresh fruit, and volunteer Tatiana Rousseau added peanut butter. The food bank’s capital campaign is continuing. To donate, visit the Feed Unite Flourish capital campaign page . Project Thanksgiving The Treasure Coast Food Bank is also a recipient of donations through CBS12 News' Project Thanksgiving . Drop off non-perishable food items at Treasure Coast iTHINK Financial bank branches to help the food bank feed families this holiday season. Treasure Coast Branches Fellsmere: 56 N. entry.title: Health Department takes another look at St. Lucie County glioblastoma cases - WPTV
entry.summary: Health Department takes another look at St. Lucie County glioblastoma cases    WPTV
entry.article_text: Nearly eight years after WPTV first investigated concerns about a possible cluster of glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County, health officials have reviewed the numbers again.The latest findings show the number of cases remains in line with what would be expected based on the county's population, but families who lost loved ones to the deadly brain cancer say important questions remain unanswered.WATCH THE REPORT BELOW: The latest review by the Florida Department of Health follows years of WPTV reporting into concerns raised by patients and families who discovered they lived near others diagnosed with the same aggressive form of brain cancer.While health officials say the data does not show a statistically significant increase in cases, the review does not examine whether patients were concentrated on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.For families who have spent years searching for answers, that distinction matters.READ THE FULL STATE REPORT BELOW: A young man's death helped spark an investigationFor Deb Johnston, the loss of her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., is still painful."It's been eight years since Lenny passed," she said.Lenny was just 33 years old when he died from glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer.He was healthy, active and loved fishing. He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis."Everybody loved Lenny. He just had this charm about him," his mother recalled.Lenny's story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18.After WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories.Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns.Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families.But it wasn't just their ages that raised questions.As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018.Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health.What did the original 2019 investigation find?The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County."You brought it to my attention. It was alarming; it was nerve-wracking," Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, told WPTV's Meghan McRoberts.Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida's cancer registry."I asked for assistance from our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss," he said. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. "We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county."According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year.The report also shows that from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected.Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations.Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns.What questions remain?Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families.Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.That means the review's broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families, determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging.Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source."I wish there was an answer," Sperber said. "I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma."As St. Lucie County's population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well.But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story.A mother's call for a closer look at her hometownFor Johnston, hearing that the state's findings have not changed was difficult."I was deflated when you told me that. I was like, oh my God," she told McRoberts.She remains grateful that health officials are continuing to review the numbers.When asked whether she was glad the state was still looking into the issue, she responded, "Yes … it gives you hope for the others that come behind us."But she wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, rather than relying on broader geographic data.When McRoberts asked where she would like additional testing conducted, her answer was immediate."In the White City area," she said.Nearly eight years after losing her son, Deb says the search for answers has taken an emotional toll."I haven't given up; it's just you get tired," she said.Millions invested in glioblastoma researchSince WPTV's initial reporting, the Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research.Deb has also worked to support research in her son's memory.Each year, she hosts a fishing tournament honoring Lenny, who loved spending time on the water.The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research.Another tournament is approaching, continuing her efforts to help other families facing the same devastating diagnosis.For Deb, the hope is that continued research and closer examination of local cases will eventually provide answers."I'm just glad you have followed through the way that you have," she told McRoberts.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Jensen Beach man sentenced to 84 years in AI child pornography, voyeurism case - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach man sentenced to 84 years in AI child pornography, voyeurism case    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 53-year-old Jensen Beach man was sentenced to more than 84 years in prison on 82 counts of child pornography in Martin County's first arrest in a case involving artificial intelligence in 2024. On Wednesday, Daniel Clark Warren was sentenced by Circuit Judge Elizabeth Metzger to 1,013.1 months in prison with credit for 1,002 days already served. The judge denied the defense's request for a downward departure from the sentence. In July, before a scheduled jury trial, he changed his plea to guilty on all counts of child sexual abuse material and video voyeurism involving a minor. Warren was arrested on Jan. 26, 2024, after detectives received an internet crime tip about child pornography. "It's pretty scary when you look at this stuff," Det. Brian Broughton said at the time about creating the images using AI. "This is our first case in Martin County where we have seen AI taking a regular headshot and then turning them into child porn and it's alarming to us," John Budensiek, chief deputy at the time and now sheriff, said. At least one image was of a child under the age of 5, according to the arrest report. "What he does is he takes the face of a child and then he sexualizes that removes the clothing and poses the child and engages them in certain sexual activity and that's the images that he's making with his AI," Broughton said. It took several months for the state to arrest him. "The reason why we waited this long to put it out is because our detectives have been working with other jurisdictions to try and figure out if there are other cases related to this," Budensiek said. The FBI warns child sexual abuse material created with content manipulation technologies, to include generative artificial intelligence, is illegal. "There's been a couple of years now we've seen the deepfakes with celebrities and politicians," Broughton said. "This is just a new level. This is scary stuff." Since then, AI has become more prominent with even better deepfakes.

entry.title: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicated its new regional operations center in Fort Pierce Thursday morning, bringing its work under one roof and expanding its capacity to serve people across four counties. The 132,000-square-foot facility at 401 Loop Road supports the organization’s food storage and fresh food programs, prepared meals, nutrition education, benefits assistance and workforce training. The food bank, which began in 1988, is the only food bank serving Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. It reaches about 250,000 people each week and works with hundreds of nonprofit partners. The center’s production kitchen has more than doubled in size, growing from 7,000 to 15,000 square feet. It can produce up to 25,000 meals a day during a disaster, while also preparing nutritious meals for the community. The new freezer area alone could fit one and a half of the food bank’s former facilities. The center is designed to help people build stability for the future as well as meet immediate needs. Adults and children can take nutrition education classes on site, and nutrition information is sent with food boxes delivered to seniors. Its three job-training programs focus on culinary, hospitality and barista skills. Students learn skills such as knife safety, food safety and making pasta from scratch. The programs offer certifications in stages, and some courses are free. See also: Project Thanksgiving: Ruth & Norman Rales Jewish Family Services helps families in need During the dedication, 10 community members took part in a ceremonial First Box packing to represent the network behind the food bank’s work. Robin Safley of Feeding Florida added fresh vegetables on behalf of the statewide hunger-relief network. Donor Dee Locke added fresh fruit, and volunteer Tatiana Rousseau added peanut butter. The food bank’s capital campaign is continuing. To donate, visit the Feed Unite Flourish capital campaign page . Project Thanksgiving The Treasure Coast Food Bank is also a recipient of donations through CBS12 News' Project Thanksgiving . Drop off non-perishable food items at Treasure Coast iTHINK Financial bank branches to help the food bank feed families this holiday season. Treasure Coast Branches Fellsmere: 56 N. entry.title: Deputies locate wanted Broward County man after Fort Pierce hotel disturbance - WPEC
entry.summary: Deputies locate wanted Broward County man after Fort Pierce hotel disturbance    WPEC
entry.article_text: A report of a woman being assaulted and pushed into a car at a Fort Pierce hotel led deputies to a Broward County man wanted in four felony probation cases, authorities said. Deputies say they were called to the Best Western in the 7900 block of South U.S. Highway 1 around 11:20 p.m. Friday after a witness reported seeing a man assault a woman, push her into a vehicle, and drive away, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . Deputies reportedly confirmed a battery had occurred and identified the suspect as 37-year-old Guyrson Maddy of Broward County. A records check found an active warrant for probation violations in four separate felony cases dating from 2017 to 2025. See also: Rescue crews search Delray Beach pond after car found submerged Court records show Maddy’s criminal history dates back to 2012. It includes cases involving battery on a law enforcement officer, grand theft of a motor vehicle, third-degree grand theft, and organized fraud. Investigators also identified a dark-colored 2025 Tesla Model Y they believed was involved. Deputies found a vehicle matching that description at a home on Palm Breezes Drive. A woman at the home confirmed she had been at the hotel and directed deputies to a bathroom where they found Maddy. Deputy Mendoza and his K-9 partner, Oso, helped find him. Maddy followed deputies’ commands and was arrested without incident, the sheriff’s office said. Maddy is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a domestic battery charge, with Broward County holds for probation violations.

entry.title: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff’s deputy turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued in connection with an off-duty crash in Vero Beach, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Read also: Road Ranger killed, hit at crash scene on I-95 near Lantana Road Deputy Tyler Horstman was driving an agency vehicle when he was involved in the crash on March 1, the sheriff’s office said. On September 9, the Sheriff’s Office received Horstman’s blood-test results. They showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit. According to the arrest report, March 1 at about 11:25pm at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach, Horstman was off-duty driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he hit a Chevy Equinox with a woman and an infant inside. Vero Beach police say Horstman was driving at 63 mph in a posted 35 mph zone and entered the intersection on a green light. The other driver entered the intersection against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital, and the infant was not injured. The arrest report says: "Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening." It says Horstman had a "faint odor of alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and later posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

entry.title: 'Have no word': St. Lucie County mourns firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge after on-duty death - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Have no word': St. Lucie County mourns firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge after on-duty death    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District is honoring the life and service of firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died Saturday while on duty. On Monday afternoon, firefighters escorted Hodge’s body from the medical examiner’s office to a funeral home in Fort Pierce. Tears, respect and a sense of loss were visible on the faces of those gathered to pay tribute. FIREFIGHTER MOURNED: Family honors late St. Lucie County firefighter’s birthday with cookout and balloon release His fellow firefighters, friends and members of the community came together to honor Hodge’s more than nine years of service. Diana Harrison, who has known Hodge’s mother since the early 1990s, shared her memories of him. “So, we actually homeschooled our kids together. Austin was just a little bitty guy back then,” Harrison said. Friends and coworkers expressed the heartbreak of losing Hodge, especially as his brother, Jarius Hodge, also a firefighter-paramedic with the St. Lucie County Fire District, died last year after falling ill while on duty. “I have no words, there’s no words, and the brokenness, the sadness — you can’t imagine losing not one son but two sons,” Harrison said. The fire district reported that Austin Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse during a shift change Saturday. Crews immediately began life-saving measures, but Hodge later died at the hospital. Lucie County Fire District holds procession for firefighter Austin Hodge Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Hodge joined the district’s firefighter challenge team in 2018 and helped the team win a world championship in 2021. "He was always a giver, even from a little bitty kid, you know. And if I remember right, even when he was a little kid, he wanted to be a firefighter, and then that's what he became," Harrison said. Howard Dunn Jr., founder of the Howard Dunn Jr. Foundation, which supports first responders, shared his personal connection to Hodge. “A couple of years ago I had a close call, and when the rescue came to me, I met Austin. I had an emergency; they transported me to the hospital. He made me feel better — I forgot what I was going for,” Dunn said. Retired lieutenant and former fire district chaplain Thomas Neiman reflected on the Hodge family’s impact on the community. “Knowing that we saw those kids as grade school kids in the library for our homeschool co-op meetings,” Neiman said. “And of course, we can’t begin to imagine what the family and mom and dad are going through, but we’re holding on to them as best we can, and they know we love them." Funeral arrangements for Austin Hodge have not yet been announced. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.article_text: An arrest has been made in a Port St. Lucie hoarding case in which 124 cats some of which were deceased were found inside of a home, according to the Port St. PSLPD says that Kimberly K. Robinson, 66, was arrested on Friday after detectives obtained an arrest warrant to charge her with 29 counts of cruelty to animals. This investigation began on Oct. 13, after Animal Control responded to a residence at the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street with concerns about the welfare of animals and unsanitary living conditions. More than 60 cats were discovered inside of the residence during the initial response, PSLPD says. Officers observed extensive accumulations of animal urine and feces, an ammonia odor, and several cats suffering from untreated medical conditions. Through multiple visits, a total of 124 cats of all ages were found. See also: Owner sought after 8-month-old shepherd mix found with injured, bleeding hind legs The cats were divided between Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County after Animal Control reached capacity, PSLPD says. Many of them required veterinary attention for numerous medical conditions. This investigation remains active, according to PSLPD.

entry.title: Jensen Beach man sentenced to 84 years in AI child pornography, voyeurism case - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach man sentenced to 84 years in AI child pornography, voyeurism case    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 53-year-old Jensen Beach man was sentenced to more than 84 years in prison on 82 counts of child pornography in Martin County's first arrest in a case involving artificial intelligence in 2024. On Wednesday, Daniel Clark Warren was sentenced by Circuit Judge Elizabeth Metzger to 1,013.1 months in prison with credit for 1,002 days already served. The judge denied the defense's request for a downward departure from the sentence. In July, before a scheduled jury trial, he changed his plea to guilty on all counts of child sexual abuse material and video voyeurism involving a minor. Warren was arrested on Jan. 26, 2024, after detectives received an internet crime tip about child pornography. "It's pretty scary when you look at this stuff," Det. Brian Broughton said at the time about creating the images using AI. "This is our first case in Martin County where we have seen AI taking a regular headshot and then turning them into child porn and it's alarming to us," John Budensiek, chief deputy at the time and now sheriff, said. At least one image was of a child under the age of 5, according to the arrest report. "What he does is he takes the face of a child and then he sexualizes that removes the clothing and poses the child and engages them in certain sexual activity and that's the images that he's making with his AI," Broughton said. It took several months for the state to arrest him. "The reason why we waited this long to put it out is because our detectives have been working with other jurisdictions to try and figure out if there are other cases related to this," Budensiek said. The FBI warns child sexual abuse material created with content manipulation technologies, to include generative artificial intelligence, is illegal. "There's been a couple of years now we've seen the deepfakes with celebrities and politicians," Broughton said. "This is just a new level. This is scary stuff." Since then, AI has become more prominent with even better deepfakes.

entry.title: Still no cancer cluster? Florida updates Treasure Coast brain cancer review - cw34.com
entry.summary: Still no cancer cluster? Florida updates Treasure Coast brain cancer review    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Florida health officials released an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review Thursday, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. But families who have spent years tracking brain tumor diagnoses say the review still does not answer all of their questions particularly about patients living on the same streets or just doors apart. This upsets me, said Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. I see family after family, and when is it enough? Like, when do we actually look into this problem? The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. I am hopeful that, after reviewing the website and the available documents, you will find reassurance in the thorough work conducted by our public health scientists, Sperber wrote. What the state found The updated assessment examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties, along with three St. Officials compared recorded diagnoses with the number expected based on statewide cancer rates, accounting for age. Lucie County, the state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, the ZIP code analysis found: 34952: 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected. 34983: 21 diagnoses, compared with approximately 20 expected. 34982: 12 diagnoses, compared with approximately 13 expected. None showed a statistically significant excess. Officials said small case numbers can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without an increase in underlying risk. The report does not determine what caused individual patients’ cancers. Questions beyond glioblastoma Ankiel said she was not surprised by the state’s conclusion. Earlier this month, she drove I-Team reporter Katie Bente through Fort Pierce neighborhoods, pointing out homes where she said brain tumor patients had lived in some cases, only doors apart. Her questions are also personal. Ankiel’s husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma in 2012. Ankiel said his cancer was later diagnosed as glioblastoma. Now, Ankiel is helping another patient with the same initial diagnosis. Amber Lee, 37, is living with oligodendroglioma, a brain tumor that is distinct from glioblastoma. The first thing I remember thinking of when they told me I had cancer was, I have a daughter, Lee said. Lee also grew up in the same Fort Pierce neighborhood as Ankiel’s husband. I realized that a lot of those people were family members of people that I grew up with, people that my family, my parents grew up with, Lee said. The shared diagnosis and neighborhood history do not establish a common cause or prove a cancer cluster. But Ankiel believes the geographic patterns deserve a closer examination. The state analyzed entire ZIP codes, not individual streets. Maybe the ZIP codes are a little bit too broad, Ankiel said. Let’s actually, let’s look at some of the streets. Why oligodendroglioma was not counted The updated review focuses specifically on glioblastoma. It excludes oligodendroglioma the tumor Lee is living with and the tumor Ankiel said her husband was initially diagnosed with. The report shows two tumor classification codes included in the state’s 2019 analysis 9450 and 9451 were excluded from the new review. The department said medical classifications have evolved and those oligodendroglioma codes are no longer included in the current glioblastoma definition. The I-Team previously asked health officials how their analysis handles patients whose diagnoses change and whether other brain cancers were examined separately. The report does not explain how a case initially classified as oligodendroglioma and later diagnosed as glioblastoma would be counted. Recent diagnoses fall outside the review The assessment does not include diagnoses from 2024 through 2026. An accompanying FAQ says 2023 was the latest finalized cancer registry year available. Officials said the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy. Lee’s diagnosis falls outside the period examined. Her tumor also would not be included in the glioblastoma analysis because it is classified as oligodendroglioma. Lee said she wants officials to continue studying brain tumor diagnoses in the area. She is especially concerned about her younger sister, who grew up in the same home. I want to know if my sister can get tested somehow before it’s too late for her, Lee said. The review also does not capture more recent glioblastoma diagnoses previously covered by the I-Team. Lucie resident Laura Cooper told CBS12 News in June that she was diagnosed with glioblastoma in November 2025, years after losing her best friend to the disease. At the time of the interview, she was undergoing treatment and participating in a clinical trial. Street-level limitations The report acknowledges limitations in the Florida Cancer Data System. The registry generally records a patient’s address at the time of diagnosis. It does not contain a complete residential history or detailed information about possible environmental exposures. That means a patient’s address at diagnosis may not reflect where that person lived years earlier or where a potentially relevant exposure occurred. The report also does not analyze whether cases are concentrated on individual streets or within smaller sections of the ZIP codes examined. Environmental records reviewed Health officials reviewed public drinking-water records, available private-well data and radiation monitoring around the St. Lucie nuclear power plant. The department reported that its water review did not identify contamination involving chemicals linked by the Environmental Protection Agency to glioblastoma or other brain-related health concerns. It also reported no increase in monitored environmental radiation levels around the plant. The documents describe reviews of existing records and monitoring data. They do not specify whether new environmental samples were collected specifically for this assessment. In Thursday’s email, Sperber highlighted the department’s conclusion that no environmental hazard in the Treasure Coast region has been shown to cause glioblastoma. The scientific journal article provided by the department is a broader review of existing research into environmental hazards and brain tumors. It is not a study of Treasure Coast patients, neighborhoods or environmental conditions. The department said it will continue monitoring cancer incidence and working with state and local partners. Ankiel said she is not trying to work against health officials and wants to work with them. But for the families she has met, the state’s statistical conclusion does not resolve the questions raised by patients living in the same neighborhoods or sometimes only a few houses apart.
