entry.title: West Palm Beach entrepreneur brings Vietnamese coffee and culture to the GreenMarket
entry.summary: The West Palm Beach GreenMarket is more than a weekend destination. For local entrepreneurs, it can also be a launching pad for growing a small business. For this week's Small Business Saturday, WPTV's Christy Waite checked out Ba Cafe, a mobile coffee company specializing in Vietnamese coffee that is now a full-time vendor at the GreenMarket. Founder Kimberly Truong was born and raised in West Palm Beach and named Ba Cafe after her late father. WATCH: West Palm Beach entrepreneur brings Vietnamese coffee and culture to the GreenMarket Ba Cafe at the GreenMarket 'We specialize in Vietnamese coffee and we are a mobile coffee company,' Truong said. For Truong, the business is about more than serving coffee. It's also an opportunity to share Vietnamese culture with the community. 'There is not a lot of Vietnamese representation so it's my mission to introduce people to our coffee and culture,' Truong said. The flavor starts thousands of miles away. Truong said she brews her coffee using 100% Robusta beans imported from Vietnam. 'I brew my coffee with 100% Robusta beans that I get imported from Vietnam,' she said. And the coffee packs a punch because the main difference is that it has double the caffeine compared to arabica beans which is mostly sold in America. Vietnamese coffee is traditionally served over ice, and Truong offers several varieties at her GreenMarket stand, including two of her most popular options like the classic Vietnamese coffee, and the salt coffee, Truong and Ba Cafe are back at the GreenMarket this year, but this time the business is there full time. 'I love the people here and interacting with them, especially since they were voted the number one market in the country,' Truong said.

entry.title: In-person early voting hits record pace for midterms
entry.summary: Early voting for the 2026 midterm election has already surpassed the number of ballots cast before Election Day in 2022, according to the University of Florida Election Lab. As of midday Saturday, more than 51.3 million ballots had been cast ahead of Tuesday's election. By comparison, 45.9 million ballots were cast before Election Day in 2022. RELATED STORY | Democrats tout momentum as early voting rises ahead of midterms The data suggest a growing preference among voters to cast ballots in person before Election Day. More than 28 million voters have already cast ballots in person, compared with about 20.5 million in-person early votes in 2022. Among states that report party registration data for early voters, Democrats account for 43.2% of ballots cast, compared with 31.7% for Republicans. Independent and unaffiliated voters make up 25.1% of the early vote in those states. Not every state releases a partisan breakdown of early voters. However, Democrats have improved their early voting turnout in 16 of the 25 states that have reported data. The University of Florida Election Lab said the 2026 election continues a broader trend of voters casting ballots before Election Day, a shift that accelerated during the COVID-19 pandemic. entry.summary: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates new Fort Pierce operations center    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicated its new regional operations center in Fort Pierce Thursday morning, bringing its work under one roof and expanding its capacity to serve people across four counties. The 132,000-square-foot facility at 401 Loop Road supports the organization’s food storage and fresh food programs, prepared meals, nutrition education, benefits assistance and workforce training. The food bank, which began in 1988, is the only food bank serving Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. It reaches about 250,000 people each week and works with hundreds of nonprofit partners. The center’s production kitchen has more than doubled in size, growing from 7,000 to 15,000 square feet. It can produce up to 25,000 meals a day during a disaster, while also preparing nutritious meals for the community. The new freezer area alone could fit one and a half of the food bank’s former facilities. The center is designed to help people build stability for the future as well as meet immediate needs. Adults and children can take nutrition education classes on site, and nutrition information is sent with food boxes delivered to seniors. Its three job-training programs focus on culinary, hospitality and barista skills. Students learn skills such as knife safety, food safety and making pasta from scratch. The programs offer certifications in stages, and some courses are free. See also: Project Thanksgiving: Ruth & Norman Rales Jewish Family Services helps families in need During the dedication, 10 community members took part in a ceremonial First Box packing to represent the network behind the food bank’s work. Robin Safley of Feeding Florida added fresh vegetables on behalf of the statewide hunger-relief network. Donor Dee Locke added fresh fruit, and volunteer Tatiana Rousseau added peanut butter. The food bank’s capital campaign is continuing. To donate, visit the Feed Unite Flourish capital campaign page . It includes cases involving battery on a law enforcement officer, grand theft of a motor vehicle, third-degree grand theft, and organized fraud. Investigators also identified a dark-colored 2025 Tesla Model Y they believed was involved. Deputies found a vehicle matching that description at a home on Palm Breezes Drive. A woman at the home confirmed she had been at the hotel and directed deputies to a bathroom where they found Maddy. Deputy Mendoza and his K-9 partner, Oso, helped find him. entry.title: Jensen Beach man sentenced to 84 years in AI child pornography, voyeurism case - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach man sentenced to 84 years in AI child pornography, voyeurism case    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 53-year-old Jensen Beach man was sentenced to more than 84 years in prison on 82 counts of child pornography in Martin County's first arrest in a case involving artificial intelligence in 2024. On Wednesday, Daniel Clark Warren was sentenced by Circuit Judge Elizabeth Metzger to 1,013.1 months in prison with credit for 1,002 days already served. The judge denied the defense's request for a downward departure from the sentence. In July, before a scheduled jury trial, he changed his plea to guilty on all counts of child sexual abuse material and video voyeurism involving a minor. Warren was arrested on Jan. 26, 2024, after detectives received an internet crime tip about child pornography. "It's pretty scary when you look at this stuff," Det. Brian Broughton said at the time about creating the images using AI. "This is our first case in Martin County where we have seen AI taking a regular headshot and then turning them into child porn and it's alarming to us," John Budensiek, chief deputy at the time and now sheriff, said. At least one image was of a child under the age of 5, according to the arrest report. "What he does is he takes the face of a child and then he sexualizes that removes the clothing and poses the child and engages them in certain sexual activity and that's the images that he's making with his AI," Broughton said. It took several months for the state to arrest him. "The reason why we waited this long to put it out is because our detectives have been working with other jurisdictions to try and figure out if there are other cases related to this," Budensiek said. The FBI warns child sexual abuse material created with content manipulation technologies, to include generative artificial intelligence, is illegal. "There's been a couple of years now we've seen the deepfakes with celebrities and politicians," Broughton said. "This is just a new level. This is scary stuff." Since then, AI has become more prominent with even better deepfakes.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie woman, 67, arrested in hoarding of 124 kittens, cats - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman, 67, arrested in hoarding of 124 kittens, cats    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie woman was arrested Friday after 124 cats and kittens were rescued from a hoarding situation in her home. Marshals Service arrested Kimberly K. Lucie Police Department detectives obtained an arrest warrant charging her with 29 counts of cruelty to animals, a third-degree felony. Robinson was arrested in Indian River County on the outstanding warrant. The arrest stems from an investigation that began on Oct. Lucie Animal Control responded to a residence in the 2500 block of Southwest Warwick Street, east of Florida's Turnpike, after concerns about the welfare of animals and unsanitary living conditions. Animal Control officers discovered more than 60 cats inside the residence. Officers observed extensive accumulations of animal feces and urine, an overwhelming ammonia odor, and numerous cats suffering from apparent untreated medical conditions. Officers then made multiple visits to the residence and ultimately removed 124 cats, including newborn kittens, juveniles up to 1 year old and adult cats. Animal Control removed the animals over three days. The animals were divided between Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County after Animal Control reached capacity. PSLPD detectives reviewed Animal Control reports, veterinary medical records and other investigative documentation. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory," Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, earlier told WPBF. "The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues." Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. The Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens.

entry.title: West Palm Beach entrepreneur brings Vietnamese coffee and culture to the GreenMarket
entry.summary: The West Palm Beach GreenMarket is more than a weekend destination. For local entrepreneurs, it can also be a launching pad for growing a small business. For this week's Small Business Saturday, WPTV's Christy Waite checked out Ba Cafe, a mobile coffee company specializing in Vietnamese coffee that is now a full-time vendor at the GreenMarket. WATCH: West Palm Beach entrepreneur brings Vietnamese coffee and culture to the GreenMarket Ba Cafe at the GreenMarket Founder Kimberly Truong was born and raised in West Palm Beach and named Ba Cafe after her late father. 'We specialize in Vietnamese coffee and we are a mobile coffee company,' Truong said. For Truong, the business is about more than serving coffee. It's also an opportunity to share Vietnamese culture with the community. 'There is not a lot of Vietnamese representation so it's my mission to introduce people to our coffee and culture,' Truong said. The flavor starts thousands of miles away. Truong said she brews her coffee using 100% Robusta beans imported from Vietnam. 'I brew my coffee with 100% Robusta beans that I get imported from Vietnam,' she said. And the coffee packs a punch because the main difference is that it has double the caffeine compared to arabica beans which is mostly sold in America. Vietnamese coffee is traditionally served over ice, and Truong offers several varieties at her GreenMarket stand, including two of her most popular options like the classic Vietnamese coffee, and the salt coffee, Truong and Ba Cafe are back at the GreenMarket this year, but this time the business is there full time. 'I love the people here and interacting with them, especially since they were voted the number one market in the country,' Truong said.

entry.summary: Early voting ends on the Treasure Coast, Okeechobee County    WPBF
entry.article_text: Early voting ended on the Treasure Coast and in Okeechobee County on Saturday for Tuesday's General Election. In Palm Beach County, residents are still able to visit any of the 28 early polling sites on Sunday. On the Treasure Coast, the early voting totals are nearly 56,000 in St. Lucie County, around 29,000 each in Martin and Indian River counties, and more than 3,700 in Okeechobee County. In addition, residents statewide have the option to vote by mail. It was a busy day at the Martin County Supervisor of Elections Office in Stuart as workers wrapped up early voting. "We've had a great turnout in Martin County," Vicki Davis told WPBF. Martin County officials say more than 40% of registered voters cast their ballots by mail or during early voting. That's already higher than the overall 29% turnout in the primary. After early voting, the only time to vote in person is on Election Day at their designated precinct. Vote-by-mail ballots can be returned to county elections offices during business hours Monday or by 7 p.m. Election officials don't go by postmarks. "The biggest concern heading into Tuesday is voters knowing where their voting location is. So voters can access their voting location by going to our website at MartinVotes.gov or giving us a cal at 772-288-5637." More than 2.8 million of 13.7 million registered Floridians have already voted early, compared with over 50 million ballots cast nationwide ahead of Election Day. Also, around 1.8 million vote-by-mail ballots have been counted in Florida. In Palm Beach County, nearly 178,000 people have submitted their ballots early. entry.title: Florida voters weigh 3 amendments impacting homestead taxes, budget stabilization, agricultural industry
entry.summary: Florida voters will decide three statewide amendments when they head to the polls on Tuesday, with a property tax proposal drawing the most attention. Amendment 1 would boost Florida's budget stabilization fund from 10% to 25% and require annual transfers into the fund of up to $750 million. Lawmakers would be allowed to use those reserves for certain critical state needs. Supporters say it strengthens the state's financial safety net, while critics argue the money is better spent addressing current needs. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida voters weigh three amendments Tuesday impacting homestead taxes, budget stabilization and the agricultural industry Another measure on the ballot, Amendment 2, would exempt agricultural equipment and other farm-related tangible personal property from property taxes. Supporters say it would help farmers and the agriculture industry. Opponents say it could reduce revenue for local services. Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Supporters say it would provide relief for homeowners and limit government spending. Opponents warn it could reduce local revenue. All three amendments need 60% approval to pass. Early voting ended Saturday in Martin and Okeechobee counties and wraps up Sunday in St. Lucie, Indian River and Palm Beach counties. Election Day is Tuesday Nov. 3. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: King tides and strong onshore winds have caused significant coastal erosion along the boardwalk in Vero Beach, with officials describing the damage as severe and warning that the weather event is not yet over. I was trying to look it up to see if there was a name, a named storm off the coast or anything, but nope, it's just weather," one observer said. Quintin Bergman is the resource manager with Indian River County. He's monitoring the situation. "So, what we're seeing here is two weather events that have aligned," Bergman said. "We're still in the middle of this. We're not through with the weather event. The forecast is showing elevated winds for a few more days, and the king tide event is still going to be affecting the tide." The erosion has impacted a section of beachfront parking on Ocean Drive, an area official have identified as one of their erosion hot spots. One couple who walked on the beach the day before said they didn’t notice the damage but weren’t surprised by the situation. "That's what nature wants to do, and that's kind of what you need to let nature do, I think. But the problem is we keep building on it. That's the interruption, not nature doing its thing," they said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Officials described the erosion as approaching severe. "I would classify this as leaning more on the severe side of erosion. It's not extreme by any means, but definitely we are very concerned," Bergman said. Authorities are contacting park officials to discuss safety measures to protect the public. Lucie County, beach erosion has also been observed, but officials credited beach replenishment projects with helping protect nearby buildings. "I mean, it certainly helped that we did a renourishment last year. Any time you lose sand, the more you have on there, the better you're going to protect your shoreline," Erick Gill, St. Lucie County public information officer, said. In parts of Martin County, residents are still dealing with flooding caused by the rough conditions. entry.summary: President Donald Trump's administration has made $15 billion worth of promises to agriculture producers in the last few weeks of the midterm elections, initiatives intended to help offset higher costs for diesel and fertilizer that farmers have endured largely due to his tariffs and the war in Iran. Whether that will motivate more voters to turn out in agricultural states where traditionally Republican seats are now seen as competitive is unclear. It may explain his increased attention on rural areas, including visits Sunday to Iowa and Kansas, two days before the election. A look at the Republican administration's pledges to farmers: Who these efforts will help Besides the more than $15 billion worth of payments and initiatives announced by Trump's Department of Agriculture, the agency plans $13.8 billion in safety net program payments for eligible producers for the 2025 crop year, offsetting shortfalls for farmers who grow key crops such as corn, soybeans, wheat and rice. Of the $15 billion, more than half will go toward an $8 billion one-time payment plan for farmers buffeted by soaring diesel prices. The USDA said it will release more details about the payments this month. It is not clear when the payments will go to farmers, who rely on diesel for trucks, tractors and combines. As a costly harvest season raises concerns, Trump heads to Kansas Gregg Ibendahl, a farm management specialist at Kansas State University, said he estimates the payments to more than cover the increase in fuel costs, and that the money could help with high fertilizer prices. At least $5 billion was announced in guaranteed loans for ranchers and fishermen. An additional $1.8 billion in payments is for producers and landowners who participated in conservation programs, $573 million will go toward fertilizer manufacturing projects and $57 million is for expanding meat processors. For specialty crop producers, $86.6 million in grants will be awarded to innovative projects. On Thursday, the agency said it would purchase up to $472.5 million in agricultural commodities to support producers and give to charitable programs. The USDA also announced other efforts, such as expanding sales of a diesel normally used only for off-road use, helping ranchers by making cattle sale data more transparent and strengthening wolf management policies to protect livestock. As a costly harvest season raises concerns, Trump heads to KansasGregg Ibendahl, a farm management specialist at Kansas State University, said he estimates the payments to “more than cover the increase in fuel costs,” and that the money could help with high fertilizer prices.At least $5 billion was announced in guaranteed loans for ranchers and fishermen. An additional $1.8 billion in payments is for producers and landowners who participated in conservation programs, $573 million will go toward fertilizer manufacturing projects and $57 million is for expanding meat processors. For specialty crop producers, $86.6 million in grants will be awarded to innovative projects.On Thursday, the agency said it would purchase up to $472.5 million in agricultural commodities to support producers and give to charitable programs.The USDA also announced other efforts, such as expanding sales of a diesel normally used only for off-road use, helping ranchers by making cattle sale data more transparent and strengthening wolf management policies to protect livestock.Why farmers are strugglingIt has been a frustrating year for farmers. Increased costs for fertilizer and fuel have made it difficult to turn a profit. Last year, tariffs drove up expenses for other equipment that farmers use, and the trade war with China resulted in a near boycott of U.S. agricultural goods.On Friday, diesel was averaging $6.32 per gallon, down slightly from its peak in September but 70% higher than the price a year ago, according to motor club AAA. Filling up a 100-gallon tank now costs $260 more than it did one year ago.“That input side risk, I think, is the thing that really has hurt farmers this year, as well as the fact that there has been a lot more uncertainty about what’s going to happen in the world,” Ibendahl said.He said he expects these ad hoc payments to be a big help for farmers who otherwise would not make a profit this year, but they do not address the broader issues driving up prices.“It’s hard to go to your lender in the next spring and say, ‘OK, well, we’re looking pretty good this year, but it’s all because of these extra temporary government payments, so how much can you make me a loan (for) next year for my crop?’” he said.Alexandra Middlewood, an associate professor of political science at Wichita State University, said she has heard mixed reactions from farmers, who are happy their business will survive this year but see these programs as one-time bailouts rather than a long-term solution.What farmers may vote onRural voters, including farmers and those who rely on the agricultural economy, have been an instrumental voting group for Trump.Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, said many rural voters like the president, but some of his policies have hurt the agriculture industry. Immigrant deportations have threatened the agricultural labor force, and cuts to foreign aid and SNAP food stamps hurt the market for agricultural products.“Some people who admire Trump really just admire the person, the man,” he said. “But it doesn’t mean they necessarily like his policies. Well, Trump himself isn’t on the ballot this year. His policies are.”RELATED STORY | High inflation and the Iran war put pressure on Republicans ahead of the midterm electionsCost of living and access to health care are top issues for rural voters, Middlewood said. She added that there is a perception the administration has not done enough to address these issues, even as Trump boasts at campaign rallies about a booming economy.Middlewood, who is based in Kansas, does not expect frustrated rural voters to shift to the Democratic Party, given how long the state has been a Republican stronghold. But some voters may decide to sit out of this election or vote independent, which would hurt Republican candidates.“Independent voters make or break elections," she said. "And so that’s really what it’s going to come down to this year is those independent voters and who they’re breaking for.”

entry.title: Beachgoers in Martin County urged to stay out of water after high levels of fecal bacteria found: Officials
entry.summary: Martin County health officials are urging beachgoers to stay out of the water this weekend after water quality tested poor in several areas of the county. The Department of Health in Martin County put a health advisory in place after water samples taken Monday came back with unsafe levels of fecal bacteria at 10 locations across the county, including: Sandsprit Park Bathtub Beach Charlie Leighton Park Stuart Sandbar Jensen Beach Causeway Stuart Causeway Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge Jensen Beach Bob Graham Beach Hobe Sound Beach Beach conditions Friday were less than ideal with choppy waters, a red flag flying and water quality concerns. For some beachgoers, the rough surf was reason enough to stay dry. 'You know, it's not safe to swim in the water, especially at this time of year when you want to be in the water,' beachgoer Dan Casamento said. Valentin Kapranoe, a snowbird, just learned that the health department is urging the public to avoid contact with the water. 'Very good waves. Very good waves. It's rough sea, but you told me something is wrong,' Kapranoe said. Once he heard about the advisory, his tone changed. 'I would be a little bit concerned for sure,' Kapranoe said. The health department says exposure could increase the risk of illness in swimmers. Officials say the poor water quality is likely tied to the recent wind, king tides and stormwater runoff from heavy rain. For beachgoer Charlene Cook, the situation was disappointing. 'What a shame especially if you're vacationing,' Cook said. She added that the broader environmental impact concerns her most. 'What bothers me the most is the runoff from the lawns and the lawn treatments and what it does to the environment,' Cook said. The health department plans to resample the water on Monday if conditions allow. Officials told us they expect water quality to stabilize as the weather clears up. entry.title: Woman, 66, charged with 29 counts of animal cruelty after 124 cats removed from Port St. Lucie home
entry.summary: A 66-year-old woman has been arrested on dozens of animal cruelty charges following an investigation that resulted in 124 cats being removed from a Port St. Lucie home , according to police. The Port St. Lucie Police Department said Kimberly K. Robinson was arrested Friday by members of the Marshals Task Force after detectives obtained a warrant charging her with 29 counts of felony animal cruelty. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Woman arrested after more than 120 cats removed from home Port St. Lucie woman arrested after more than 120 cats removed from home The investigation began Oct. 13, when Animal Control responded to a home in the 2500 block of Southwest Warwick Street over concerns about the animals' welfare and unsanitary conditions, police said. Officers initially found more than 60 cats inside the home, according to police. Investigators said there were extensive accumulations of animal feces and urine, a strong ammonia odor and numerous cats that appeared to have untreated medical conditions. Authorities ultimately removed 124 cats, including newborn kittens, juvenile cats and adult cats. The animals were divided between Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County. Police said many required veterinary treatment for conditions including respiratory and eye infections, elevated temperatures, fleas and ear mites. Some cats also had open and infected wounds. Investigators reviewed Animal Control reports, veterinary records and other evidence as part of the case. Police said the 29 felony charges against Robinson are based on veterinary findings involving the first 29 cats that were evaluated. The investigation remains ongoing as authorities review medical findings involving the remaining animals. Police said additional charges could be considered.

entry.title: Martin County man charged with attempted murder after roommate slashed in neck with box cutter
entry.summary: A 32-year-old man is facing an attempted murder charge after deputies say a dispute between roommates ended with a man being slashed in the neck with a box cutter. The Martin County Sheriffs Office said Bradley Martin was arrested Thursday night following the attack in the 2800 block of Southeast Indian St. According to the sheriffs office, Martin used a box cutter to slash an acquaintance, described as a man in his 40s, in the neck during a violent dispute between the roommates. Despite his injuries, the victim attempted to drive himself to a hospital, authorities said. Deputies and Fire Rescue personnel intercepted him and took him to a trauma hospital. The sheriffs office said the victim was in stable condition and is expected to recover. Deputies located Martin shortly after the incident and took him into custody. Martin has been charged with attempted murder. The sheriffs office did not provide additional details about what led to the dispute.

entry.title: Multiple-fatality crash involving tractor-trailer closes I-95 northbound in Martin County - WPEC
entry.summary: Multiple-fatality crash involving tractor-trailer closes I-95 northbound in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Three people, including a 5-year-old boy, were killed in a crash involving a car and a parked tractor-trailer on northbound Interstate 95 in Martin County late Saturday night. The Florida Highway Patrol says the crash was reported around 11:05 p.m. According to investigators, a 2017 Toyota Camry was traveling in the outside northbound lane when, for reasons still undetermined, it moved onto the right shoulder and collided with the rear of a parked 2012 Kenworth tractor-trailer's 53-foot trailer. The impact caused the Camry to spin across all three northbound lanes before coming to rest on the left shoulder. Three passengers in the Camry died: a 34-year-old man, a 5-year-old boy and a woman whose age was not provided. All three were from Port St. The driver, a 31-year-old Port St. Lucie woman, suffered non-incapacitating injuries. An 11-year-old girl who was also in the car suffered incapacitating injuries. FHP says the driver was transported by ground, while the child was flown by LifeStar. The 60-year-old Miami man driving the tractor-trailer was not injured. The truck was parked on the right shoulder at the time of the crash. The crash remains under investigation.

The remarkable show of support for President Donald Trump's backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., had said hours earlier.Dueling church services: Stevens defects as Democrats preach unityStevens was initially set to join the nominee and U.S. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina at a church event. Turkish said last week that he was going to vote for Rogers, arguing that El-Sayed had not done enough to address the Jewish community's concerns.The appearance stunned Democrats across the political spectrum, coming just days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed that she would vote for El-Sayed.Meanwhile, El-Sayed attended a separate church service alongside Dingell, South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Democratic Senate primary before voting began.El-Sayed spoke for nearly 10 minutes at the service, but did not address the latest controversy.“It’s in churches like this, in pews like the ones in which you sit, that the foundation of my life was built,” El-Sayed said.Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance in hopes of bringing together Democrats in the final days before Tuesday's vote, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that.“I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," Dingell said a telephone interview Sunday before Stevens' appearance. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.”"The bishop was getting upset, because this is a real church service,” Dingell added.The latest and late-stage infighting comes as Democrats look to drive turnout among Black and Jewish voters in key strongholds. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party's effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump's second term.Dingell and other Democrats insist the party is united behind El-Sayed. Early voting has been underway since Oct. 24, before the latest tensions erupted. Stevens defeated El-Sayed in both counties in the August primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition.How did we get here?The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offense to an outside group’s ad accusing him of disrespecting women.Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his summer win.Their lack of joint appearances was particularly notable as some Jewish voters and leaders continued to criticize El-Sayed over his comments about Israel, past rhetoric and campaign appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.The divisions spilled into public view again Wednesday when Stevens’ fiancé told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Hours later, Stevens appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.”Dingell had been working to bring them together at church alongside Clyburn, one of the nation’s most prominent Black Democrats.But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices.“Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”El-Sayed then responded: “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand.”He repeated Saturday evening that the ad was not made by his campaign and “I do not agree with the contents of that ad.”Michigan Democrats insist they are unitedDespite the latest tensions, El-Sayed planned to move ahead with a series of church visits Sunday alongside Clyburn and other prominent Black Democrats.The appearances will also include Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield, Garlin Gilchrist II, the nominee for secretary of state, and several Michigan bishops, according to campaign advisories obtained by AP.Democrats are seeking to drive turnout in Detroit, where roughly three-quarters of residents are Black and strong support is essential to Democratic success statewide.

entry.title: Florida voters weigh 3 amendments impacting homestead taxes, budget stabilization, agricultural industry
entry.summary: Florida voters will decide three statewide amendments when they head to the polls on Tuesday, with a property tax proposal drawing the most attention. Amendment 1 would boost Florida's budget stabilization fund from 10% to 25% and require annual transfers into the fund of up to $750 million. Lawmakers would be allowed to use those reserves for certain critical state needs. Supporters say it strengthens the state's financial safety net, while critics argue the money is better spent addressing current needs. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida voters weigh three amendments Tuesday impacting homestead taxes, budget stabilization and the agricultural industry Another measure on the ballot, Amendment 2, would exempt agricultural equipment and other farm-related tangible personal property from property taxes. Supporters say it would help farmers and the agriculture industry. Opponents say it could reduce revenue for local services. Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Supporters say it would provide relief for homeowners and limit government spending. Opponents warn it could reduce local revenue. All three amendments need 60% approval to pass. Early voting ended Saturday in Martin and Okeechobee counties and wraps up Sunday in St. Lucie, Indian River and Palm Beach counties. Election Day is Tuesday Nov. 3. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: Three people, including a 5-year-old boy, were killed in a crash involving a car and a parked tractor-trailer on northbound Interstate 95 in Martin County late Saturday night. The Florida Highway Patrol says the crash was reported around 11:05 p.m. According to investigators, a 2017 Toyota Camry was traveling in the outside northbound lane when, for reasons still undetermined, it moved onto the right shoulder and collided with the rear of a parked 2012 Kenworth tractor-trailer's 53-foot trailer. The impact caused the Camry to spin across all three northbound lanes before coming to rest on the left shoulder. Three passengers in the Camry died: a 34-year-old man, a 5-year-old boy and a woman whose age was not provided. All three were from Port St. The driver, a 31-year-old Port St. Lucie woman, suffered non-incapacitating injuries. An 11-year-old girl who was also in the car suffered incapacitating injuries. FHP says the driver was transported by ground, while the child was flown by LifeStar. The 60-year-old Miami man driving the tractor-trailer was not injured. The truck was parked on the right shoulder at the time of the crash. The crash remains under investigation.

entry.title: Florida mom fights wrongful death law after daughter dies hours after leaving hospital
entry.summary: Two years after her only daughter died just hours after leaving a Florida hospital, Beth Miller says she is still searching for answers. She also wants to make sure another family does not face the same barriers she has encountered. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida mom fights 'free kill' law after daughter's death Florida mom fights 'free kill' law after daughter's death 'I would like to be the only one,' Miller said. 'I know what it feels like. I don't want anybody else to have to go through this.' Miller's daughter, Dawn Miller, was 49 when she died after undergoing gallbladder surgery. A previous WPTV investigation found medical records showed Dawn initially 'tolerated the procedure well.' But her condition later changed. Her hemoglobin dropped. Doctors confirmed sepsis, a potentially life-threatening response to infection, and lab results the morning of her discharge showed decreased kidney function. Records also show Dawn twice resisted leaving the hospital, telling medical staff she felt 'weak' and 'not ready to go home.' She was discharged anyway. Minutes after arriving home, she collapsed. 'I couldn't get her to breathe,' Beth Miller recalled. 'And I just felt so helpless. You know, and then you're staring at your daughter trying to do CPR, and nothing's happening.' Dawn was pronounced dead about two hours after leaving the hospital. Dr. Gerald Feigin, a medical examiner and forensic pathologist who reviewed Dawn's medical records for WPTV, said he believes she should not have been discharged. 'She should have been given emergency transfusions and [they should] figure out why she was bleeding,' Feigin said. 'Possibly had additional surgery.' Feigin also said the hospital should have performed an autopsy. It did not. WPTV previously reported Beth Miller requested an autopsy after her daughter's death, but the hospital declined to perform one. The hospital also declined to answer WPTV's questions about Dawn's case. 'I don't have an answer to this day,' Miller said. 'It's on your mind 24/7.' A legal barrier to seeking damages Miller hoped she might find answers through the legal system. But Florida law creates another obstacle. A provision of the Florida Wrongful Death Act restricts which surviving family members can recover certain damages in medical malpractice cases. Critics have dubbed it Florida's 'free kill' law. Under the provision, parents generally cannot recover certain damages for the medical malpractice death of an adult child age 25 or older.

But her condition later changed.Her hemoglobin dropped. Doctors confirmed sepsis, a potentially life-threatening response to infection, and lab results the morning of her discharge showed decreased kidney function.Records also show Dawn twice resisted leaving the hospital, telling medical staff she felt "weak" and "not ready to go home."She was discharged anyway.Minutes after arriving home, she collapsed."I couldn't get her to breathe," Beth Miller recalled. "And I just felt so helpless. You know, and then you're staring at your daughter trying to do CPR, and nothing's happening."Dawn was pronounced dead about two hours after leaving the hospital.Dr. Gerald Feigin, a medical examiner and forensic pathologist who reviewed Dawn's medical records for WPTV, said he believes she should not have been discharged."She should have been given emergency transfusions and [they should] figure out why she was bleeding," Feigin said. "Possibly had additional surgery."Feigin also said the hospital should have performed an autopsy.It did not.WPTV previously reported Beth Miller requested an autopsy after her daughter's death, but the hospital declined to perform one. The hospital also declined to answer WPTV's questions about Dawn's case."I don't have an answer to this day," Miller said. "It's on your mind 24/7."Miller hoped she might find answers through the legal system.But Florida law creates another obstacle.A provision of the Florida Wrongful Death Act restricts which surviving family members can recover certain damages in medical malpractice cases.Critics have dubbed it Florida's "free kill" law.Under the provision, parents generally cannot recover certain damages for the medical malpractice death of an adult child age 25 or older. Adult children also face restrictions on recovering those damages for the death of a parent.Dawn was unmarried, in her 40s, and had no children."Unless she had kids or a spouse, there's nothing I can do," Miller said.Jordan Dulce, a West Palm Beach trial attorney who previously defended hospitals in medical malpractice cases, is among the critics calling for the law to change."It's completely arbitrary," Dulce said.Dulce said potential liability is something hospitals consider as part of risk management."I can tell you, from a risk management perspective, it's very much on their radar," he said.Critics argue the law can reduce the potential financial consequences when alleged medical negligence results in the death of certain patients compared with others.Dulce argues that it can weaken one of the financial incentives intended to promote accountability and patient safety."It's not meaning that you're intending to hurt someone," he said. "But obviously, when you don't have those guardrails up, certainly the quality of health care suffers."Florida enacted the provision in 1990 amid concerns over the cost and availability of medical malpractice insurance.Federal data show Florida had the sixth-highest number of medical malpractice claim payouts in the country that year.A Yale Journal on Regulation study also found average malpractice premiums had more than quadrupled over a four-year period, from about $4,300 to $18,000.At the time, proponents of the law argued rising malpractice costs were threatening access to doctors and driving physicians out of the state.But some of those claims later came under scrutiny.A 2003 U.S. Government Accountability Office report examined reports of physician shortages in Florida and other states and found some widely cited claims were "anecdotal" or "inaccurate."In one example, medical society officials reported two Florida counties had lost all of their neurosurgeons. GAO investigators found at least five neurosurgeons were still practicing in each county.The report also found the number of new medical licenses in Florida had increased while the number of physicians per capita remained relatively unchanged."There's been no actual studies or evidence or support for this law actually doing what it was intended to do," Dulce said.Florida's medical malpractice insurance market has since stabilized.A 2026 report from Florida's Office of Insurance Regulation found the industry was "doing well," with annual premium increases far below the triple-digit increases seen during the insurance crisis of the late 1980s.The report, however, attributed much of that stabilization to malpractice reforms enacted in 2003 — more than a decade after the wrongful-death provision took effect.Florida also remains among the most expensive states in the country for medical malpractice insurance, ranking third nationwide."No matter what we try to do to limit the victim's right to courts, that has never stopped the insurance industry from continuing to increase their prices because that's their model," Dulce said. "At the end of the day, trying to value life from the Legislature's standpoint, I think, is always improper."WPTV reached out to several local state lawmakers to share Miller's story and ask about the law. None have yet agreed to sit down for an interview.For Miller, the debate is more than a question of insurance rates, liability or state policy.It is about the daughter she still pictures lying on the floor of her home."It will always be difficult," Miller said. "I see her laying on that floor all the time."She said she will continue speaking publicly in hopes of convincing lawmakers to change the law."To get this point across, to make it so other people don't have to go through this suffering," Miller said.Last year, Florida lawmakers passed legislation that would have repealed the provision, but the bill never took effect.In the next part of WPTV's investigation, investigative reporter Kate Hussey examines what happened to that effort — and shares the stories of other Florida families who say they have encountered the same legal barrier.

entry.summary: A Learjet carrying nine people crashed in a residential area near Cresthaven on Sunday afternoon, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Nine people were on board, according to the FAA. The agency said its information is preliminary and subject to change. Gov. Ron DeSantis visited the scene Sunday and described the crash as 'cataclysmic,' saying the aircraft appeared 'like a missile going down' and left a large crater along Military Trail. He praised Palm Beach County first responders for their quick response. Officials said they had not received reports at the time of the news conference of people on the ground being killed or injured by the crash or debris. DeSantis said the debris field stretched a significant distance. Palm Beach County officials said approximately 600 people in a nearby mobile home community are expected to be relocated because the crash site is considered a crime scene while authorities investigate. Officials said two shelters were on standby and Palm Tran was prepared to transport residents once law enforcement allowed the evacuation to begin. Military Trail closed until further notice Palm Beach County said Military Trail between 10th Avenue North and Purdy Lane/Alameda Drive will remain closed until further notice. Only emergency vehicles will be allowed into the closed area. Law enforcement will redirect traffic and assist residents as needed. Drivers are being asked to use 10th Avenue North and Purdy Lane/Alameda Drive for east-west travel and Haverhill Road and Kirk Road for north-south travel. County officials said they are also working on an alternate traffic pattern expected to be released as the response continues. During Sunday's news conference, a county commissioner said the crash created a massive crater on Military Trail and cautioned that portions of the roadway could face an extended closure. County officials stressed that the timeline will also depend on the federal investigation. The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the crash. entry.summary: Deputies locate wanted Broward County man after Fort Pierce hotel disturbance    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A report of a woman being assaulted and pushed into a car at a Fort Pierce hotel led deputies to a Broward County man wanted in four felony probation cases, authorities said. Deputies say they were called to the Best Western in the 7900 block of South U.S. Highway 1 around 11:20 p.m. Friday after a witness reported seeing a man assault a woman, push her into a vehicle, and drive away, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . Deputies reportedly confirmed a battery had occurred and identified the suspect as 37-year-old Guyrson Maddy of Broward County. A records check found an active warrant for probation violations in four separate felony cases dating from 2017 to 2025. See also: Rescue crews search Delray Beach pond after car found submerged Court records show Maddy’s criminal history dates back to 2012. It includes cases involving battery on a law enforcement officer, grand theft of a motor vehicle, third-degree grand theft, and organized fraud. Investigators also identified a dark-colored 2025 Tesla Model Y they believed was involved. Deputies found a vehicle matching that description at a home on Palm Breezes Drive. A woman at the home confirmed she had been at the hotel and directed deputies to a bathroom where they found Maddy. Deputy Mendoza and his K-9 partner, Oso, helped find him. Maddy followed deputies’ commands and was arrested without incident, the sheriff’s office said. Maddy is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a domestic battery charge, with Broward County holds for probation violations.

entry.title: Florida voters weigh 3 amendments impacting homestead taxes, budget stabilization, agricultural industry
entry.summary: Florida voters will decide three statewide amendments when they head to the polls on Tuesday, with a property tax proposal drawing the most attention. Amendment 1 would boost Florida's budget stabilization fund from 10% to 25% and require annual transfers into the fund of up to $750 million. Lawmakers would be allowed to use those reserves for certain critical state needs. Supporters say it strengthens the state's financial safety net, while critics argue the money is better spent addressing current needs. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida voters weigh 3 amendments Another measure on the ballot, Amendment 2, would exempt agricultural equipment and other farm-related tangible personal property from property taxes. Supporters say it would help farmers and the agriculture industry. Opponents say it could reduce revenue for local services. Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Supporters say it would provide relief for homeowners and limit government spending. Opponents warn it could reduce local revenue. All three amendments need 60% approval to pass. Early voting ended Saturday in Martin and Okeechobee counties and wraps up Sunday in St. Lucie, Indian River and Palm Beach counties. Election Day is Tuesday Nov. 3. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: The West Palm Beach GreenMarket is more than a weekend destination. For local entrepreneurs, it can also be a launching pad for growing a small business. For this week's Small Business Saturday, WPTV's Christy Waite checked out Ba Cafe, a mobile coffee company specializing in Vietnamese coffee that is now a full-time vendor at the GreenMarket. WATCH: West Palm Beach entrepreneur brings Vietnamese coffee and culture to the GreenMarket Entrepreneur brings Vietnamese coffee and culture to GreenMarket Founder Kimberly Truong was born and raised in West Palm Beach and named Ba Cafe after her late father. 'We specialize in Vietnamese coffee and we are a mobile coffee company,' Truong said. For Truong, the business is about more than serving coffee. entry.summary: Deputies locate wanted Broward County man after Fort Pierce hotel disturbance    WPEC
entry.article_text: A report of a woman being assaulted and pushed into a car at a Fort Pierce hotel led deputies to a Broward County man wanted in four felony probation cases, authorities said. Deputies say they were called to the Best Western in the 7900 block of South U.S. Highway 1 around 11:20 p.m. Friday after a witness reported seeing a man assault a woman, push her into a vehicle, and drive away, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . Deputies reportedly confirmed a battery had occurred and identified the suspect as 37-year-old Guyrson Maddy of Broward County. A records check found an active warrant for probation violations in four separate felony cases dating from 2017 to 2025. See also: Rescue crews search Delray Beach pond after car found submerged Court records show Maddy’s criminal history dates back to 2012. It includes cases involving battery on a law enforcement officer, grand theft of a motor vehicle, third-degree grand theft, and organized fraud. Investigators also identified a dark-colored 2025 Tesla Model Y they believed was involved. Deputies found a vehicle matching that description at a home on Palm Breezes Drive. A woman at the home confirmed she had been at the hotel and directed deputies to a bathroom where they found Maddy. Deputy Mendoza and his K-9 partner, Oso, helped find him. Maddy followed deputies’ commands and was arrested without incident, the sheriff’s office said. Maddy is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a domestic battery charge, with Broward County holds for probation violations.

entry.summary: Early voting ends Saturday on the Treasure Coast, Okeechobee County    WPBF
entry.article_text: Early voting ended on the Treasure Coast and in Okeechobee County on Saturday for Tuesday's General Election. In Palm Beach County, residents were still able to visit any of the 28 early polling sites on Sunday. On the Treasure Coast, the early voting totals are nearly 56,000 in St. Lucie County, around 29,000 each in Martin and Indian River counties, and more than 3,700 in Okeechobee County. In addition, residents statewide have the option to vote by mail. It was a busy day at the Martin County Supervisor of Elections Office in Stuart as workers wrapped up early voting. "We've had a great turnout in Martin County," Vicki Davis told WPBF. Martin County officials say more than 40% of registered voters cast their ballots by mail or during early voting. That's already higher than the overall 29% turnout in the primary. After early voting, the only time to vote in person is on Election Day at their designated precinct. Vote-by-mail ballots can be returned to county elections offices during business hours Monday or by 7 p.m. Election officials don't go by postmarks. "The biggest concern heading into Tuesday is voters knowing where their voting location is. So voters can access their voting location by going to our website at MartinVotes.gov or giving us a cal at 772-288-5637." More than 2.8 million of 13.7 million registered Floridians have already voted early, compared with over 50 million ballots cast nationwide ahead of Election Day. Also, around 1.8 million vote-by-mail ballots have been counted in Florida. In Palm Beach County, nearly 178,000 people have submitted their ballots early. entry.title: Three dead in crash on Interstate 95 in Martin County - WPBF
entry.summary: Three dead in crash on Interstate 95 in Martin County    WPBF
entry.article_text: Three people were killed following a crash on Interstate 95 in northern Martin County late Saturday. The Florida Highway Patrol released additional information about the crash on Sunday morning just south of St. According to the report, around 11:05 p.m. on Saturday, a Toyota Camry was traveling north in the outside lane of I-95 at mile marker 112. A tractor-trailer was parked on the right paved shoulder of I-95 at mile marker 112. For an unknown reason, the Camry exited the outside lane onto the right paved shoulder that was occupied by the tractor trailer. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 According to the FHP report, the front right of the Camry collided with the rear left of the tractor-trailer. After the collision, the Camry rotated across the three lanes on I-95 and stopped on the left paved shoulder. Those who died in the crash were passengers in the Camry, including a 34-year-old man, a 5-year-old boy, both from Port St. Lucie, along with an unidentified woman. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. The FHP report notes that the driver, a 31-year-old woman from Port St. Lucie, was transported by ground to St. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach, while an 11-year-old girl was transported by helicopter to St. The driver of the tractor-trailer, a 60-year-old man from Miami, was not injured. Following the crash, all northbound lanes of Interstate 95 at mile marker 112 were closed, and traffic was diverted off the highway at SW Martin Highway. Martin County Fire Rescue and the Martin County Sheriff’s Office also responded to the scene of the crash. The northbound lanes reopened after 5 a.m.

entry.article_text: Election officials have spent months preparing to run the 2026 vote — and bracing for what could disrupt it. They’re training workers, tightening security and readying legal challenges for threats that could stretch well beyond Election Day.“Lately we have to take into account really horrible, worst-case scenarios, whether that is outside actors or foreign actors,” Maricopa County Supervisor Thomas Galvin said. “But the most important thing is that we have to be prepared.”WATCH | FBI reminds agents to avoid polling sites ahead of election dayPlanning for trouble is part of running elections. But this year’s preparations by state and local officials come amid a ramped-up campaign by President Donald Trump and his allies to undermine confidence in voting integrity and assert greater federal control over elections.“Sadly, a new hazard on the list this time that’s never been on the list before is the possibility that our own federal government would try to interfere somehow, directly or indirectly,” Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon, a Democrat, told CNN.What Trump could doOfficials have spent months considering what that might look like: a last-minute executive order, ballot seizures, federal agents at the polls or efforts to undermine trust in the results.Trump and his allies continue to allege widespread noncitizen voting and election fraud, including in midterm voting already underway. They have threatened to prosecute election officials who fail to secure the vote or allow noncitizens to cast ballots and have filed lawsuits to restrict the counting of disputed ballots in California and the certification of results in Alaska.“The more this stuff comes up, and the fact that it is based on so much disinformation or half-truths, it’s incredibly frustrating,” said Matt Crane, the Executive Director of the Colorado County Clerks Association and a Republican. “We’re going to keep working our asses off to make sure the election runs well on Tuesday and that people can have confidence in the process.”RELATED STORY | Trump bets on his rallies to help Republicans defy midterm historySome election leaders have prepared for the administration to potentially take even more drastic steps on or after Election Day, like disrupting polling places, confiscating ballots or election equipment, challenging the results or going after election administrators.So far, however, Trump’s attempts to interfere have mostly played out in the courts and with letters demanding that election officials set aside certain ballots so that those who cast them could be investigated — requests administrators have been rebuffing. Early in-person voting has been underway in states across the country — in some states, for weeks — and there have been no reports of major disruptions involving the federal government.But officials are prepared in case that changes.Last week, Trump attacked Minnesota’s elections, as he has other states’, writing on Truth Social that a Republican candidate could lose only “if they cheat by playing games with the Ballots as they come in.”“The Federal Government will be watching closely,” Trump wrote.For Minnesota leaders, it only validated their concerns and preparations, which included two trips to closed-door conferences this year where they met with officials from other states to game out doomsday scenarios — and how they’d respond.“We are sort of shadow boxing here,” Simon said. “We don’t know when or if the blow will land, and hopefully it never will. But we would be foolish not to be thinking through worst case scenario.”Others fear the biggest threat of federal disruption could come after the midterms, fueled by challenges to the results and allegations of fraud.“What’s the administration going to say to try to put a cloud over everything?” Crane said. “And then as all that rhetoric ratchets up over here, the concern is always that violence against election officials and our facilities increases as that disinformation increases too.”Fearing disruptions at the pollsState and local leaders have been drilling poll workers and coordinating with local police on how to respond if ICE officers or other federal agents show up at voting sites.Wisconsin’s Elections Commission advised poll leaders to alert municipal clerks, inspect badges or warrants, document encounters and keep agents outside when possible. Cherokee County, Georgia, led by a Republican election director, added similar training for its poll workers after its Trump-aligned State Election Board asked the administration to investigate Georgia’s election systems.Arlington County, Virginia, sued to keep armed federal officers away from its polling places. In Arizona, the voting-rights group LUCHA has trained election observers to watch for immigration agents.Minnesota officials have spent months reassuring voters that polling places are safe and officials are ready if ICE shows up, following a major immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis earlier this year.Some local leaders have rehearsed an even more disruptive scenario: federal agents arriving to seize ballots or voting equipment. Boulder County, Colorado conducted trainings for election officials on what federal warrants look like and encouraged them to strategize with the county attorney’s office on how to respond. Others in the state focused on airtight chain-of-custody records so they can pinpoint what’s been taken if ballots are seized.“This is new territory, I think, for just about everybody,” Boulder County Clerk Molly Fitzpatrick told CNN. “So, we’ve provided guidance around making sure that you always follow the law.”IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Trump administration promises US farmers $15 billion in weeks before the midtermsFor Fulton County, Georgia, that concern follows the FBI search of an election hub in January, when agents took hundreds of boxes of ballots and records from the 2020 election. County Board Chairman Robb Pitts says he still doesn’t know where the records are and is fighting to recover them. He fears another intervention on Election Day.“Worst possible scenario: Election Day, before the votes are counted, they come in, confiscate the ballots, take them off. What do we do now?” Pitts told CNN. “People say that’s impossible. Well, what I’ve learned with this administration: the impossible is always possible. We’re prepared, though.”The Justice Department plans to send more than 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states has opened another front. They’re federal lawyers — not law enforcement — with narrowly defined powers, but election leaders fear a DOJ reshaped under Trump could push past those limits.Minnesota and Wyoming are among several states barring DOJ monitors from direct access to polling places. Wyoming’s Republican leaders accused two monitors of overstepping during the August primary by seeking to question voters and workers and inspect voting machines.Colorado offered access with conditions, including an escort from the secretary of state’s office. DOJ declined and will keep its monitors outside. Meanwhile, Minnesota is sending state observers to keep tabs on their federal counterparts — effectively monitoring the monitors.The administration says its monitors, a longstanding presence in US elections, won’t disrupt voting. Their role is to observe and document potential problems for post-election investigations and challenges.“What’s concerning is that they are looking for something. Something no other election monitor has ever been able to find,” Ingham County, Michigan Clerk Barb Byrum told CNN.Byrum has served in her post since 2013 and has never seen DOJ monitors in her county until this year. She said she was suspicious of their presence during the August primary – because the DOJ’s justification included incorrect claims about long lines and improper balloting in her county – but things went smoothly.“They didn’t see anything out of the ordinary,” she added. “So why are they coming back? Well, they’re coming back, I think, to cast more doubt on the integrity of our elections.”Lawsuits ready to goStates have pre-drafted potential legal challenges before any confrontation occurs. Others have preemptively hired outside attorneys. They’re prepared to rush to court and get immediate relief or an injection if federal interference becomes a reality.Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar described preparing “Mad Libs” legal filings, leaving names and jurisdictions blank so lawyers can move quickly, especially if agents come to the polls or attempt to confiscate machines or ballots.“We made sure to have pre-drafted legal finds and a lot of legal research completed and ready to go to be able to respond in moments if something is actually occurring,” Aguilar said. “And the top two major issues was one, federal agents had polling locations, and two, the feds coming in and taking the machines and the ballots.”Nevada is already under federal scrutiny. The Department of Homeland Security says it identified thousands of possible noncitizens registered to vote there — figures state leaders dispute.Nevada officials have received seven grand jury subpoenas in recent months, though they declined to discuss details, citing legal constraints. Aguilar says he has been told he is under DOJ investigation.His staff is juggling those demands with the work of running an election.“It’s mostly having to reassure them that we will work to protect them,” he said.DOJ issued subpoenas to California election officials and sued the state last month, alleging that roughly 20,000 possible noncitizens are on its voter rolls and may be voting in the midterms. The administration wants those ballots separated and withheld from the count until citizenship can be verified.Crane, the Republican head of the Colorado County Clerks Association, said the local officials he works with have those subpoenas “in the back of their minds” as they try to carry out the election.“There’s more pressure now because you know one little mistake can be amplified into a national disinformation campaign,” Crane told CNN.‘They want us talking about it’Election officials are walking a delicate line heading into Election Day: preparing for the worst without making voters fear the polls.Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes pushed back on concerns about federal action, saying he thinks fear is part of the administration’s strategy — and its threats run up against legal limits.“The threats themselves are the voter intimidation. The idea that voters are worried means that the administration is getting what they want,” Fontes told CNN. “I don’t mean to be blithe about it, but the reality is that until something happens, it’s just an empty threat.”Other election leaders share his concern that the administration’s promises to scrutinize the midterms could keep voters home. They stress that they have no evidence of planned Election Day disruptions that would prevent people from casting ballots.Their preparations, they say, are a precaution — not a reason to stay away.Still, Fontes has spent months making sure local officials understand states’ authority over elections and that local law enforcement is prepared to enforce the boundaries of federal oversight.His message: Anyone who interferes with voters will face consequences, whether an activist or a federal agent.“If they’re breaking the law, we’re going to prosecute them,” he said. “It’s just that simple.”Safety concerns for poll workersElection officials are also preparing in case private citizens, activists or partisan observers disrupt disrupting polling places and ballot-counting sites.Online, activists are already pushing recycled claims of rigged elections and alleged problems with ballots and voting machines. Minnesota charged two right-wing influencers, including James O’Keefe, with felony counts of unlawful voting and identity theft for a stunt they recorded at several polling places during the August primary.Officials fear those narratives could become ammunition to challenge results or undermine public trust in the outcome.Election offices have spent years strengthening their defenses against threats with added cameras, bullet-resistant glass and tighter access controls. In recent weeks, Georgia election workers have handled mail wearing gloves and masks after suspicious letters reached election offices and lawmakers nationwide.In Irwin County, Georgia, poll workers are getting another piece of equipment for Election Day: panic buttons.The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

entry.article_text: Three people, including a 5-year-old boy, were killed in a crash involving a car and a parked tractor-trailer on northbound Interstate 95 in Martin County late Saturday night. The Florida Highway Patrol says the crash was reported around 11:05 p.m. According to investigators, a 2017 Toyota Camry was traveling in the outside northbound lane when, for reasons still undetermined, it moved onto the right shoulder and collided with the rear of a parked 2012 Kenworth tractor-trailer's 53-foot trailer. The impact caused the Camry to spin across all three northbound lanes before coming to rest on the left shoulder. Three passengers in the Camry died: a 34-year-old man, a 5-year-old boy and a woman whose age was not provided. All three were from Port St. The driver, a 31-year-old Port St. Lucie woman, suffered non-incapacitating injuries. An 11-year-old girl who was also in the car suffered incapacitating injuries. FHP says the driver was transported by ground, while the child was flown by LifeStar. The 60-year-old Miami man driving the tractor-trailer was not injured. The truck was parked on the right shoulder at the time of the crash. The crash remains under investigation.
