But right now, he can't get to his house, his vehicle or the tools he needs to work."I have a regular life like everybody does, and all of us just want a little bit of our lives back, I guess," Perez said.Perez was home when the Learjet crashed and remembers feeling the impact before he fully understood what was happening."If you could visualize, if you could feel noise, then that's how I felt. I felt the noise in my body," Perez said. "I felt the pressure that sent through my walls when I was sleeping."Within minutes, neighbors were coming out of their homes, trying to figure out what had happened.Eventually, residents learned a jet had gone down nearby. Then came the evacuation.Perez said residents were given time to grab the necessities for a couple of days. He took clothes, his passport, a toothbrush and other hygiene products. His vehicle, however, stayed behind, along with the tools and equipment he uses to make a living."Working materials are there. My screwdrivers, my drills, my saws, they're stuck there," Perez said.Perez works as a handyman, making access to those tools and his vehicle especially important. He said the longer he remains displaced, the more worried he becomes about the financial impact."Please help us as soon as possible, please, and help us with what is really needed," Perez said. "We're not asking for nothing else but the necessary that's been lost or gonna get lost because of this, because my job wages, when rent comes down, who is gonna be, is my landlord or the people who I pay for that lot gonna say, ‘Oh, we feel sorry for you to have a discount?’ No, full payments are gonna have to be made."Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said residents have not been allowed back because the area is still being investigated."They're combing through all the evidence. Once that is clear, they'll gain access," Flores said. "We're hoping to try to see if there's a way that we can get their vehicles out once that crime scene is gone through, but at this point in time we don't really know when."Flores said that the crash happened near the entrance of the mobile park and said there's no way to go in or out without interfering with the scene."You know, it could be up to two weeks. We don't really know," Flores said. "I'm trying to get people to at least get their vehicles."Around 50 people stayed overnight at the Greenacres Community Center, according to Flores. The county initially opened two shelter sites but later consolidated them into one.Perez was among those who stayed at the community center."It wasn't bad, Joel. They did the best they can for us, and they have, and I hope they still do," Perez said.While WPTV was on scene, emergency officials brought mobile showers to the shelter and is working on other forms of assistance. Flores said he's trying to secure hotel vouchers as well as food and Palm Tran vouchers for people who do not have access to their vehicles.The problems extend beyond the investigation itself.Flores said a water main broke, causing a water outage in the neighborhood and nearby businesses. Crews need to pump water out before reaching some of the debris, and rain has made that work more difficult."Because of the water main breaking, we have to pump all the water out so that we're able to get to the debris, and with the rain last night and we're expecting more rain, it's making the process go a lot slower," Flores said.Florida state Rep. Debra Tendrich said debris from the aircraft has been scattered throughout the surrounding community, stretching roughly two miles."Some of those pieces are very sharp," Tendrich said. "And so in order for us to make sure our community is safe, we also want people to look out in their backyards and around their homes to make sure that when they're out with their kids or walking their dogs that they're not stepping on these items."Residents who find potential evidence or witnessed the crash can report it by calling 561-688-3375, Tendrich said.She's also looking ahead to another problem residents could face when they're finally allowed home: food.With power shut off in the affected area, Tendrich said some families may return to refrigerators filled with food that has to be thrown away."What's happening with their electricity being cut off and the power grid shut down, you're looking at people returning to their homes and having to throw out their entire refrigerator full of food that they might have just purchased or that they need to fill now," Tendrich said.For families already dealing with displacement, she said that's another expense she doesn't want them to have to shoulder alone."The last thing that you want to worry about is how are you going to feed yourself, your family, and your children after a tragedy like this," Tendrich said.For Perez, getting back home also means getting back some sense of normalcy. While he understands investigators still have a job to do, he said the uncertainty is taking a toll financially and mentally."I understand that there's lives and things that happened, but I'm alive too," Perez said. "Our lives are tied up in an investigation."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. In Indian River County, County Administrator John A. Titkanich Jr. issued the emergency order in response to ongoing flooding, deteriorating weather conditions and continued rainfall. The county said numerous roads have become impassable, creating public safety concerns. The Indian River County emergency order took effect at 2:30 p.m. Monday and will remain in effect until further order. County officials said the declaration gives the county authority to take emergency actions, coordinate response efforts and address hazardous conditions as they develop. St. Lucie County's Emergency Operations Center is operating under a Level 2 partial activation. Public Safety personnel are coordinating with law enforcement, water management agencies and local governments in response to the flooding. Officials are asking residents to refrain from traveling Monday evening if possible and warning motorists not to attempt to drive through flooded roads. Crews are working to address problems across St. Lucie County as several streets and neighborhoods experience flooding. entry.summary: Flooding from heavy rainfall has forced election officials to relocate polling places in Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Indian River counties ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. Palm Beach County Polling Changes Voters in two precincts will report to different locations on Election Day. Precinct 6401 voters who normally cast ballots at Casa Rio Clubhouse have been reassigned to: Riviera Beach Preparatory and Achievement Academy 7071 Garden Road Riviera Beach, FL 33404 Precinct 7628 voters who normally vote at Ironhorse Country Club have been reassigned to: North County Senior Center 5217 Northlake Blvd. Palm Beach Gardens, FL 33418 Election officials said affected voters will receive an email and/or text message about the change if the elections office has their contact information. Signs will also be posted at the original polling places directing voters to their new locations. entry.summary: Days of relentless rain have flooded streets and homes in Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community, leaving residents struggling to salvage their belongings as the city declared a state of emergency amid continued heavy rain. WPTV's Michael Hoffman found streets deep underwater as he entered the neighborhood. Residents carried belongings in trash bags and on rafts, while one person used a kayak to make their way down a flooded street. Many residents were unable to get back into their homes as the rain continued. 'A disaster,' Ortiz said. Ortiz told Hoffman she has lived there for 21 years and never expected to see flooding like this. 'We didn't know it was going to happen because, since, like I said, we've been here 21 years and never happened, so we didn't expect this,' Ortiz said. Another resident told Hoffman the water was already waist-high just trying to reach their home and worried that continued rainfall could make conditions even worse. 'That's what we're worried about. We're worried about it getting even higher than this, because just to get into my house, it's waist high,' the resident said. 'Just imagine it going higher than that.' Riviera Beach declares state of emergency The City of Riviera Beach declared a state of emergency as flooding continued across the area. Other local governments across WPTV's five-county viewing area also declared states of emergency, including St. Lucie, Indian River and Martin counties. Flooding was not confined to residential neighborhoods. Hoffman also documented severe street flooding on Military Trail approaching Okeechobee Boulevard. First responders and emergency officials urged people to stay off flooded roads whenever possible and warned motorists never to drive through standing water. The guidance is simple: Turn around, don't drown. entry.article_text: Both Okeechobee County and Martin County Public Schools will be closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, as flooding and severe weather continue to create unsafe travel conditions across the region. MARTIN COUNTY SCHOOLS CLOSED All Martin County School District-operated schools will be closed Tuesday, which will also include all after-school activities. School officials said in a Facebook post that conditions vary significantly across the region, with some communities experiencing serious flooding and difficult travel conditions. The district said many of its employees and families live outside Martin County and commute into the county each day. Those conditions in neighboring communities played an important role in the decision to close schools. Throughout Monday, the district received reports of employees and families driving through floodwaters to get home, abandoning vehicles because of impassable roads and making alternate overnight accommodations because they could not safely remain in their homes. Officials said they also considered whether employees would be able to safely travel to and from campuses and whether schools would have enough staff and resources to safely support students throughout the day. The district said the decision follows Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis' declaration of a state of emergency covering Martin County and surrounding counties. "We encourage everyone to use caution and prioritize their safety as conditions continue to affect our region," the district said. Families are being asked to monitor the Martin County School District's website and social media accounts for additional updates. OKEECHOBEE COUNTY SCHOOLS CLOSED Okeechobee County district officials announced Monday evening that lingering floodwaters continue to make some campuses and bus stops unsafe. In a Facebook post, the district said crews spent Monday assessing school campuses and their accessibility following widespread flooding across the county. Officials had hoped water levels would fall enough to reopen schools Tuesday, but floodwaters were still preventing safe access to some campuses Monday evening. The district also said flooding has created unsafe conditions in several areas where students would normally wait for school buses. After consulting with the Okeechobee County Emergency Operations Center, district officials said there was no guarantee conditions would improve enough overnight to safely reopen. "To avoid further delay and inconvenience to parents and the community, we have determined that keeping schools closed Tuesday is the safest decision for our students, families, and staff," the district said. District teams will continue checking conditions Tuesday and will provide additional information about when schools can reopen. Officials said the district will also announce in the coming days whether any makeup days will be necessary. The continued closure comes after heavy rainfall caused significant flooding across Okeechobee County, leaving neighborhoods underwater and roads difficult to navigate.

In Indian River County, County Administrator John A. Titkanich Jr. issued the emergency order in response to ongoing flooding, deteriorating weather conditions and continued rainfall. The county said numerous roads have become impassable, creating public safety concerns. The Indian River County emergency order took effect at 2:30 p.m. Monday and will remain in effect until further order. County officials said the declaration gives the county authority to take emergency actions, coordinate response efforts and address hazardous conditions as they develop. entry.title: Brightline temporarily suspends service between Orlando and West Palm Beach due to high water
entry.summary: Brightline temporarily suspended train service between Orlando and West Palm Beach because of high water along its rail corridor in Brevard County. The rail company said maintenance crews are at the scene and service will not resume until Tuesday at 8:30 p.m. Brightline said its rail infrastructure teams are monitoring conditions along the corridor in coordination with Florida East Coast Railway. Passengers with reservations affected by the suspension will be contacted directly about their travel options. Brightline is encouraging passengers to check its website, mobile app and social media channels for the latest service information. The disruption comes as heavy rain affects parts of Florida's east coast, bringing flooding concerns to portions of the state.

entry.title: NTSB: Learjet 60 crew reported icing, turbulence shortly before deadly Palm Beach County crash
entry.summary: The crew of a Learjet that crashed in Palm Beach County on Sunday reported icing, moderate turbulence and precipitation minutes before the aircraft rapidly descended and crashed, killing all nine people aboard, federal investigators said Monday. During a Monday afternoon news conference, National Transportation Safety Board Member Tom Chapman laid out a preliminary timeline of the Learjet 60's final flight and said weather conditions will be a major focus of the investigation. WATCH INVESTIGATIVE REPORTER KATE HUSSEY'S REPORT BELOW: Weather may have played role in Florida Learjet crash, NTSB says Investigators also have some evidence that the aircraft began breaking apart before impact, although Chapman stressed the NTSB is still working to determine exactly what happened. The Learjet 60 was operated by Aurora Aviation doing business as Upper Jets, according to Chapman. The plane left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport at approximately 10:37 a.m. ET Sunday, bound for North Eleuthera in the Bahamas. There were nine people aboard, including two flight crew members and seven passengers. The NTSB said at approximately 12:47 p.m., the crew told air traffic controllers they were encountering light clear icing that they considered manageable, along with moderate turbulence. The aircraft was flying at 35,000 feet when the crew reported altitude deviations of approximately 700 feet. They also reported an outside temperature of minus 53 degrees Fahrenheit. WATCH THE NTSB news conference below: NTSB holds news conference on Learjet crash in Palm Beach County Shortly afterward, the crew reported encountering precipitation and asked to climb to 37,000 feet. Air traffic control approved the request. 'Less than 30 seconds later, a transmission from the airplane announced the descent, followed by a mayday call,' Chapman said. At about 12:48 p.m., investigators said the crew reported the aircraft was in an overspeed condition and descending. Later communications indicated it was rapidly losing altitude. The plane crashed at approximately 12:51 p.m. near Greenacres and Palm Springs. All nine people aboard were killed. Allan Filgueiras confirmed to NBC News that his daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, was serving as the co-pilot on the deadly flight. Chapman said investigators are examining whether the icing and turbulence played a role in the crash. WATCH BELOW: Gov. DeSantis speaks about tragedy Gov. entry.article_text: The crew of a Learjet that crashed in Palm Beach County on Sunday reported icing, moderate turbulence and precipitation minutes before the aircraft rapidly descended and crashed, killing all nine people aboard, federal investigators said Monday.During a Monday afternoon news conference, National Transportation Safety Board Member Tom Chapman laid out a preliminary timeline of the Learjet 60's final flight and said weather conditions will be a major focus of the investigation.WATCH INVESTIGATIVE REPORTER KATE HUSSEY'S REPORT BELOW:Investigators also have some evidence that the aircraft began breaking apart before impact, although Chapman stressed the NTSB is still working to determine exactly what happened.The Learjet 60 was operated by Aurora Aviation doing business as Upper Jets, according to Chapman.The plane left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport at approximately 10:37 a.m. ET Sunday, bound for North Eleuthera in the Bahamas. There were nine people aboard, including two flight crew members and seven passengers.The NTSB said at approximately 12:47 p.m., the crew told air traffic controllers they were encountering light clear icing that they considered manageable, along with moderate turbulence.The aircraft was flying at 35,000 feet when the crew reported altitude deviations of approximately 700 feet. They also reported an outside temperature of minus 53 degrees Fahrenheit.WATCH THE NTSB news conference below:Shortly afterward, the crew reported encountering precipitation and asked to climb to 37,000 feet. Air traffic control approved the request."Less than 30 seconds later, a transmission from the airplane announced the descent, followed by a mayday call," Chapman said.At about 12:48 p.m., investigators said the crew reported the aircraft was in an overspeed condition and descending. Later communications indicated it was rapidly losing altitude.The plane crashed at approximately 12:51 p.m. near Greenacres and Palm Springs.All nine people aboard were killed. Allan Filgueiras confirmed to NBC News that his daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, was serving as the co-pilot on the deadly flight.Chapman said investigators are examining whether the icing and turbulence played a role in the crash.WATCH BELOW: Gov. DeSantis speaks about tragedy"The weather conditions are a major focus of the investigation," Chapman said, adding that investigators still need to determine what conditions were like at the plane's cruising altitude.The NTSB has not yet confirmed whether the aircraft flew through an active thunderstorm.Chapman said investigators have "some indication that the aircraft was breaking before impact," but cautioned that the investigation remains in its early stages.The debris field was described as roughly a half-mile by four-tenths of a mile, with debris found around ball fields, businesses and residences.Investigators have not yet identified all of the aircraft pieces recovered from the scene.NTSB Investigator-in-Charge Timothy Monville said one person on the ground suffered a leg injury. The person had been inside a vehicle leaving the area immediately adjacent to the crash site, according to information provided to investigators.Investigators are also trying to determine whether a cockpit voice recorder was aboard the aircraft when it crashed.Chapman said maintenance records indicate one had been installed, but investigators still need to confirm it remained aboard the plane.If recovered, Chapman said information from the recorder could become an important part of the investigation.About 20 NTSB investigators began arriving in Palm Beach County Sunday evening, with additional personnel arriving Monday.The investigative team includes specialists in aircraft systems and structures, recorders, weather and air traffic control, as well as a drone pilot.Monville said one of the biggest challenges will be recovering the main wreckage from the impact crater in the roadway. Water in the crater following heavy rainfall is complicating access to the wreckage.Investigators expect their work at the scene to continue for several days.The NTSB is asking anyone who witnessed the crash or has relevant photographs or video to contact investigators at witness@ntsb.gov. Anyone who finds aircraft debris is being asked not to move it and instead contact authorities.Chapman emphasized that investigators will not determine the probable cause while working at the scene."Our mission is to understand not just what happened, but why it happened and to recommend changes to prevent it from happening again," Chapman said.

OKEECHOBEE COUNTY Highway 78 East closure: Highway 78 East road closure will occur at the 1600 block to allow crews to place a pump capable of moving up to 25,000 gallons of water per minute. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office has established a traffic plan with signs directing motorists to detours. Additional law enforcement officers are en route to assist with traffic control. PALM BEACH COUNTY WEST PALM BEACH: The West Palm Beach Police Department advises travelers to avoid Village Boulevard and 45th Street, Haverhill Road and Tyler Lakes Boulevard, Cumberland Drive and Military Trail, 45th Street and Military Trail, Shenandoah Drive and Military Trail. TOWN OF PALM BEACH: South Ocean Boulevard is closed due to flooding from the 1200 block to the 2200 block of South Ocean Blvd. The town asks travelers to avoid the area. RIVIERA BEACH: The City of Riviera Beach is advising residents and motorists to avoid the intersection of Garden Road and Blue Heron Boulevard due to a water main break. Crews are working to complete repairs, which are expected to be finished by 6 a.m. Please use alternate routes and exercise caution when traveling near the affected area. BOYNTON BEACH: The area from Gateway Boulevard and Seacrest Boulevard to the 1900 block of North Seacrest Boulevard is currently experiencing severe flooding. Motorists are urged to avoid the area and seek alternate routes until conditions improve. Please use caution and never attempt to drive through flooded roadways. BOCA RATON: The city of Boca Raton said on Monday evening that the heavy rains produced standing water in several areas of the city, including: NW Second Avenue and NW 28th Street NW Second Avenue and NW 35th Street Multiple areas of Dixie Highway NW Second Ave from NW 20th Street to Yamato Road The city added that other major roadways across the city are impacted as well, and city staff are actively monitoring the situation. Calls for service are being handled without interruption. LANTANA: Due to heavy rainfall this evening, the Town is experiencing isolated flooding in several areas. Residents are encouraged to stay off the roads and avoid unnecessary travel until conditions improve. Please use caution and do not drive through flooded streets. LAKE PARK: The town of Lake Park said that the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office advises all motorists to avoid Congress Avenue until further notice due to hazardous flooding conditions. The town also asks motorists to avoid Water Tower Road as the road is flooded. 2, at 7 p.m., the following major roadways are closed, with many smaller streets around Port St. Lucie also closed: The intersection of California and Savona boulevards Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Aviation Avenue Eastbound Prima Vista Boulevard, west of Airoso Boulevard. Lucie County has closed westbound Prima Vista Boulevard, east of Airoso Boulevard. entry.summary: Flooding prompts St. Lucie County closures, could affect Election Day voting    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County officials are urging residents to stay off the roads unless travel is necessary, as significant rainfall and flooding affect the area. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of widespread flooding and threats to public safety and critical infrastructure. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said numerous roads are flooded or impassable, with more rain expected through Monday night and Tuesday. Deputies and other personnel remain on duty and are coordinating with the Emergency Operations Center, the agency said. See also: NTSB: Learjet crew reported ice, turbulence before deadly Florida crash The sheriff’s office urged residents to stay home, never drive through floodwaters, and avoid moving or driving around barricades and road-closure signs. Residents should also stay away from downed power lines and standing water near electrical equipment, and monitor official sources for weather alerts and road updates. Lucie County Public Schools , county government offices and courthouses will be closed Tuesday, Nov. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections announced temporary polling-place changes for the Nov. 3 General Election because flooding has affected road access to some locations. Voters in the following precincts should go to their temporary voting locations: Precinct 12 , originally at Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge: Days Inn Midtown, 3224 S. Precincts 49 and 71 , originally at Oak Hammock K-8 School, and Precinct 51, originally at Disabled American Veterans Hall: Port St. Lucie Community Center, 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Access is from Airoso Boulevard. Precincts 67 and 86 , originally at St. Lucie West Centennial High School: Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence, 500 NW California Blvd., Port St. Access is from Peacock Boulevard. Precinct 83 , originally at Paula A. Lewis Library, and Precinct 92, originally at The Brennity at Tradition: Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. For more information about voting or vote-by-mail ballots, visit stlucievotes.gov or call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 . The agency thanked deputies, dispatchers, emergency personnel, and community partners responding to the conditions and urged residents to look out for their neighbors.

entry.article_text: Heavy rain has led to widespread flooding in Port St. Lucie, creating hazardous driving conditions and prompting police to urge residents to stay home. According to a Facebook post, the Port St. Lucie Police Department is responding to numerous calls involving vehicles stranded in floodwaters. Authorities are asking the community to avoid traveling unless absolutely necessary. Flooded areas include SW Airoso Boulevard, SE Thornhill Drive and surrounding side streets, Southworth Boulevard and Jeanette Drive, Country Club Estates, SW Discovery Way and Community Boulevard in Tradition, and LTC Parkway. PSLPD issued several safety reminders: "Do not drive through flooded roadways. Never underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters. Just a few inches of moving water can be dangerous. If your vehicle becomes stranded in floodwaters and you are not in immediate danger requiring an emergency rescue, you may contact a towing company directly for assistance." Officers and emergency personnel are working to respond to calls throughout the city. For questions regarding school closures, residents are advised to contact schools directly. "Please be patient and stay safe. If you don't need to be on the road, please don't be," PSLPD said. The department expressed appreciation for the community's cooperation during these challenging weather conditions. entry.title: Drainage systems overwhelmed as water covers roads, lawns and driveways in Vero Beach - WPEC
entry.summary: Drainage systems overwhelmed as water covers roads, lawns and driveways in Vero Beach    WPEC
entry.article_text: Several neighborhoods in Vero Beach were flooded Monday after rounds of heavy rain moved through the area. The scene along 41st Avenue and 12th Street, about a mile from Glendale Elementary School, showed water covering roads, front lawns and driveways. Neighbors said they have never seen flooding this severe in the area before. Residents say the steady rain throughout the day overwhelmed drainage systems, leaving water with nowhere to go but into neighborhood streets and yards. A photo shared by the sheriff's office showed just how high the water rose at one point, with only the roof of an SUV visible above the floodwaters. Authorities have not said whether anyone was inside the vehicle. See also: See updated polling locations due to severe weather across South Florida Deputies are urging residents to stay off the roads and avoid driving through flooded areas, warning that conditions remain unsafe. A CBS12 News crew will be back in affected neighborhoods Tuesday morning to assess any damage as residents continue waiting for floodwaters to recede.
